text:
Reassured an uncertain buyer

As a realtor, sometimes offers and closings aren’t as clean and easy as you’d expect. Some situations need a little extra…incentive. 

Shortly after graduating college in 2024, I was helping a family purchase a home in the Pittsburgh area for about $650,000. It was at the upper end of their budget but it was their forever home and in a location with great schools. Everything was moving along fine until the inspection. It’s always the inspection!!!

The roof’s underlayment had some damage and was leaking into the attic. The damage was small but the roof would need to be replaced shortly after closing. The buyers wanted the sellers to fix it. The sellers wouldn’t fix it. Since it was a sellers market at the time, they also wouldn’t adjust the price, basically saying “tough shit.”

I met the husband at the house to take a closer look at the roof from inside the attic and decide how he wanted to proceed. This was going to be my biggest sale yet and I really didn’t want to lose out on a nice payday. We went up into the attic and sure enough you could see the spots with a flashlight. About 4 individual damaged spots in total. And there was moisture in the attic that the sellers were clearly trying to hide with a dehumidifier running full time up there. 

He felt the spots and wasn’t sure what to do. It was hot as fuck in the attic so we climbed back down to chat about it. I was wearing a romper and the buyer (Frank) was wearing shorts and a t shirt. He was in his late 30s, bigger sized guy with short hair. He wasn’t fat but he wasn’t fit either. He was super kind but usually very stressed. He worked long hours (often had to miss house showings where I’d meet his wife and kids instead) and was financially stressed because his wife didn’t work and they were obviously trying to save up for a down payment on a new home. Despite being stressed he was a super kind person. Never got mad at me and always treated me with tons of respect and kindness. But I could see the cost of a new roof running through his mind and the math wasn’t mathing. 

We stepped down off the attic latter and closed the door to the ceiling and continued talking in one of the empty bedrooms (the sellers had already moved out). My mom was a realtor before me and passed on many of her clients. This client I had gotten from a mortgage broker I was working with. But I remember my mom telling me sometimes buyers needed a little…persuasion. And this seemed to be one of those times. 

I stepped close to Frank and gave him a hug. It felt so nice with how big he was. It was like hugging a bear lol and he was surprised by it too. I told him everything is going to work out even if things seem difficult now. I couldn’t take the stress away but I could try to relieve some in the moment. I felt him close the hug around me and rest his head on top of my head. Honestly sometimes guys just need a hug lol but it didn’t stop there. I felt him inhale and he commented on how good my hair smelled. I chuckled and thanked him and commented that he smelled good too. (He didn’t smell good, but it was the nice thing to say lol) I rubbed my hand along his back and he kissed the top of my head which seemed awkward but I didn’t mind. It was sweet. 

As I stepped back from the hug I noticed his shorts had a tent in them. And even worse, he noticed that I noticed. I looked up and our eyes met and he immediately went to adjust himself and apologized for having an erection. I laughed and said it wasn’t my first time seeing one. Which made him laugh. Then I commented that I was surprised a hug did that to him.  He replied that married life isn’t like college, hinting at my recent past. We talked a little bit and he admitted that he and his wife hadn’t had sex in 2 months and over the past year, it’s only been about three times. 

I was shocked he told me that but I didn’t mind talking about it since I grew up in a very sex positive household.

text:
@ScottPresler First off, this is not directed at you. You busted your ass for us all.  Weknow this and appreciate you for everything you do . But this is my message to the administration and the Republican party in general, more so than Trump. The man can only do so much. That being said - 

My heart is heavy today. I know I’m not alone in that. This is a message from an average American voter that I hope will find its way to you. 

Last night’s midterm results offer three clear lessons:

Messaging - Republicans still lack a coherent, forward-looking message that speaks to the daily struggles of ordinary people.

Messengers - Too many of the faces carrying the message, particularly in places like South Carolina and Texas, failed to connect with voters who are open to change.

Approach - The Republican Party continues to operate under a fatal conceit: that top-down messaging and national talking points are enough. They are not.

Democrats spent two decades building from the ground up: school boards, city councils, state legislatures. Conservatives have largely stayed top-down. We need both.

That means primarying the old-guard neocons out of Congress while simultaneously running strong America First candidates for state and local office. Both efforts have to address the concrete problems hitting everyday Americans and offer solutions that produce tangible results. People vote on emotion when they’re struggling, and many of us are. Telling someone who can’t put food on the table that their pain is necessary for the long-term good does not work. Vague promises of a better future do nothing for them. And a promise of 5k doesnt help or fix the underlying problem of affordability for people drowning in debt.

Running solely on “Democrats are bad” and “woke is bad” is not enough. We already know that. We need to reach the voters who simply want their situation to improve and are willing to try the other side’s answers. How do you think you got elected the first time, Mr. President? In case you forgot, it was the fed up Americans who voted for you.

Average Americans have work to do too. We have to show up in the communities we live in and engage our neighbors, even the ones we disagree with on social issues. That is how ground-up change actually happens.

I know you’re angry. I am too. So let’s channel that into concrete plans. Use your voice and your reach to rally people like me and start changing minds. We do that through clear communication, community engagement, and by turning policy into durable law, not executive orders that vanish with the next administration.

One last point: Preaching to the choir accomplishes little if the message never leaves the church. If we remember that, 2028 can still be a massive success.

Sincerely,
An Average American

text:
FERMI $FRMI FELL TO $1.82. THE CO-FOUNDER SOLD AGAIN:

Fermi (FRMI) at $1.82, -$0.22 / -10.57% on Wednesday.

Fermi stays off the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5, and the day after our Tuesday post added reasons instead of removing one. The shares closed at $2.04 when we wrote and set a new low on Wednesday with nothing from Fermi during the session, as the companies building data centers in Texas fell on the state's new governor. Toby Neugebauer, Fermi's co-founder and largest holder, completed the sale we wrote about and filed to sell more at a lower price. After the close, Fermi disclosed the vote count from its October 30 annual meeting and said it believes the Neugebauer shares were cast against the board's own nominee, former Texas governor Rick Perry.

Deep-Value and Special-Situations wants a dated event and the money to meet it, and Fermi at $1.82 offers the price without either: the TensorWave lease has no new closing date, and the construction loan it needs is still a condition rather than a signature. The shares are 91% under their October 2025 listing price; a price alone does not earn the seat. What would put it on the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5 has not changed: the lease taking effect with a named lender behind the construction loan. With no sales yet, Fermi is not on the Momentum, Quality-Value, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es, and the Quality Len5 needs a gross profit that cannot exist before a tenant pays rent.

Neither of Wednesday's disclosures was out before the close. The low was $1.80, the lowest since the shares listed, on 37.1 million shares against a 22.8 million daily average over the past month. Our read: Fermi fell with the companies building data centers in Texas. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who defeated Governor Greg Abbott on Tuesday, wants an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state, CNBC reported, and she takes office January 19. Fermi's campus sits on about 5,000 acres leased from the Texas Tech University System outside Amarillo, and the buildings TensorWave would rent are not yet financed. Cipher Digital (CIFR) at $6.50, -$1.62 / -19.95% on Wednesday. Formerly Cipher Mining, it rents out data centers it built in West Texas. Cipher is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es: it lost money over the past year and pays no dividend.

We wrote Tuesday that Neugebauer had filed to sell up to 2.56 million shares at the lowest price yet. He sold them that day, at about $2.04, split evenly between the Melissa A. Neugebauer 2020 Trust and Vicksburg Investments Management, both of which he runs. On Wednesday evening the trust filed to sell 94,000 more at $1.82.
- October 13: 2.75M shares, $10.3M.
- October 14 and 20: 1.72M shares, $5.4M.
- November 3: 2.56M shares, $5.2M.
- November 4 notice: 94,000 shares, $171,080.
Four sales in three weeks have brought $20.9 million, each at a lower price than the one before, and Wednesday's notice is the smallest and the cheapest.

The vote count shows neither director up for re-election on October 30 reached the majority of all shares that Fermi's rules require.
- Rick Perry, the former Texas governor and Fermi co-founder: 249.4M votes for, 197.6M against.
- Jeffrey S. Stein, a Fermi director: 261.0M for, 185.6M against.
- Needed: 320.6M, a majority of the 641.3M shares outstanding.
Both stay on the board until someone is elected in their place. Fermi says the trust and TMNN Manager LLC, Neugebauer entities with 98.9 million shares between them going into the vote, were bound by a September 2025 agreement with the company to vote for Perry, Caddis Capital's nominee, and believes they voted against him; those shares would have carried him past the threshold, and Fermi "reserves all rights and remedies." Those investors, through their lawyers, dispute that the agreement required it, and Neugebauer told Taylor Goldenstein of The Texas Tribune that he did not campaign to have Perry removed and that the agreement's conditions had not been met.

Fermi now has two directors its shareholders did not elect, a co-founder selling at every lower price, and a tenant whose lease waits on a loan nobody has signed. The November 12 call, at 9am ET, can change only the third.

Not investment advice.

FERMI $FRMI ELECTED NO ONE AND CLOSED NOTHING:

Fermi (FRMI) at $2.21, -$0.40 / -15.52% on Monday.

Fermi stays off the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5. Of the two things we said Monday's open would trade on, a first vote count came Friday and elected no one, and the lease did not close. The shares fell to a new low, 14.7% under where we flagged them.

Deep-Value and Special-Situations wants a catalyst with a date and the money to meet it; Fermi's date came and went with no lender named for the building. It is on no other Len5 we weigh; it has no sales yet. What would put it on the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5: the lease closing with a named construction loan, or a signed agreement to sell the company.

Rick Perry, the former Texas governor who co-founded Fermi, and director Jeffrey S. Stein won a majority of votes cast, Fermi said, and still lost, because its bylaws require more than half of all 641M shares; both stay until successors are elected. Fermi says Toby Neugebauer, its co-founder, former chief executive and 22% holder, voted against Perry in breach of a founders' agreement; he told the Texas Tribune its conditions were never met.

The TensorWave lease was due to close Saturday, October 31, and by Tuesday's premarket Fermi had announced no closing, extension or end.

Fermi owes the certified count by Thursday, November 5; the September quarter lands November 12, and we are watching for a word on the lease before then.

🔬 1. Upstream Chemicals, APIs, and Raw Materials (7 Actions)

• Vietnamese Rare Earth Consortiums: Establish public-private processing hubs to refine heavy rare earths, bypassing Chinese refining dominance for critical electronics components.
• South Korean Chemical Aggregators: Form state-backed buying consortiums for basic organic chemicals, using bulk purchasing power to secure long-term alternative supply contracts from the Middle East.
• Taiwanese API Industrial Parks: Build specialized mega-parks for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) with zero-cost common effluent treatment plants, allowing local firms to compete with cheap Chinese key starting materials.
• US-style Semiconductor Substrate Rebates: Provide 50% capital subsidies for plants manufacturing high-end silicon wafers and chemical gases, securing the foundation of electronic manufacturing.
• Danish Eco-Chemical Substitutes: Fund massive academic-corporate research grants to develop bio-based, non-petrochemical alternatives for industrial solvents traditionally imported from China.
• Japanese Strategic Mineral Stockpiles: Create a state-managed physical reserve of 30 critical minerals (like lithium, cobalt, and antimony), insulating Indian factories from sudden Chinese export bans.
• Israeli Synthetic Diamond Technology: Scale up lab-grown industrial diamond production to replace Chinese abrasive dust imports used heavily in the domestic cutting and polishing industries.

. Component Localization and Capital Goods (7 Actions)

• Japanese 'Meister' Machine Tool Program: Subsidize advanced engineering training to reverse-engineer and locally build high-precision CNC machines, heavy molds, and dies currently dominated by Chinese manufacturers.
• Taiwanese PCB Cluster Model: Form a hyper-localized cluster exclusively for Multi-Layer Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs), providing plug-and-play factories to instantly replace Chinese circuit board assemblies.
• German Passive Component Mandates: Offer specific tax credits to electronic assemblers who buy Indian-made resistors, capacitors, and diodes, building the micro-component ecosystem from the ground up.
• US Component-Specific PLI Expansion: Redesign the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme to reward the actual local production of low-value, high-volume sub-components rather than final product assembly.
• South Korean Display Glass Alliances: Co-invest with private tech giants to build domestic display glass and polarizer factories, breaking the absolute reliance on Chinese TV and smartphone panels.
• Italian Machinery Leasing Trusts: Set up government-backed asset leasing firms to let Indian MSMEs lease high-end European textile and injection-molding machinery at affordable interest rates, avoiding cheap Chinese equipment purchases.
• Global Open-Source Automation Hubs: Standardize industrial automation protocols using open-source architectures, eliminating reliance on proprietary Chinese industrial software and controllers.

3. Logistics, Supply Chain, and Tariff Re-engineering (6 Actions)

• Singaporean Automated Custom Vaults: Deploy AI-driven customs scanning at ports to instantly detect and penalize trans-shipment routes where Chinese goods are rerouted through ASEAN nations via free trade agreements.

text:
The ultimate guide to prepping

Source: Daily Mail
Published: 5 November 2026

British households are being encouraged to prepare for emergencies, including severe storms, cyberattacks and potential disruptions to essential services, by keeping at least three days' worth of food and drinking water at home.

KEY POINTS

• Three-day supplies: Households are advised to store enough non-perishable food for at least 72 hours, prioritising products that require little or no cooking.

• Drinking water: The recommended allowance is three litres per person daily — 36 litres for a family of four over three days.

• Essential carbohydrates: Rice, pasta, porridge oats, couscous and crackers provide filling meals, although ready-to-eat rice is preferable if cooking facilities are unavailable.

• Protein supplies: Tinned tuna, salmon, mackerel, beans, chickpeas, lentils and canned meats offer protein and essential nutrients.

• Fruit and vegetables: Stock tinned tomatoes, vegetables, potatoes, fruit in syrup and dried fruit to maintain nutritional variety.

• Healthy fats: Olive oil, oily fish, nuts and seeds provide energy and important nutrients.

• Flavour essentials: Salt, pepper, stock cubes, herbs, spices, vinegar and Worcestershire sauce help turn basic ingredients into meals.

• Emergency extras: Long-life milk, honey, peanut butter, chocolate, tea, coffee and electrolyte tablets are among the recommended supplies.

• Storage precautions: Check expiry dates, rotate supplies regularly and avoid buying large quantities of products that require refrigeration once opened.

• Cooking without electricity: A suitable camping stove or barbecue can provide an alternative cooking method, provided it is used safely outdoors.

THE ARTICLE'S SHOPPING CHECKLIST

For a family of four, supplies include:

• Rice: 500g dry plus four ready-cooked pouches.
• Pasta: 1kg.
• Porridge oats: 1kg.
• Baked beans: Two tins.
• Chickpeas: Two jars.
• Lentils: Four pouches.
• Tuna: Four tins.
• Mackerel and salmon: Two tins each.
• Chopped tomatoes: Four tins.
• Vegetable soup: Four tins.
• Long-life milk: Six litres.
• Bottled water: 36 litres.
• Tea or coffee: 40 bags.

The full checklist also includes additional proteins, vegetables, fruit, condiments, baking ingredients, snacks and sweet treats.

Central advice is to stock food your household already enjoys, choose ingredients suitable for several different meals and avoid unnecessary purchases.

An emergency cupboard should provide practical food and drink during a disruption without relying entirely on electricity, refrigeration or complicated cooking.

Mary herself said she needed a Saviour.

Luke 1:46-47 (KJV) And Mary said, My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.

A person without sin does not need a Saviour.

Paul wrote that all have sinned, and he made no exception for Mary.

Romans 3:23 (KJV) For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;

Romans 5:12 (KJV) Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:

After Jesus was born, Mary went to the temple for her purification and offered the sacrifice the law required.

Luke 2:22-24 (KJV) And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord; (As it is written in the law of the Lord, Every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord;) And to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.

2 Corinthians 5:21 (KJV) For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.

1 Peter 2:22 (KJV) Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth:

Jesus was conceived of the Holy Ghost, and that is why He was without sin.

text:
Stupid Is as Stupid Does

The picture is a still from a film. A girl of about seven sits by a bus window with her chin down and her eyes slid sideways at someone just out of frame. Across the top, in heavy white letters: “My response when someone tells me they used AI.” Under her chin, in smaller type, is the line she’s about to say: “Are you stupid or something?”

Anyone who has seen Forrest Gump knows her. She’s young Jenny Curran, played by Hanna Hall, in the 1994 film. In the meme her sideways look is a verdict. Reaching for a machine to help you think is proof that you can’t. It’s a fair question for a meme to put, even rudely. What actually makes a mind stupid, or not? And does using a tool tell you which kind of mind you’re looking at?

The scene itself answers first, so start by putting back what the meme cut. It’s Forrest’s first day of school. His mother sends him off at the bus stop. On the bus, the other children turn him away from their seats one after another. Then a voice: “You can sit here if you want.” Jenny asks about his legs, and about the shoes he’s wearing, the heavy braces he walks in. Then she asks the question in the caption. Forrest answers, “Momma says stupid is as stupid does.” She holds out her hand. “I’m Jenny.”

The meme keeps the middle of that exchange and drops both ends: the seat she offered before the question, and the answer that came after it.

The answer matters, because the film makes it a theory. Forrest has been diagnosed with an IQ of 75, and his mother’s line is her argument against the number. Don’t judge a person by a score or a look, the line says. Judge him by what he does. That’s a real claim about intelligence, and a century of research gives us places to test it.

Start where the meme points, at the machine. Its charge is that using AI is itself the mark of stupidity, and there’s now research on whether these tools change how people think. In 2025 a team at the MIT Media Lab led by Nataliya Kosmyna had students write essays with ChatGPT, with a search engine, or with no tools at all, and recorded their brain activity with EEG. The students who wrote unaided showed the strongest and most widely connected brain networks. The ChatGPT group showed the weakest, and its members struggled to quote accurately from essays they had just written. Over four months, the authors report, the ChatGPT users underperformed at neural, linguistic and behavioral levels.

That sounds like the meme’s case made in a lab. But the study was small, 54 participants with 18 completing the last session. It was posted as a preprint, and it measured brain connectivity and memory during one writing task, not intelligence. And its last session complicated the result. When the groups switched, students who had first written on their own and then used ChatGPT showed stronger recall and broader brain activity than those who had used it from the start. The tool alone didn’t settle the outcome. The order of use did, and so did what the writer had already done unaided.

A second study, the same year, makes that point directly. Hao-Ping Lee, Advait Sarkar, Lev Tankelevitch, Ian Drosos, Sean Rintel, Richard Banks and Natasha Wilson, from Carnegie Mellon and Microsoft Research, surveyed 319 knowledge workers who use these tools at least weekly. They collected 936 real examples of tasks done with AI. People who trusted the AI more reported putting less effort into thinking critically about its output. People who trusted their own abilities more reported putting in more. For the careful ones, the work of thinking didn’t disappear. It moved, from gathering information to verifying it, and from doing a task to overseeing it. It’s a survey of what people say they do, not a test of what they can do. But neither study finds that picking up the tool marks a person as stupid. Both find that what the person does with it decides the outcome. That’s Forrest’s mother’s line, with a sample size.

Under the meme’s verdict sits an older assumption: that smart is a single quantity a person either has or lacks, readable from the outside. Psychologists have been taking that apart for decades, and one finding cuts especially close. Keith Stanovich of the University of Toronto and Richard West of James Madison University studied myside bias, the habit of weighing evidence in favor of what you already believe. Across experiments with nearly fifteen hundred university students, they found very little sign that higher cognitive ability reduced it. In a later review with Maggie Toplak, Stanovich reported that the bias appeared on fifteen different policy questions, and on none of them was it smaller among the higher-ability students. A high score didn’t protect anyone from favoring their own side.

The physicist Richard Feynman named the skill those tests miss. In his 1974 commencement address at Caltech, he told the graduates that the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. Intelligence doesn’t guarantee that habit. It has to be practiced, and it shows in what a person does.

It’s tempting to go a step further, and this is where the argument needs care. If intelligence doesn’t protect against fooling yourself, maybe it doesn’t matter much at all, and character is the real thing. The favorite evidence for that conclusion is one of the most famous footnotes in psychology. In the 1920s the Stanford psychologist Lewis Terman began following a large group of high-IQ California children through their lives. Two boys who were tested but scored too low for the study, William Shockley and Luis Alvarez, both grew up to win the Nobel Prize in physics. None of Terman’s chosen children did. The story is usually told as proof that IQ tests fail at the top.

It doesn’t hold up. In 2020 Russell Warne, Ross Larsen and Jonathan Clark simulated Terman’s selection process to see how likely he was to have caught a future Nobelist. The answer was very unlikely, whatever the test’s merits. Nobel prizes are so rare, and Terman’s cutoff was so high, that the test was bound to miss them. The miss shows how rare the prize is, not that the test was useless. The researchers drew a broader conclusion as well: predicting the highest levels of achievement means measuring a range of things, cognitive and non-cognitive together.

The best-measured case shows what “together” means. Philip Tetlock and Barbara Mellers ran forecasting tournaments for the American intelligence community and found a small group of amateurs who predicted world events better than almost anyone, the people they called superforecasters. These forecasters were more actively open-minded than the others, more willing to consider that they might be wrong. They also had higher fluid and crystallized intelligence than the average forecaster. The habit of questioning yourself didn’t stand in for intelligence. It came along with it. Intelligence set how far a mind could go, and the other habits decided how much of that range got used.

What are the other habits? One clue comes from the very top of science. In 2008 Robert Root-Bernstein of Michigan State University and his colleagues read the biographies of elite scientists and counted their adult arts and crafts hobbies, from painting to woodworking to music. Nobel laureates were significantly more likely to have one than members of the Royal Society and the National Academy of Sciences. Those members, in turn, were more likely than ordinary working researchers in the Sigma Xi honor society, who were more likely than the general public. Every step up in eminence came with more breadth, and every group in the comparison was already highly intelligent. The data have gaps. For about a fifth of the laureates, the researchers found no record of hobbies either way. But the gradient points somewhere the score alone doesn’t.

The newest work on polymaths, people who range across many fields, tries to say what that breadth consists of. In February 2026 Irina Trofimova and Michael Araki described polymathy as breadth, depth, and the ability to integrate them across domains, built on the same mental machinery as intelligence. They tested the old picture of the polymath as scattered and easily distracted, and found the reverse. People who scored high on their measure of polymathy showed more sustained attention, not less, along with greater intellectual endurance. They also noted that many polymaths in history didn’t earn exceptional grades in school. Teachers judging by grades might have wondered whether they were stupid or something.

That brings the research back to the bus. Forrest’s mother gave her son a sentence to carry against a number. The research has spent a century reaching a more careful version of it. The number is real, and it matters. It doesn’t settle what a person is. What settles it is what they do: whether they check their own work, whether they correct it, whether they stay with a hard problem, and, with a new tool in their hands, whether they let it think for them or use it to think more.

The scene the meme was cut from shows that before it states it. The children who turned Forrest away from their seats had already answered the question for themselves, without asking it. Jenny made room first, asked second, and listened to the answer. Then she put out her hand, and the film says they were together from that day on.

The meme stops at the question mark. The girl’s eyes are still turned sideways, the white letters still ask it, and the seat she offered is just out of frame.

No new legislation is assumed. All county participation is voluntary. Primary election administration and local government authority remain with the states and counties.

**Cohort**

text:
Texas counties maintain early voting rosters and election day rosters under the Texas Election Code (including Sec. 87.121 for early voting). These typically include:
•  Name
•  Address
•  Voter registration number (VUID)
•  Precinct
•  Date voted (and method, such as in-person early or mail)
Many counties post them online as PDFs or spreadsheets (examples include Collin, Reeves, Tom Green, and others). You can also request them for public inspection. The Texas Secretary of State aggregates turnout data and hosts portals for early voting and election day figures; counties upload the underlying rosters.
Statewide voter registration lists (which can include voting history) are available from county voter registrars (any person can request them; certain commercial uses are restricted) or via subscription from the Secretary of State. Some counties (such as Travis) also offer downloads of registered voters with election history.

text:
We Win on the 80 Percent Issues

The path forward at the state and federal level is not complicated. We win on the issues that large majorities of Americans already agree on—issues that bring together Republicans, independents, libertarians, and even moderate Democrats who are tired of the excesses. These are not fringe positions. They are common-sense positions that affect the guy who works for a living, the mom who is working two jobs just to keep food on the table, and the couples who cannot get ahead no matter how hard they try.

Equal justice under the law means the Epstein list gets fully exposed and prosecuted where the evidence warrants it. No more foreign wars that drain blood and treasure without clear purpose or end. Getting the woke ideology out of our schools so that children can learn reading, writing, math, and history instead of political theory. Protecting girls’ sports and private spaces so that fairness and safety are not sacrificed to ideology.

These four points, executed with clarity and consistency, would have given people a reason to show up and vote in places where the other side has been winning by default. Instead, too many candidates at the state and federal level treated the public like they were already satisfied. They said the economy was fine while families on the ground saw prices stay high and wages fail to keep pace. They offered typical politician talking points instead of a clear plan that would make life better for ordinary people.

I saw this firsthand in Texas. When Paxton and Abbott spoke, neither delivered the kind of message that gives people hope or a sense that someone in power understands the daily struggle. It left me wondering whether that was the best Texas could offer. Too many candidates believe they can spend their way to victory. They forget that the real issues live at the ground level. They gaslight the base instead of staying disciplined on the points that actually matter. The state and federal levels told people everything was fine. The people at the bottom knew there was no real plan and no real hope.

What Happened in 2024 and Why 2026 Felt Different

In 2024, many people had been called terrorists. Some had been jailed. Others lost jobs or were silenced for speaking about COVID policies, parental rights, or basic fairness. For a large number of those voters, Donald Trump and the Republican Party represented the only remaining hope. They showed up.

By 2026, that sense of urgency had faded for too many on our side. People felt safe. They assumed the talking points were enough and that grassroots work on the ground was optional. Meanwhile, the other side ran energetic “No Kings” style rallies that united their extreme wing with moderates. Their base showed up. Our side did not fully unite. Some of our weaker candidates in the middle did not want to be called names. Some on the farther right sat out. And the occasional voters who had turned out in 2024 because they finally had hope did not feel the same pull.

We lost because the other side gave their people hope and a reason to vote. We did not rally our full base. We did not execute on the issues we campaigned on at the federal level. And some of the local candidates who lost simply did not work hard enough. If school board candidates are out-working people running for city and county seats, then those city and county candidates are not putting in the effort required to win. Running for local office means treating it like your life depends on it: twenty hours a week, seven days a week, from now until Election Day.

🇺🇸 USADAY250 | VETERANS MONTH 2026 🇺🇸
THE HEART OF A WARRIOR — DAY 3
November 4, 2026

INTEGRITY — Doing What Is Right When No One Is Watching

A warrior’s greatest victories are not always won on the battlefield. Sometimes they are won in the quiet moments when character is tested and no one is watching.

Courage may carry a warrior into battle.

Honor may inspire a warrior to serve.

But INTEGRITY determines who that warrior truly is.

Integrity is the unwavering commitment to truth, even when dishonesty offers an easier path.

It is keeping a promise when circumstances make that promise difficult.

It is accepting responsibility when excuses would be more comfortable.

It is doing what is right—not because someone is watching, not because recognition awaits, but because conscience demands nothing less.

🇺🇸 A LESSON FROM AMERICAN MILITARY HISTORY

In December 1777, General George Washington led the Continental Army into winter quarters at Valley Forge National Historical Park.

The soldiers faced bitter cold, inadequate clothing, food shortages, and disease. Many had enlisted for limited periods. Others questioned whether the struggling Revolution could succeed.

Washington faced enormous challenges as commander.

His leadership was far from flawless, but his persistence through that winter demonstrated an essential principle: responsibility does not disappear when circumstances become difficult.

The army endured. Training and organization improved. And in June 1778, the Continental Army emerged from Valley Forge better prepared to continue the struggle for independence.

Yet Washington’s most enduring example of integrity came years later.

In December 1783, after the Revolutionary War, he voluntarily surrendered his military commission to Congress.

The victorious general relinquished his command and returned to civilian life.

At a time when military leaders throughout history had used victory to seize political power, Washington chose a different path.

He placed the principles of the new republic above his personal authority.

That decision helped establish a foundational American tradition: military power must remain accountable to civilian government.

It was leadership guided by restraint, responsibility, and principle.

And it remains a powerful example of the integrity we should expect from those entrusted with great authority.

🇺🇸 THE QUIET STRENGTH OF A TRUE WARRIOR

Integrity is not reserved for generals or celebrated heroes.

It lives in the service member who tells the truth even when admitting a mistake carries consequences.

In the officer who refuses to compromise ethical standards.

In the soldier who protects the dignity of others, even in the harshest circumstances.

In the veteran who continues to serve with honesty and compassion long after leaving the military.

It is the quiet strength of people who understand that doing what is right matters more than being seen doing it.

As we commemorate America’s 250th anniversary, we must remember that the strength of our republic depends upon more than military might.

It depends upon character. Upon trust. Upon responsibility.

Upon citizens and leaders who understand that principles must never become negotiable simply because circumstances become inconvenient.

A warrior may be remembered for courage in battle. But the true measure of character is the integrity demonstrated throughout a lifetime.

To our veterans: Thank you for your service, your example, and the sacrifices you have made for our nation.

May we honor you by living with the same commitment to responsibility, truth, and principle that military service asks of those who wear the uniform.

🇺🇸 INTEGRITY — DOING WHAT IS RIGHT WHEN NO ONE IS WATCHING.

Because a nation’s freedom is protected by its defenders, but its future is strengthened by the character of its people.

God bless our veterans. God bless America. 🇺🇸

#TheHeartOfAWarrior #VeteransMonth #Integrity #Honorourveterans

text:
BERTRAND’S BOX 
US–IRAN 

ASYMMETRIC ASSESSMENT
4 NOVEMBER 2026

STRATEGIC JUDGEMENT

The ballot has changed Washington’s political geometry but not yet its military capacity. Democratic control of both houses will constrain future funding and widen scrutiny of the Iran campaign, but the new Congress has not assumed office. President Trump therefore retains a narrow window in which he can order further action using forces already deployed.

Iran’s immediate advantage is not conventional strength. It is uncertainty: Washington cannot determine whether the next tanker incident, Kurdish strike, Saudi alert, cyber disruption or proxy operation is an isolated event, an Iranian warning or the opening move of coordinated retaliation. Tehran benefits whenever the United States must defend everything while Iran need only threaten selectively.

The apparent choice remains between diplomacy and renewed war. That is misleading. The real contest concerns who controls escalation while negotiations, maritime attrition and deniable attacks continue simultaneously.

THE THREE CUPS

One ball - escalation control - is moving beneath three outwardly similar cups.

BOX EE 
EXCHANGE AND EXIT

What Washington thinks it selects: reopening Hormuz, limiting sanctions relief and converting the Qeshm strike into leverage without conceding strategic defeat.

What Tehran thinks it selects: relief from the port blockade, oil sanctions and frozen-asset restrictions before making irreversible nuclear or maritime concessions.

What the box may contain: an interim transactional pause, not peace. Iran could reopen selected shipping lanes while retaining mines, coastal missiles, proxy forces and the ability to close them again. Washington could suspend limited measures while preserving the blockade architecture.

Qatar reports that proposals are still moving between the parties, but Tehran says the American response remains inadequate. Iran continues to demand sequencing in which Washington acts first. 

Why it is being chosen: both governments need economic relief and political breathing space without admitting that coercion failed.

Likely outcome: a reversible arrangement that postpones rather than resolves the nuclear, missile, proxy and maritime disputes.

Assessment: most likely strategic box; fragile implementation.

BOX KK 
CALIBRATED KINETIC CONTAINMENT

What Washington thinks it selects: limited attacks on clearly defined Iranian military systems, followed by a return to diplomacy.

What Iran may see: proof that every pause is merely preparation for another strike.

The limited US attack on Qeshm reportedly targeted air-defence equipment. Trump says no immediate follow-on attack is planned, but the precedent has been established: Washington may now strike Iranian territory while describing the action as contained. Tehran has warned that another attack would produce an immediate and geographically wider response.

Why Washington might choose it: it offers visible resolve without the initial cost of a major campaign.

Why the choice is dangerous: the attacker controls the opening strike, not the opponent’s valuation of the damage. An apparently minor action could kill senior personnel, expose concealed capabilities or compel Iran to answer publicly.

Likely outcome: another limited strike remains plausible after American deaths, a major maritime attack or evidence of preparations against US forces. It would probably expand rather than close the confrontation.

Assessment: moderate likelihood; high escalation sensitivity.

1/5 maybe 6

Hormuz has become a diplomatic scoreboard.

An Iranian parliamentary official says ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar have been exempted from Iran’s Hormuz transit restrictions.

India brings medicines. China brings political backing. Iraq brings deep connections with Tehran. Qatar brings a working channel for negotiation.

Four countries named for passage. Four relationships with practical value.

Then comes the glaring omission from this announcement: PAKISTAN.

My reading? Islamabad’s embrace of Trump risks making it look more like his messenger than an independent mediator. Access to Washington does not automatically buy trust in Tehran.

Pakistan’s military rulers have repeatedly cultivated American presidents. In my view, the attraction is straightforward: military strongmen offer Washington compliance without the inconvenience of democratic scrutiny. Following orders may earn presidential favour. It does not earn diplomatic independence.

Has Pakistan confused proximity to power with influence?

Being welcomed in Washington is one thing. Being trusted in Tehran is another. Pakistan’s leadership needs to understand the difference.

#Hormuz #Iran #Pakistan #India

text:
THE LAST DISTRACTION IS THE MOST DANGEROUS.

Imagine this.

Tomorrow morning, you have a meeting at 9:00 AM.

Not just another meeting.

This one could change your entire life. Your career, your future, everything you've been working toward.

You planned everything the night before. You were supposed to wake up early, get ready, and arrive ahead of time.

But life had other plans.

7:30 AM.

You wake up late.

SHIT.

You jump out of bed, get dressed, grab your keys, and rush out on your bike.

You're already behind schedule, but you still have a chance.

Then suddenly...

BAM! 💥

A minor accident.

A few scratches. Some pain. Nothing serious.

You could give up and go home.

But you don't.

You get back on your bike and keep moving.

A few minutes later...

A traffic officer stops you.

Another obstacle.

More wasted time.

You explain, negotiate, and somehow manage to get moving again.

Your heart is racing.

You check the time.

You're almost there.

JUST FIVE MINUTES AWAY.

You've survived the late start.

You've survived the accident.

You've survived the police stop.

Nothing could stop you now.

Or so you thought.

Suddenly, a cute little dog appears beside the road. 🐕

You love dogs.

You stop for a second to pet it.

Just a minute. What's the harm?

Then you notice something else nearby.

Something you've loved since childhood.

Something you've always wanted to experience.

And then another interesting thing catches your attention.

For the first time that morning, you're not thinking about the meeting.

You're enjoying yourself.

One minute becomes five.

Five becomes fifteen.

And suddenly...

You look at your watch.

9:17 AM.

Your smile disappears.

OH SHIT. THE MEETING.

You rush back to your bike.

But it's too late.

The opportunity is gone.

And here's the crazy part.

The accident didn't defeat you.

The police didn't defeat you.

Being late didn't defeat you.

You fought through every obstacle life threw at you.

But in the final five minutes...

Something you LOVED defeated you.

---

THE LESSON.

When you're about to achieve something great, not every obstacle will look like an obstacle.

At first, life might test you with pain, failure, rejection, and setbacks.

And if you're determined enough, you'll overcome them.

But sometimes, the final test doesn't come as suffering.

It comes as pleasure.

Something beautiful.

Something exciting.

Something you've always wanted.

Something that makes you forget why you started.

And that's what makes it so dangerous.

Not everything that destroys your future will look like an enemy. Sometimes, it will look like everything you've ever wanted.

You can overcome a hundred obstacles and still lose everything to one distraction.

Because success isn't just about surviving the hard days.

It's about remembering your destination even when the journey offers you a thousand reasons to stop.

REMEMBER:

Stay focused.

Stay locked in.

Ignore the noise.

Resist the temptation.

You don't have to chase every opportunity, enjoy every pleasure, or respond to every distraction.

Some things can wait.

Some things must be sacrificed.

And some doors only open once.

The last five minutes can cost you everything you've fought for during the last five years.

Your life. Your choices. Your future.

It's in your hands.

Don't lose your destination because you fell in love with a distraction along the way.

Legends aren't made by those who never face temptation. They're made by those who remember what matters more.

STAY LOCKED IN. 🐈‍⬛

THE BEAUTIFUL CONTRADICTION OF BEING HUMAN.

This world has constructed so many layers of psychological programming that humanity has become architecturally conditioned to identify with its own illusions.

Ego, pride, arrogance, insecurity, superiority, inferiority. 

We inherit labels, internalise expectations and spend much of our existence defending identities we barely understand ourselves.

And the irony?

The majority of humanity, myself included, are walking contradictions.

We speak of fear as though experiencing it is something to be ashamed of. We associate vulnerability with weakness, weakness with inadequacy, and inadequacy with an assault upon the ego we've spent our lives constructing.

Well, fuck it.

Fuck the labels. Fuck the expectations. Fuck the psychological boxes humanity has invented to categorise the complexity of human existence.

I experience fear. I experience anger. There are things I hate. I have felt jealousy. I can be impulsive, outspoken and brutally direct when I disagree with something or feel disrespected.

I am human.

Yet I can love in extraordinary abundance. I can empathise with suffering. I can understand perspectives that contradict my own. I carry a depth of compassion that sometimes exceeds my ability to express it.

I spend many of my days battling depression, not because I cannot recognise the beauty of existence, but because I struggle to reconcile that beauty with the greed, superficiality, corruption and deliberate cruelty humanity has normalised.

I can be profoundly grateful for life while simultaneously grieving what humanity has made of it.

Like the yin and yang, I exist within polarity.

I desire love, yet I fear the vulnerability of receiving it because of the wounds left by those who once claimed to offer it.

And why should that make me a hypocrite?

Why have we become so obsessed with appearing consistent that we deny ourselves the freedom to evolve?

Every experience reveals another layer. Every moment offers an opportunity to discover something we previously misunderstood about ourselves.

We are not finished masterpieces hanging motionless in some gallery of human perfection.

We are living, breathing, evolving expressions of existence.

And I am tired of watching people suffocate their individuality beneath the weight of societal approval.

There is no fucking box.

The box is an illusion.

Perfection is an illusion.

The idea that human beings must conform to some universally approved psychological architecture to be worthy of acceptance is an illusion.

Do you genuinely believe that when God breathed existence into this universe, He intended humanity to spend its fleeting time categorising, condemning and measuring one another against arbitrary standards of perfection?

I accept people regardless of race, culture, religion or the circumstances that shaped their existence.

But acceptance does not mean surrendering discernment.

I will never understand the gratification some people derive from deliberately inflicting suffering upon another human being who has done them no harm.

And I never will.

Because compassion does not require me to excuse cruelty, just as authenticity does not absolve me of responsibility for my own imperfections.

To acknowledge our contradictions is not to glorify them. 

It is to recognise them honestly enough to continue evolving.

Life is but a fleeting candle in the wind.

So why squander it performing an identity designed to satisfy the expectations of people who are themselves struggling to understand who they are?

Why spend an entire lifetime forcing a circle into a square when neither was ever intended to become the other?

Nah. I'll pass.

I love being a walking contradiction.

I would rather spend my existence discovering the truth of who I am than waste it perfecting the illusion of who the world expects me to be. 

If that makes me a contradiction? 

So be it.

At least I'm living authentically enough to admit it. 💯🙏

text:
The court is indoors, in Nicetown, in the north of Philadelphia. Painted across it is the name of a boy who was 13 years old.

He never played on it. The building opened ten years after he was gone.

Above the court hangs a mural, 70 feet of it, and the face on the wall belongs to his older brother.

His name is Joel Embiid.

Before any of this, in Cameroon, he was a kid who wanted soccer and kept sneaking out of the house to go find a game of it. His father had a different plan for him.

"Nobody in Cameroon plays basketball," his dad told him. "You can play volleyball."

So he spent his teenage years on a volleyball court instead, which is the only court anybody in his family expected him to end up on.

He was 16 when Luc Mbah a Moute, a Cameroonian who had made the league, came home to run a basketball camp and asked him to come to it. He had been playing the sport for roughly three months. A high school in Florida offered him a place anyway.

"When I came over from Cameroon at 16, I didn't know any English," he said.

He learned to shoot off YouTube clips. One season at Kansas. Third pick in the 2014 draft. Then two surgeries on the same foot and no professional game until October of 2016.

In 2014, while he was in America, his family lost Arthur. The boy was 13.

Joel had been gone from home for years by then. When he went back, what he got handed was other people's memories of his own brother.

"It's funny, all the stories that I heard, because I hadn't been around since I left Cameroon," he said.

"He was someone that cared about everybody."

In 2020 he and Anne had a son, and they named him Arthur Elijah.

Then came the floor. The Alan Horwitz Sixth Man Center opened in Nicetown in 2024, and the court inside was dedicated to the Embiid family and given the name In Memory of Arthur. That September they held a block party in the building and pulled the sheet off the mural.

"It's still tough, thinking about the whole thing," Joel said. "He's also one of the reasons why I'm doing this."

TONIGHT the Sixers beat Detroit and moved to 8-1, the best record in the Eastern Conference. Joel Embiid is 32 years old and he has an MVP and an Olympic gold medal.

"There's no way, starting at 16, that I was supposed to be here," he said.

None of it was ever likely. A kid steered toward volleyball because basketball was not a thing people did where he lived now has a 70 foot face on a wall in North Philadelphia.

And on the court underneath it, where kids from Nicetown run drills on weeknights, a 13 year old's name is in the paint.

text:
In The 5,000 Year Leap, the Founders’ 3rd Principle is clear: the most promising way to secure a virtuous and morally stable people is to elect virtuous leaders. 📜

Samuel Adams warned that “neither the wisest constitution nor the wisest laws will secure the liberty and happiness of a people whose manners are universally corrupt.” The true friend of liberty “will not suffer a man to be chosen into any office of power and trust who is not a wise and virtuous man.” Officials must have experience, training, proven virtue, and demonstrated wisdom; not mere ambition, money, or name.

Jefferson distinguished the “natural aristocracy” of virtue and talents from the artificial one based on wealth and birth alone. The best government selects the former into office.

The Founders also warned of a deeper failure: the day when the best-qualified people refuse the tedious, arduous, and sometimes unpleasant task of filling important public offices. The natural tendency is to encourage others to run while staying on the sidelines. They knew strong self-government would be impossible unless that changed. It should be counted an honor to be drafted into politics. 

After the 2026 midterms, the question is straightforward: Do the candidates offered (and the ones who win) reflect standards of wisdom, virtue, experience, and moral character over money, name, or political machinery? Are the good and able still sitting out, leaving the field to those less fit?

A constitutional republic thrives only when the wise and virtuous step forward to lead, not merely push others. Choices driven by anything less risk the liberty and stability the Founders built. The remedy remains what they prescribed: elect the wise and virtuous, and if you are among them, stop sitting on the sidelines and step up.

What do you see when you measure today’s choices against that standard?

Do you feel that the midterm elected were chosen because of their virtue and goodness?

text:
C. H. Spurgeon's Morning Reading (November 5th)

"No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper." — Isaiah 54:17

This day is notable in English history for two great deliverances wrought by God for us. On this day the plot of the Papists to destroy our Houses of Parliament was discovered, 1605.

"While for our princes they prepare

In caverns deep a burning snare,

He shot from heaven a piercing ray,

And the dark treachery brought to day."

And secondly—today is the anniversary of the landing of King William III, at Torbay, by which the hope of Popish ascendancy was quashed, and religious liberty was secured, 1688.

This day ought to be celebrated, not by the saturnalia of striplings, but by the songs of saints. Our Puritan forefathers most devoutly made it a special time of thanksgiving. There is extant a record of the annual sermons preached by Matthew Henry on this day. Our Protestant feeling, and our love of liberty, should make us regard its anniversary with holy gratitude. Let our hearts and lips exclaim, "We have heard with our ears, and our fathers have told us the wondrous things which Thou didst in their day, and in the old time before them." Thou hast made this nation the home of the gospel; and when the foe has risen against her, Thou hast shielded her. Help us to offer repeated songs for repeated deliverances. Grant us more and more a hatred of Antichrist, and hasten on the day of her entire extinction. Till then and ever, we believe the promise, "No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper." Should it not be laid upon the heart of every lover of the gospel of Jesus on this day to plead for the overturning of false doctrines and the extension of divine truth? Would it not be well to search our own hearts, and turn out any of the Popish lumber of self-righteousness which may lie concealed therein?

text:
🇺🇸 WE DIDN’T LOSE THE VOTERS. WE LOST THEIR TRUST.

On Tuesday, November 3, 2026, I stood in line for hours to vote in Florida. And I listened.

A woman standing in front of me said something that stayed with me. Her family had always voted Republican. This time, she was voting the other way.

Think about that.

Texas elected Democrat James Talarico to the Senate and Gina Hinojosa as governor. 

Ohio elected Amy Acton, ending a 20-year Democratic drought in its governor’s race. 

Michigan went Democratic. 

Florida’s governor’s race was far closer than it should have been. 

Alaska was still too close to call as of Wednesday.

These aren’t isolated warning signs. 
They’re a message.

I don’t believe Americans stopped caring about their country. 
I believe too many of our candidates stopped giving people a compelling reason to believe in them.

We have mistaken endorsements for credibility, campaign money for competence, television advertising for personal connection, and name recognition for leadership.

And perhaps worst of all, we haven’t explained clearly enough what we stand for.

So let me put it plainly.

The Constitution. 
Individual liberty. 
Free enterprise.
Equal justice under the law. Limited government. 
Fiscal responsibility. 
Economic opportunity. 
A country that works for ordinary Americans.

These aren’t campaign slogans. They’re principles worth defending.

We need candidates with demonstrated records of service, integrity, competence, and conviction.

Not people selected because they have the largest war chest or the right political connections.

We need to identify those candidates early, support them, put them in front of the people, and hold them accountable.

Get out of the studios. 
Get out of the consultants’ offices. 
Get out into the communities.

Knock on doors. 
Listen. 
Have conversations. 
Answer difficult questions. 
Earn trust.

And stop assuming that voters owe us their loyalty.

They don’t. 
We have to earn it.

Politics isn’t supposed to be a business of selling personalities. 
It’s supposed to be the business of public service.

We lose when we offer voters a name and a war chest.

We win when we offer them principles, competence, character, and something worth believing in.

This is bigger than one election. 

It’s about rebuilding a political movement that remembers why it exists.

Hearts and minds. 
One voter at a time.

Let’s get to work.

text:
As a Republican, I am not going to pretend we didn't have this coming. This year I got to see the party from a different perspective: from the inside… and though the eyes of my young adult children. 

We didn't lose because our principles failed. We lost because so many of our leaders drifted from them.

The light is growing dim, and the weakening torch is being guarded, not passed to the next generation. 

The next generation doesn't feel heard, known, valued, or respected. I know, because I'm a mom of 15. My kids are passionate and principled individuals, ages 11 to 27, and they want a ballot full of leaders who fight for them, not against them.

What matters most?

As I listen to my adult kids and the young parents around me, it comes down to something like this: 

Liberty. Life. Free speech. Justice. 
The freedom to pursue one’s own happiness without government overreach. They want low taxes. Less red tape, more trust. Less potholes. 

Clean air, clean water, clean food, safe medicine, vibrant main streets, diverse farms, safe and affordable communities, and real food on the table.

This generation wants sidewalks that go places. Not wider roads, not more asphalt and not bigger parking lots. 

They want the government out of their business, their bedroom, and their medicine cabinet. 

They don't want to be coerced into vaccinations, and they don't want to be punished keeping chickens or for selling eggs to a neighbor. They don't want to be burdened with the debts of the previous generation's out-of-control spending. 

They don't want wars in Iran and Ukraine, and a legacy of broken promises.

They want the freedom to give their kids a better education than public schools currently offer, and they don't think children should have to be medicated just to sit still through boring lessons. 

They want neighborhood schools their kids can walk to, where they learn skills over standardization. 

They don't want politicians to look the other way when their buddies are getting drunk on private islands and doing things they ought not. They are tired of the waste, fraud and abuse. 

They don't want AI robots running the country. They don’t want data centers that look like prisons. They don’t want eminent domain used against them and in favor of private companies. 

They want to get back to basics and raise families on one income instead of two, so someone can create a home for the kids. 

They want faith that's spiritual and churches that take a stand. They want leaders they are not ashamed of. They want the criminals off the streets and out of public office. 

They want to raise up the next generation in a country where a mother's womb is not a dangerous place for a child.

Those are not new ideas. 

They are the ideas this nation was built on. 

Many of these values are based on the foundation of liberty… that the Republican Party has always claimed to stand on. These are the principles our soldiers went to battle for. Last night, a nation that still holds on to the principles that made us America told us it no longer believes we, the GOP, do too.

text:
For some reason, I’m reminded of Neil Gorsuch’s opinion on the case that ended Trump’s IEEPA tariffs.

Many of you are going to be mad that power may be chiseled away from Trump. But his own appointee wrote quite brilliantly why this is a feature, not a bug.

“For those who think it important for the Nation to impose more tariffs, I understand that today’s decision will be disappointing. All I can offer them is that most major decisions affecting the rights and responsibilities of the American people (including the duty to pay taxes and tariffs) are funneled through the legislative process for a reason. Yes, legislating can be hard and take time. And, yes, it can be tempting to bypass Congress when some pressing problem arises. But the deliberative nature of the legislative process was the whole point of its design. Through that process, the Nation can tap the combined wisdom of the people’s elected representatives, not just that of one faction or man. There, deliberation tempers impulse, and compromise hammers disagreements into workable solutions. And because laws must earn such broad support to survive the legislative process, they tend to endure, allowing ordinary people to plan their lives in ways they cannot when the rules shift from day to day. In all, the legislative process helps ensure each of us has a stake in the laws that govern us and in the Nation’s future. For some today, the weight of those virtues is apparent. For others, it may not seem so obvious. But if history is any guide, the tables will turn and the day will come when those disappointed by today’s result will appreciate the legislative process for the bulwark of liberty it is.”

🇺🇸 Rubio–DeSantis 2028 🇺🇸
     The Potential Benefits

A presidential ticket featuring Marco Rubio and Ron DeSantis would bring together two prominent Florida Republicans with different governing experiences, policy backgrounds, and political constituencies.

Whether Rubio headed the ticket with DeSantis as vice president—or the reverse—would matter considerably.

Here are the principal potential advantages, along with the challenges that would need to be addressed.

1. Complementary experience
Marco Rubio — Foreign policy and national security
Rubio's experience in the U.S. Senate and executive branch provides a background in diplomacy, intelligence, international relations, and national security.
Supporters could emphasize his familiarity with China, Latin America, international alliances, and U.S. strategic interests.
Ron DeSantis — Executive leadership and domestic policy
DeSantis brings experience as Florida governor, a former member of Congress, and a military veteran.
His record provides concrete examples for voters to evaluate on taxes, education, immigration, disaster response, and the use of state executive authority.

2. A combination of national and state-level perspectives
Rubio's federal experience and DeSantis's state executive experience could allow the ticket to present a broad governing agenda.
For example, Rubio could emphasize diplomatic and national-security priorities, while DeSantis could discuss how federal decisions affect states, businesses, schools, and local governments.

3. Overlapping but distinct conservative constituencies
Both politicians have established relationships within the Republican Party, but their political profiles differ.
Rubio has a long history of engagement with foreign-policy conservatives and Cuban American political communities. DeSantis has developed a national profile through conservative state-level policy initiatives and his 2024 presidential campaign.
A joint ticket could seek to bring those constituencies into one coalition, although shared support cannot be assumed.

4. Policy continuity with the Trump administration
Rubio's role as Secretary of State gives him direct experience implementing the administration's foreign-policy agenda. DeSantis has pursued several overlapping conservative priorities in Florida.

For Republicans interested in continuing parts of Trump's policy agenda after 2028, the two politicians offer records that can be examined on immigration enforcement, regulatory policy, national security, and education.
However, voters would also need to examine where their approaches differ, particularly on foreign intervention and the appropriate scope of government power.

5. A significant constitutional complication
Both Rubio and DeSantis are Florida residents.
Under the 12th Amendment, Florida's presidential electors cannot vote for both a presidential candidate and vice-presidential candidate who are Florida inhabitants.
Florida has 30 electoral votes in 2028. A ticket involving two Florida residents would therefore need to address this issue, potentially through a genuine change of residency by one candidate.

From Observing Consciousness:

“My election observations... I'm titling it... "The Rope-a-Dope"... 

Trump is leaning against the ropes, congratulating the people throwing punches at him, while an entirely different fight unfolds around the ring...

Three days before the midterms, Trump posted Muhammad Ali's 1971 defeat against Joe Frazier... that caught my attention because Ali's greatest strategic masterpiece came three years later against George Foreman... the rope-a-dope...

Ali absorbed punishment against the ropes, allowing Foreman to exhaust himself while the crowd watched what appeared to be a losing fighter... then, in the eighth round, Ali came off those ropes and knocked Foreman out...

Now look at November 3... Dems capture Congress, the media celebrates, and Trump congratulates his opponents, praises their performance, and offers cooperation...

He distances himself from the losses, reminding everyone he wasn't on the ballot and still possesses presidential veto authority...

See the positioning? He's absorbing the blows while his opponents inherit responsibility for what follows...

Meanwhile another sequence was unfolding... in September, DOJ issued litigation holds covering election records in 29 states and Washington, D.C. On October 26, Trump announced a proposed $1 million election fraud reward, alongside DOJ's separate $10,000 to $30,000 fraud incentive program...

On October 29, DOJ reinforced the 22-month federal election record preservation requirement, warning against deliberate destruction... 

Then just one day before the election, a Michigan judge permanently blocked deletion of original electronic pollbooks after certification, preserving underlying data and metadata... "watch Michigan"...

Election evidence was being legally protected before the outcome was known...

Simultaneously ~1,000 DOJ monitors and observers covered 126 jurisdictions across all 50 states...

Hegseth mobilized military intelligence, Cyber Command, and the NSA against foreign interference, while DOJ's voter registration litigation tested federal authority against state sovereignty and privacy protections...

Election Day produced localized scanner failures, ballot shortages, bomb threats, and disruptions. Federal cyber monitoring reported limited threats and no identified foreign influence operations by late election night... preserved records now provide a foundation for lawful audits and investigations...

Zoom out and connect the systems... federal monitoring expanded as courts enforced constitutional boundaries... cyber defenses operated alongside evidence preservation... Congressional power shifted while the presidency retained its executive authority... and Trump is congratulating the Democrats...

Ali understood this dynamic... Foreman's aggression, confidence, and energy expenditure became variables influencing the fight... the punches were landing while conditions for Ali's counterattack developed...

Trump's Ali posts, his election response, and the institutional activity surrounding November 3 create a striking parallel...

The congressional defeat is real, legal processes continue, election records remain preserved, and Trump retains his constitutional powers...

Trump has absorbed the immediate political damage while positioning himself for the next phase...

The Democrats have their victory, the spotlight, and the illusion of victory... Trump is about to move off the ropes and come out swinging...”

text:
10 PM Top-of-the-Hour News

Democrats are now mapping out plans for the new year – a day after the Midterm elections.  In Minnesota, Senator Amy Klobuchar is detailing the next few months as she makes the transition from Washington back to Saint Paul – where she will take over as governor in January.  She said she's ready to push policy and change – and cast politics aside.: “I am committed as ever to moving our state forward, not moving our state to the left or to the right, but moving our state forward. ”
It’s not clear who will succeed Klobuchar in the Senate.  The process will take shape – when Klobuchar formally resigns from her seat.  Some analysts think her first decision as governor may be appointing a replacement – to fill the last four years of her term.

After a decisive win by Democrats in the midterm election, the presumed next Speaker of the House,  Democratic Congressman Hakeem Jeffries sees this as an opportunity for Congress to reintroduce a power balance between President Trump and the legislative branch: “The days of the House of Representatives functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over. House Democrats are going to lead a Congress that does serve as a check and balance on an out of control executive branch. ”
If Jeffries is elected Speaker of the House by his fellow Democrats he will become the first black Speaker.

President Trump is pushing back against any notion that the midterm results are a referendum on his leadership.
On social media, the President deflected blame onto individual GOP candidates, claiming his personal support simply did not transfer over.
Instead, he argues the night would have looked very different if his name had appeared on the ballot: “If I were on the ballot, we would have won. You saw the people that were packed, thousands and thousands of people at every rally, and if I was on the ballot, we would have won, but they just, you couldn't transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies. It was incredible, and we weren't able to transfer the love to candidates. ”
Trump's hand-picked candidates ultimately lost several key swing-state races.

The President is standing by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth – after the so-called Blue Tsunami which many attribute to voter anger over the Iran war.  Asked whether he was considering replacing Hegseth, whom he has described as a champion of the war, Trump told reporters no and that he thinks he's doing a very good job."
The response contrasted with then-President George Bush, who fired Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld the morning after the 2006 midterm elections.  That's when voter discontent over the Iraq war helped Democrats win control of Congress.
Sources add Trump could still replace Hegseth as Republicans continue to assess their losses.

Police in Western Pennsylvania say a 42 year old man threw his two children, ages 8 and 6, off the top of a parking garage in Allegheny County, then jumped.  All three died. Mount Lebanin Police Chief Jason Haberman...: “There will be a significant amount of trauma associated with this event to the community. Our condolences to everybody involved, victims' families, friends, everybody within the Mount Lebanon community will know somebody involved in this incident. ”

It's not just food storage being affected by hackers in France.  Brad Gibson is in Paris: “Officials said the attack earlier this week was detected before damage was done. A supervisor reportedly stopped it by carrying out a remote control on three different freezing and cooling units that stored blood and blood plasma. We're being told that no blood was affected and no health had been harmed, but what the hackers reportedly did in this cyberattack was turn the temperature gauge from -22 to 230 °F. ”

With open enrollment underway, the Federal Trade Commission is issuing a warning about potentially misleading health insurance ads and scams.
The agency says some companies who promise comprehensive plans actually provide limited benefits and services.
Other companies offer medical discount cards instead of healthcare insurance.
Ads impersonating the government and reputable insurance companies have also appeared on the internet.
The FTC urged people to be cautious about calls, texts, social media messages and online search results.
