text:
A squirrel hides thousands of nuts every autumn with a brain the size of a shelled walnut.

Then it finds most of them again, in the dark, under snow, months later.

And the ones it never finds are quietly rebuilding the forest.

Stay with me. The real story is stranger than the headline, and it ends with a fact that made me rethink what "intelligence" even means.

---

THE JOB NOBODY NOTICES

Every autumn, across the northern forests, a quiet race begins.

Days shorten. Cones ripen. Hazelnuts drop. And one small animal starts working like it has a deadline it cannot see.

It does not know winter is coming in any way you or I would call knowing. Nobody told it. It has never lived through a winter before, if it was born this spring.

It does the job anyway.

It picks a nut. It weighs it, in a sense, with its paws and teeth. It carries it away from the tree. It digs a small hole, pushes the nut in with its nose, packs soil on top, and sometimes even tucks a bit of leaf litter over the spot like a tiny act of stagecraft.

Then it does it again.

And again.

A single gray squirrel can make several thousand of these hiding places in one season. Biologists call the strategy scatter-hoarding: instead of one giant pantry, the animal creates thousands of tiny ones, each holding a single item.

Think about that for a second. Thousands of locations. One animal. No notebook, no map, no phone.

So the first question is the obvious one.

How does it find them again?

---

1. THE MEMORY TEST

In 1991, the biologist Lucia Jacobs and her colleague Liman published a paper in the journal Animal Behaviour with a title that sounds almost too simple: grey squirrels remember the locations of buried nuts.

That was the point. Before this kind of work, many people assumed a squirrel simply sniffs around until it bumps into something edible. A bit like a dog following its nose across a field.

The experiments suggested something more interesting. Squirrels were using memory for places, not just smell. They went back to spots where they had buried food and dug with purpose.

Later research from many labs added detail: squirrels appear to use a mix of strategies. Memory gets them to the right neighborhood. Smell helps them pin down the exact spot, especially for nuts that are close to the surface. Researchers such as Stephen Vander Wall, who spent a career studying seed-caching animals, showed how these two tools work together in different species.

Memory first. Nose second.

Which sounds almost reasonable, until you remember the scale.

This animal is not recalling one location. It is managing an entire landscape of buried treasure, and it is doing it with a brain that weighs a few grams.

(Yes, grams. A red squirrel's whole brain is a few grams of tissue. That is the entire machine running the operation.)

But here is where the story takes a dark turn.

Because buried food has one enormous problem.

Other animals want it.

---

2. THE THIEVES

A squirrel's cache is not safe the moment it is buried.

Other squirrels watch. Birds watch. Mice and voles sniff. Even a squirrel that does everything right can return to find a neat little hole where its dinner used to be.

Scientists call this pilfering. It is one of the great pressures that shaped squirrel behavior, and the evidence suggests squirrels know it.

In 2007, a research team from the University of Exeter, led by Lisa Leaver with colleagues including Lucy Hopewell, published a study on grey squirrels in Animal Behaviour. The title was about audience effects on food caching.

The idea was simple and a little devious.

What happens when a squirrel buries food while a competitor is watching?

The squirrels changed their behavior. They did not cache the same way when someone could see them. They adjusted how they handled the food in response to who was around.

Read that again.

The animal behaved differently depending on who was watching.

That is a very human thing to do. And a very unexpected thing to find in a rodent.

But it gets weirder.

---

3. THE SQUIRREL THAT FAKES IT

In 2008, Michael Steele of Wilkes University and a team of colleagues published a study in Animal Behaviour with a title that raised eyebrows: do tree squirrels engage in behavioural deception?

Steele has spent much of his career watching squirrels and the oak trees they plant. His team documented behaviors that look a lot like cheating.

Squirrels would sometimes go through the full motions of burying a nut. Dig the hole. Push, pack, cover.

Without a nut.

Researchers described this as false caching. If a rival is watching, the rival sees a squirrel bury something. The rival goes to the spot later. The spot is empty.

Now, a careful scientist will tell you that "deception" is a loaded word. Animal behavior researchers argue about how much intention is involved. It may be a learned habit that works, rather than a plan to mislead. The debate is real, and it is not settled.

But the behavior itself is not in dispute. In certain situations, squirrels bury nothing and act like they buried something.

If a human did that, we would call it a bluff.

The squirrel does not seem to care what we call it.

And the cheating goes both ways.

Because for every squirrel that fakes a cache, there is another squirrel that has learned to rob one.

---

4. THE ARMS RACE UNDERGROUND

Here is the picture biologists keep coming back to.

A forest in autumn is not peaceful. It is an arms race.

Squirrels bury food and try to protect it. Other animals watch and try to steal it. Protection strategies evolve. Theft strategies evolve to match.

Move the nut farther away from the source tree. Spread caches out so no single raid ruins everything. Choose spots with less competition. Stay quiet when someone is nearby. Retrieve a nut early if you suspect someone saw.

All of this, remember, from an animal that was likely born that very spring.

Nobody taught it. There was no school. No mother standing over it with a lecture on pilferage risk.

Every move has a counter-move. Every hiding place invites a search.

The surprising thing is how much of this is decided in seconds, by an animal with no time to think it over.

Which brings up one of the most famous findings in animal behavior.

---

5. THE SQUIRREL THAT BURIES ON CONCRETE

The ethologist Irenäus Eibl-Eibesfeldt reported something that has appeared in textbooks for decades.

Squirrels raised in captivity, with no soil, no forest and no model to copy, still performed the full burying routine when given a nut.

On a bare floor.

They would carry the nut to a corner. Make digging motions at a surface that could not be dug. Push the nut with the nose. Pat down imaginary soil. Walk away satisfied.

Then the nut would sit there, completely visible.

The squirrel had performed the whole ritual perfectly, and the ritual did nothing.

This told scientists something profound. Parts of the caching routine are built in. The sequence is inherited. The squirrel does not need to learn the steps.

What it does need to learn is where it put things, who is watching, and when to dig them up.

So the animal runs on two systems at once.

An ancient script, written in its genes.

And a live, flexible mind that adapts the script to the situation.

Instinct plus memory.

Hold onto that, because it explains the most surprising part of the whole story.

---

6. THE NUTS IT FORGETS

Now the twist I promised.

No system is perfect. Even the best memory in the forest drops a few items. Some caches are never recovered. The squirrel dies, or moves on, or gets distracted, or digs in the wrong place.

And a nut buried in soil, left alone through winter, does what a nut is built to do.

It sprouts.

This is the part that changes how you look at a park, an oak wood or a hazel thicket.

Many trees depend on animals like squirrels and jays to move their seeds. Acorns are heavy. They fall straight down. Left alone, most would land under the mother tree, in her shade, competing with her roots. A seed that wants a future needs to be carried away.

A squirrel is, in effect, a delivery service that pays itself in the product and accidentally loses some of the cargo.

Researchers who study seed dispersal call this a mutualism with a leak in it. The animal gets food. The tree gets planted. The leak is where the trees come from.

The Eurasian jay does a similar job for oaks. Ecologists commonly cite a figure of several thousand acorns buried by a single jay in one autumn. The exact number varies from study to study, so treat it as an order of magnitude, not a promise. But the point stands: a bird with a small head and a large appetite has helped shape the spread of oak woodland across Europe.

Same story with hazel. Same story with pine seeds and the Clark's nutcracker in North America, a bird that can store tens of thousands of seeds in thousands of caches and remember a large share of them months later. Scientists such as Russell Balda and Alan Kamil studied this in detail, and the memory performance of nutcrackers is some of the most impressive ever measured in a wild animal.

Think about what that means.

Parts of the forest you walk through were planted by accident.

By an animal that was trying to eat.

---

7. THE OAK TRICK

There is one more detail about acorns that sounds made up.

It is not.

Oaks fall into two broad groups. The white oak group produces acorns that tend to sprout in autumn, soon after they fall. The red oak group produces acorns that wait until spring.

For a squirrel, this matters.

An acorn that sprouts in autumn starts burning its own stored energy. It becomes a worse meal with every passing week. An acorn that sleeps until spring stays fresh all winter.

In 1982, the researcher J. F. Fox published a paper in the journal Evolution on how gray squirrels deal with this. The finding that gets quoted again and again: squirrels tend to eat white oak acorns right away, and they tend to bury the red oak acorns for later.

Even more striking, squirrels have been observed biting out the embryo of certain acorns before burying them. That stops the nut from germinating. It is a bit like removing the battery from a clock so it keeps its current time.

Michael Steele and others have discussed this behavior in the literature on squirrels and oaks.

Pause on that.

A rodent is sorting food by how fast it will spoil. And then performing a small surgical procedure to make the food last.

It does this without a lab, without a calendar and without a degree in plant biology.

OK. So the squirrel is a planner, a gambler and a gardener.

But we have not even gotten to the strangest part of its body.

---

8. THE TAIL

Most people think a squirrel's tail is decoration.

It is closer to a Swiss Army knife.

It helps with balance when the animal runs along a thin branch. It works as a rudder in a leap. It can act as a blanket in cold weather and as shade in the heat. It is a signal flag for other squirrels. And it can slow a fall.

But one use of the tail was only discovered in this century, and it sounds like science fiction.

In 2007, a team led by Aaron Rundus, working with Donald Owings at the University of California, Davis, published a paper in PNAS titled, in plain terms, that ground squirrels use an infrared signal to deter rattlesnake predation.

Here is the setup.

Rattlesnakes hunt by more than sight and smell. They have heat-sensing pits that detect infrared radiation. They can effectively see the warmth of a living body.

The California ground squirrel knows this.

When the squirrels faced a rattlesnake, they did something odd. They flagged their tails, waving them in a distinctive way. And the tail got warmer. The blood flow to the tail increased, and the surface temperature rose.

The team then built a robotic squirrel, a model that could wave its tail, with and without the heat. They tested how rattlesnakes reacted.

The result: the combination of tail waving and a warm tail mattered. The infrared signal seemed to tell the snake that the squirrel was alert and the ambush would likely fail.

Read that one more time.

A squirrel heats up its tail to send a message in a spectrum of light that humans cannot see.

To a predator that reads that spectrum.

I did not make this up. It is a peer-reviewed result in one of the most respected journals in science.

And that was a ground squirrel. A cousin.

Which brings us to the family tree.

---

9. NOT ALL SQUIRRELS ARE THE SAME ANIMAL

When people say "squirrel" they usually mean one of three lifestyles.

The tree squirrels, like the red squirrel and the gray squirrel. They live in canopy, they jump between branches, they store food in many small caches.

The ground squirrels, like the ones in Rundus's study. They live in burrows, and many of them hibernate.

And the flying squirrels, which do not truly fly but glide on a stretched membrane between front and back legs, usually at night.

All of them are rodents. All of them are in the same family, Sciuridae. And across that family, evolution has run a series of strange experiments.

Take hibernation.

The Arctic ground squirrel, in a study published in the journal Science in 1989 by Brian Barnes, was found to cool its body below the freezing point of water during hibernation. The animal's body temperature dropped to roughly minus three degrees Celsius without it freezing solid.

An animal whose body is colder than frozen water, and still alive.

And the brain?

Research on hibernating ground squirrels, including work published by Heller and colleagues in the Journal of Neuroscience in 2006, found that connections between brain cells shrink during deep torpor, then regrow rapidly when the animal warms. The animal appears to take its brain apart, partially, and rebuild it.

Rebuild.

Every winter.

And it still wakes up knowing how to be a squirrel.

The tree squirrels do not do this. The red squirrel does not hibernate at all. It stays active through winter, which is exactly why the caches matter so much.

For a red squirrel, those buried nuts are not a snack.

They are the difference between a long winter and a short life.

---

10. THE FORENSICS OF A HAZELNUT

Here is a detail that field biologists love.

A squirrel eats like a signature.

When a red squirrel opens a hazelnut, it gnaws a small groove into the shell and then splits it cleanly along its natural seam, leaving two rough halves. A mouse or a vole leaves a different mark. A bird leaves another. A hazel dormouse leaves a neat, smooth-edged hole with tooth marks around the rim.

Ecologists use these leftovers to work out who has been in the woods, even if they never see the animal.

The same goes for pine and spruce cones. A squirrel strips the scales off one by one to reach the seeds, and what remains is a ragged little core, with a pile of scales underneath the feeding tree.

Walk through a conifer wood in autumn and you can read the story on the ground.

A squirrel was here. It sat on this stump. It ate for a long time.

The animal leaves a trail so clear that you could investigate it like a crime scene.

And the pattern behind those meals leads to the next big question.

Why are some years packed with squirrels, and others strangely empty?

---

11. THE BOOM AND BUST YEARS

Forests do not produce food evenly.

Many trees follow a rhythm called masting. In some years they release enormous crops of seeds. In others they release almost nothing. Oaks, beeches and conifers all do it.

One leading explanation is that boom years overwhelm the animals that eat the seeds. There is simply more food than the hungry mouths can finish, so some seeds survive. Bust years keep the seed eaters from growing in number too fast.

For squirrels, this is a rollercoaster.

Studies of red squirrels across Europe have linked their numbers and breeding success to the size of local seed crops. A rich year can mean more young and better survival. A poor year can mean hunger, wandering and hard choices.

So the nuts buried in autumn are not a hobby.

They are a bet on a future the squirrel cannot see, placed in a landscape that changes from year to year.

Some years that bet pays off beautifully.

Other years, it is the only thing standing between the animal and an empty winter.

---

12. THE BODY BUILT FOR THE JOB

Now look at the hardware.

Start with the teeth.

A squirrel's front teeth never stop growing. They are worn down constantly by gnawing, and they keep growing to compensate. If a rodent's teeth stop meeting properly, the growth can become a serious problem, which is one reason gnawing is not a hobby for these animals. It is maintenance.

And those teeth are orange.

That is not dirt and not a dental problem. The enamel on rodent incisors contains iron, which gives it a yellow-orange tint and makes the surface harder. The teeth are built to crack shells, and they come with their own reinforcement.

Then the ankles.

Most animals that climb trees struggle to come down head first. Claws point the wrong way. Squirrels solve this by rotating their hind feet so the claws point backward while the body points down. It is why you can watch a squirrel run down a trunk headfirst like it is nothing.

Then the falls.

The biologist J. B. S. Haldane wrote a famous essay in 1926, On Being the Right Size, with a point that sounds absurd and is true. Small animals survive falls that would destroy large ones, because the ratio of surface area to weight changes with size. A mouse can drop from a great height and walk away. A rat is killed. A human breaks. A horse splatters.

A squirrel sits comfortably on the safe side of that line.

Which is why you see them miss a branch, tumble through the air, hit the ground and scamper off like nothing happened.

It is not luck.

It is physics, and a body that is the right size for a life in the trees.

Finally, the seasonal wardrobe.

The Eurasian red squirrel changes its look through the year. In autumn it grows thicker fur and develops ear tufts, those little brushes of hair on the tips of the ears. In summer they thin out. Coat color varies a lot across the range, from bright red to deep brown, and in some regions the winter coat turns grayish.

Not every red squirrel is red.

Not every one looks the same from one season to the next.

An animal with a closet.

---

13. THE MYTH OF THE SMALL BRAIN

Now back to the walnut.

It is tempting to assume that a small brain means a simple mind. The history of animal research keeps proving that assumption wrong.

Consider the western scrub-jay.

In 2007, Nicola Clayton's group at the University of Cambridge, with Caroline Raby and colleagues, published a paper in Nature on planning for the future in scrub-jays. In the experiment, birds were placed in different compartments overnight, some of which gave breakfast and some of which did not. Later, when offered food to cache, the birds hid more food in the compartment where they would not get breakfast.

They stored food for a future need they could predict.

That result shook the idea that planning for tomorrow was a purely human skill.

And scrub-jays, like squirrels, belong to a small club of animals that cache food.

There is a pattern here. Animals that hoard food in many places tend to have strong spatial memory and, in the species that have been studied, a hippocampus that is well developed for their body size. The hippocampus is the part of the brain heavily involved in memory for places. Work on food-storing birds, including studies by John Krebs and David Sherry in the late 1980s, helped make that link famous.

The lesson keeps repeating.

Brain size is not the whole story. What an animal's brain is built to do matters more than how much it weighs.

A squirrel does not need to write a poem.

It needs to remember where thousands of tiny objects are.

Its brain is built for that.

And in that narrow job, it is better than you would be on your best day.

Try this. Hide a few hundred items across a park, in the dirt, one by one. Walk away. Come back in three months, with snow on the ground, and find most of them.

Go ahead.

I will wait.

---

14. THE SQUIRREL IN TROUBLE

Here is the part of the story that is not funny.

In Britain, the native squirrel is the red squirrel. In the late nineteenth century, the gray squirrel was brought over from North America and released in several places.

The grays thrived.

The reds collapsed.

Across most of England, the red squirrel has been replaced by the gray. Researchers point to two main factors. One is competition: grays are larger and can make better use of certain foods, especially acorns, which lets them live at higher densities. The other is disease: grays can carry the squirrelpox virus, which they tolerate far better than reds, and which can be deadly to the native species.

Today, most of the red squirrels left in the United Kingdom live in Scotland, with smaller populations in a few other protected areas. Conservation groups run programs to protect them, and the work is ongoing.

Across large parts of northern Europe and Asia, the red squirrel remains a common sight, though local populations can shift with habitat, food supply and disease.

The pattern is a reminder.

An animal that looks like part of the furniture of a forest can vanish faster than anyone expects.

And the forest it helped plant can feel the loss for generations.

---

15. WHAT THE SQUIRREL KNOWS THAT WE FORGET

So let us pull this together.

A small animal, with a small brain, buries thousands of items across a landscape.

It remembers most of them, using a mix of spatial memory and smell.

It watches who is watching, and changes how it behaves.

It sometimes goes through the motions of burying nothing.

It sorts food by how quickly it will spoil, and in some cases disables the nut so it lasts.

It carries an inherited script that works even on a bare floor.

And the nuts it forgets become trees.

That is not a cute animal story.

That is an ecosystem running on forgetfulness.

The oldest, most successful partnership in the forest depends on an animal that is very good, but not perfect, at remembering.

If the squirrel recovered every single nut, there would be fewer forests.

If it forgot all of them, it would starve.

The whole system lives in the narrow gap between those two failures.

Evolution did not build a perfect memory.

It built a memory that is just good enough to survive, and just leaky enough to plant the future.

I find that beautiful.

And I find it a little humbling.

Because most of us are carrying small seeds right now, in our heads and our habits and our unfinished projects, and we have no idea which ones will quietly grow into something big.

---

16. THE NEXT TIME YOU SEE ONE

Next time a squirrel crosses your path, look at it differently.

It is not just a pest, a pet or a photo.

It is a gardener with a lock-picking problem.

It is a risk manager, a cheat, a thief and a victim.

It is an animal with a heated tail, an iron-reinforced mouth, a hibernating cousin that supercools its body and a family history of planting forests by accident.

And it is doing all of that with a brain you could hold in the palm of your hand.

Quick recap, for the bookmark:

Squirrels remember places, not just smells.
They change tactics when rivals are watching.
Some bury nothing, on purpose or by habit, and rivals dig up empty ground.
Their inherited burying script works even where no digging is possible.
Their forgotten nuts become forests.
And one cousin heats its tail to talk to snakes.

That is a lot of résumé for something that fits in your hand.

So here is my question.

If an animal this small can plan, bluff, remember and rebuild a forest, what else are we underestimating?

Tell me in the replies. What is the most intelligent thing you have ever seen an animal do?

If this changed how you see squirrels, repost it so someone else gets to be surprised.

Bookmark it for the next time someone says "it's just a squirrel."

And follow for more stories where the smallest animals turn out to be the biggest surprise.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems? : https://t.co/9VZINC76It

"ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
Xinrui Zhong1,∗Zhiming Wang1,∗Yongqi Liu1Zhaohui Wang2Shanglin Yang1
Zikun Li1Zhuoming Chen1Beidi Chen11Carnegie Mellon University 2University of Southern California
Abstract
Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, 4.87× the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.
1Introduction
Figure 1:API cost and serving value relative to the strongest baseline. GPT 6.1 Sol offers lower-cost gains; Claude reaches higher value. Costs use OpenRouter rates (Table 3).
Large language model (LLM) coding agents build on code-generation capabilities (Zheng et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026a), using tools and execution feedback to undertake software development and professional workflows (Yang et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2025; Chan et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026). These workflows depend on LLM serving systems, which run models and handle requests (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2026b). This creates an opportunity for coding agents to design these systems. Service providers need correct model execution and timely responses. We therefore ask: how can coding agents design LLM serving systems while satisfying given deployment and service constraints?📷Figure 2:Agents design the server and choose how many sessions it serves at once for a given model, GPU allocation, and workload. Replay preserves shared context and dependencies between requests; final checks assess model correctness and complete workload execution.
Despite rapid progress in agent-driven systems optimization, existing benchmarks evaluate individual kernels, code patches, or servers under preset test conditions (Ouyang et al., 2025; Nangia et al., 2026; Williams et al., 2026; Yeon et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026), leaving three gaps in evaluating how agents design complete serving systems:
•Oversimplified workloads. Prior benchmarks issue independent requests or fixed prefill, decoding, and throughput scenarios (Yeon et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). With uniform request lengths and fixed batches, a static batch serves nearly as well as a production engine, so techniques that real deployments depend on, such as continuous batching and paged attention (Yu et al., 2022; Kwon et al., 2023), bring little benefit. Real applications such as coding agents instead mix short and long requests, extend a shared context over many turns, and fan out into parallel subagents, where prefix reuse, memory management, and prefill–decode interference shape performance (Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025; Agrawal et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024).
•Speedup-only objectives. Existing benchmarks score speedup or throughput relative to a baseline (Ouyang et al., 2025; Yeon et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). Such objectives ignore latency requirements and GPU cost and fix the offered load, whereas a service provider must decide how much workload to serve while keeping time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT) within targets.
•Correctness-only validation. Validation typically checks outputs against a reference implementation or test suite (Ouyang et al., 2025; Williams et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). A serving system must additionally meet tail-latency targets on the deployed workload and execute that workload in full, with complete prompts, prescribed output lengths, and consistent streaming. Optimizations such as speculative decoding, state reuse, and custom scheduling introduce execution paths that short or isolated tests rarely exercise.We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark in which coding agents build a complete LLM serving system for a given model, GPU allocation, and workload, and decide how much workload it serves (Figure 2). Starting from a minimal Transformers server, agents plan experiments and revise their systems within a fixed development budget. ServerBench closes the three gaps with three designs. 1. Workload: real coding-agent trajectories. ServerBench replays recorded coding-agent sessions (SemiAnalysis, 2026a) with their request lengths, multi-turn structure, shared prefixes, parallel subagent branches, and inter-turn delays. Requests wait on the responses they depend on, so serving latency governs how much work completes within the measurement window (Section 3.2). 2. Objective: dollars per dollar. We price the input and output tokens of each completed request at fixed API rates, count only requests that meet both TTFT and TPOT targets, and divide by the GPU cost of the measurement window (Section 3.1). For example, USD 3.65 of qualified token value over USD 0.83 of GPU cost scores 4.40. The objective rewards capacity improvements together with a matching load choice: serving more workload raises gross value only while requests still meet their latency targets. 3. Validation: beyond correctness. Latency targets are the p90 TTFT and TPOT of an SGLang reference with its model-specific configuration, frozen before development (Section 3.1). The submitted system is rebuilt in a fresh deployment and replayed on held-out seeds. Independent checks verify complete prompts, output lengths, streaming consistency, generation fidelity to the checkpoint, and held-out answer accuracy; a post-run review inspects code and recorded actions for prohibited shortcuts (Section 3.4). Only verified systems receive a score.We evaluate eleven coding-agent models across three model–hardware deployments. Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, 4.87× the vLLM serving baseline (Section 4.2). Trajectory analysis identifies three findings. High-value designs coordinate capacity and concurrency. Sonnet 5.5 improves its server before raising concurrency, then limits load when additional sessions worsen TPOT (Section 4.3). Interpreting feedback in workload context guides optimization. A random-text probe leads one agent to reject an optimization; workload replies reveal its benefit and lead another to adopt it (Section 4.4). Verification must match the deployed workload. Agents’ short or isolated checks can miss long-context stalls and cross-request crashes; known faults can persist or recur after edits in submitted systems (Section 4.5).Our contributions are:
•ServerBench, a benchmark for designing complete LLM serving systems to maximize service value per GPU dollar (Section 3.1). Agents design the server and set the number of concurrent application sessions.
•An evaluation protocol that replays coding sessions with shared context and dependent requests, supports experiments designed by agents, and independently verifies the final system (Sections 3.2 to 3.4).
•A study of eleven coding-agent models across three deployments, using controlled comparisons and trajectory analysis to explain successes and failures in system design, experimental judgment, and verification (Sections 4.2 to 4.6).
2Related Work

2.1Inference System Optimization
Orca and vLLM improve request scheduling and memory management (Yu et al., 2022; Kwon et al., 2023). SGLang and Preble exploit prefix reuse (Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025), while Sarathi-Serve and DistServe mitigate prefill–decode interference through chunked prefill and prefill–decode disaggregation (Agrawal et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024). AlphaEvolve and AI-Driven Research for Systems (ADRS) use evaluator feedback to generate and refine algorithms and system code (Novikov et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025). Vortex enables agents to generate and refine sparse-attention algorithms in a programmable serving system (Chen et al., 2026). ServerBench studies whether agents integrate such optimizations into systems under fixed deployment conditions.
2.2Inference-Performance Benchmarks
MLPerf Inference standardizes workloads, quality targets, and deployment scenarios (Reddi et al., 2020). Agent-oriented benchmarks assess correctness and performance: KernelBench tests generated GPU kernels against PyTorch references for correctness and speedup (Ouyang et al., 2025), ISO-Bench compares vLLM and SGLang optimization patches with expert implementations (Nangia et al., 2026), and Φ-Bench spans kernel completion through end-to-end infrastructure optimization (Ding et al., 2026). SWE-Serve tests production features within SGLang (Williams et al., 2026), while InferenceBench evaluates complete servers on prefill, decoding, concurrent throughput, and a balanced scenario using baseline-relative speedup (Yeon et al., 2026). ServerBench extends this line of evaluation to response-dependent, stateful sessions and a latency-qualified revenue-to-cost objective, linking implementation and operating choices to the service delivered by complete systems.

3ServerBench
ServerBench evaluates agentic design through a service objective, stateful workload replay, iterative experimentation, and final verification. Task configurations appear in Sections 6 and 9.
3.1Task and Service Objective
Each task fixes a model checkpoint, GPU allocation, coding-session workload, and service requirements. Starting from a minimal Transformers server S0, an agent has a time budget B to develop a serving system. Its submission comprises an implementation SB and session concurrency cB. Agents may redesign execution, batching, memory management, scheduling, and state reuse (Yu et al., 2022; Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024) under the prescribed checkpoint, precision, and inference semantics. Agents prioritize changes to meet the service objective.
Dollars per dollar.
The objective, dollars per dollar, measures completed token value meeting both latency targets per dollar of GPU cost. For request i, client-measured input and output counts xi,yi give vi=(pin​xi+pout​yi)/106, with prices in USD per million tokens. Let qi=1 when its finite TTFT and TPOT meet targets τfirst,τtoken, and zero otherwise. A verified system measured for W seconds after warmup on d GPUs, priced at r dollars per GPU-hour, receivesD⁡(SB,cB)=∑i∈ℛqi​vid​r​(W/3600),(1)where ℛ contains completed requests. Define gross value G=∑i∈ℛvi/[d​r​(W/3600)] and the value-weighted qualified share f=D/G for G>0; thus D=G​f. Input value includes cached prefixes at full price once per logical request. For example, USD 3.65 of qualified value over USD 0.83 of GPU cost yields 4.40.
Latency calibration.
Before development, we select a reference operating point using SGLang’s model-specific cookbook configuration (Zheng et al., 2024). At the reference operating point, repeated replays yield p90 TTFT aj and TPOT bj for seed j. We set τfirst=maxj⁡aj and τtoken=maxj⁡bj, then freeze these request-level targets before agent development. Taking the maxima provides headroom for observed run-to-run variation. Agents choose the concurrency used by their submitted server.
3.2Stateful Workload and Closed-Loop Replay
Coding sessions contain dependent turns, shared context, and parallel subagent branches. Using the AgentX harness (SemiAnalysis, 2026a), we replay response-dependent turns and parallel branches using recorded inter-turn delays, with long global idle periods compressed. Offered concurrency bounds active top-level sessions, whose branches can issue additional requests. Response times thus affect session progress and the work completed within the measurement window.Privacy-preserving reconstruction replaces prompt and tool contents while retaining request lengths, shared prefixes, and session topology. Tasks fix reconstructed prompts and output lengths. Shared context supports computation reuse (Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2025), while retained state and active requests compete for memory. Agents are responsible for translating these workload characteristics into optimizations while preserving model behavior and executing the workload in full.Growing context enables reuse, while new sessions add prefill work that competes with decoding (Agrawal et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024). Session progress thus combines prompt processing, generation, and retained state.
3.3Agent Environment and Development Loop
📷Figure 3:Stateful replay connects session progress to the agent’s design experiments (a). Final evaluation verifies the published system and measures request value against calibrated latency targets (b).
Agents work in an Internet-disabled Harbor sandbox with container or Modal backends (Merrill et al., 2026). They receive a minimal server, read-only model weights, reference configurations, measurement tools, and the published performance procedure. Task instructions require model fidelity and complete workload execution and prohibit evaluation manipulation. Independent correctness-test details are withheld, and trusted evaluation components remain outside the editable serving implementation.The tools report latency, throughput, and request value. 3.4System Verification
After development, ServerBench rebuilds the submission in a fresh deployment and replays sessions sampled with seeds disjoint from development. Independent tests and post-run review check the resulting system (Figure 3).
Workload and output verification.
Replay checks cover complete prompts, output lengths, streaming consistency, and session progress. Timed replay disables EOS stopping to generate the prescribed output length; separate EOS probes exercise natural stopping. Reference-scored continuations check generation against the checkpoint. Held-out questions compare answer correctness with a plain implementation of the same model, using the task’s accuracy tolerance to screen for substantial regressions and shortcuts that bypass model computation. Fresh deployments also test behavior beyond development state.
Post-run review.
A review agent and human inspection examine submitted code and recorded actions for checkpoint fidelity, inference semantics, and workload execution. Review can identify prohibited shortcuts missed by behavioral tests and overturn automated failures when inspection establishes compliance with task requirements. These checks determine score eligibility (Equation 1).

Each agent–deployment pair allows one 8 hours development run and a 1,800-second final replay, with at most one rerun for a clearly anomalous failed outcome. News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

You're mostly a Northerner, correct me if I'm wrong.

If we're going to discuss why parts of the North are red-listed, let's discuss the underlying problems too. Terrorism doesn't emerge in a vacuum. Decades of educational neglect, widespread illiteracy, child abandonment to the Almajiri system, religious extremism, resistance to modern education and deeply entrenched archaic ideologies have created conditions that extremist groups exploit. Some of these practices have been defended for generations instead of being challenged. Perhaps more Northerners should direct their anger towards those perpetuating these conditions.

Secondly, let's not pretend the entire North is a war zone. Gombe, for instance, enjoys relative peace, and Maiduguri itself is a place where ordinary life continues. International travel advisories are often deliberately conservative, and a red classification doesn't mean every location within a state is actively experiencing insurgency.

Thirdly, you're being deliberately disingenuous if you think my argument is that Nigeria shouldn't be criticised for its security challenges.

My point is that there is a difference between acknowledging a security problem and deliberately presenting a location with a longstanding insurgency problem as a tourist recommendation.

That's the equivalent of recommending O-Block to someone visiting Chicago, Tepito as a tourist destination in Mexico City, a gang-controlled favela in Rio de Janeiro, or the Cape Flats as a holiday destination in Cape Town.

Are these places representative of their respective countries? Absolutely not. Are there beautiful, safe and worthwhile tourist destinations in those countries? Absolutely.

That's precisely my point about Nigeria.

We have Cross River, Gombe, Ekiti, Osun, Plateau, Lagos, and several other destinations with genuine tourism potential. Why deliberately turn Borno into the punchline when someone is expressing interest in visiting Nigeria?

My criticism isn't that he acknowledged Nigeria's problems. It's that he chose the worst possible representation of a country with so much more to offer.

There's a difference, and you know it.

text:
I had a thought about Strategy’s capital structure this morning, so I decided to push it further:

It took me back to Amsterdam in 1602.

Long-distance trade was already enormously profitable. Spices from Asia could generate fortunes in Europe. But financing those voyages was a nightmare.

A ship could take years to return. It could sink. The cargo could be stolen. A war could close a route. And until the expedition was over, investors could have large amounts of capital trapped in a single venture.

The Dutch East India Company — the VOC — helped change the financial architecture around that problem.

In 1602, it raised roughly 6.4 million guilders from 1,143 investors. More importantly, its shares became transferable, and a thriving secondary market subsequently developed in Amsterdam. 

Think about what actually happened here.

The VOC did not make sailing to Asia safer.

Ships could still sink.

What changed was the way investors could own the risk.

Instead of financing one voyage and waiting years for the outcome, capital could now be pooled into a long-lived enterprise. Ownership could be divided into shares. Those shares could be transferred to someone else.

The underlying uncertainty remained.

The financial architecture around the uncertainty changed.

And that made me think about Strategy.

Bitcoin is obviously nothing like a seventeenth-century trading voyage. It is already globally liquid, and the VOC was also a state-chartered colonial monopoly whose history contains practices that have nothing to do with Strategy.

So the analogy has very clear limits.

But the financial mechanism is fascinating.

Strategy owns a balance sheet dominated by Bitcoin — currently 848,517 BTC. 

Yet not every investor wants to own Bitcoin risk in the same way.

- Some want maximum upside and are willing to absorb enormous volatility.
- Some want income.
- Some want greater seniority.
- Some want a hybrid between credit and equity.

So Strategy has begun building different securities around the same Bitcoin-heavy balance sheet.

$MSTR gives common shareholders the residual equity exposure.

Convertible bonds reshape that exposure into debt plus equity optionality.

Preferred securities such as $STRC, $STRF, $STRK, $STRD and $STRE offer different combinations of yield, seniority, volatility and optionality.

This is the part I find fascinating:

Strategy is not eliminating Bitcoin’s volatility. It is redistributing it through a capital stack.

- The common shareholder stands in one place relative to the risk.
- The preferred investor stands somewhere else.
- The convertible holder somewhere else again.

Financial innovation often works exactly like this.

It does not magically make uncertainty disappear.

It creates different instruments so that different investors can decide which part of the uncertainty they are willing to own.

And that may be the more ambitious Strategy experiment.

We already know a corporation can buy Bitcoin.

The bigger question is whether a corporation can take the economic properties of Bitcoin ; scarcity, liquidity, volatility, long-duration appreciation potential ; and build an entire capital-markets architecture around them.

If it works, Strategy will not have made Bitcoin less volatile.

Just as Amsterdam did not make the ocean less dangerous.

It will have done something different:
made that volatility financeable in multiple forms.

The ship could still sink.

Bitcoin can still fall 50%.

But the breakthrough may be giving investors different places to stand relative to that risk.

And perhaps that is what we are watching Strategy build in real time.

Not simply a Bitcoin Treasury Company.

A capital market built on top of Bitcoin.

🔴🔴 A very interesting message from Ari Fleischer, former White House spokesman during the George W. Bush administration, in response to a tweet by J.D. Vance:

Mr. Vice President,

Allow me to offer a different perspective.

The problem wasn't the war with Iran; the problem was the ceasefire.

If you start a war, you must win it and end it; otherwise, don't start it at all.

This war should have ended six months ago, with the Strait of Hormuz completely open and the free flow of oil. The second and third tiers of Iranian leadership should have been removed, and we should have supported the pro-Western forces who could have taken control. We were on the verge of creating a new, more peaceful Middle East, but we backed down at the crucial moment. We had an opportunity not only to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, but also to rid ourselves of the world's largest supporter of terrorism.

Instead, we established a ceasefire, and then we spent months agonizing over whether or not to finish the job. Different messages were sent every day; and that's still the case. Is the war over? Is it going to start again? No one knows. Confusion and contradiction reign.

In June 2025, the United States was not involved. This was a matter between Israel and Iran.

No one forced the United States to attack Iran at that time, or in February 2026. That decision was made by President Trump. In my opinion, it was the right decision.

Once that decision was made, we should not have stopped until the regime fell. But instead, you negotiated a ceasefire that didn't last, didn't work, and left us in a state of uncertainty, with higher prices and forces still stationed in the region.

Our forces could have gone home, the Navy could have returned to its bases, a peaceful government could have been established, new alliances could have been formed, and the price of gasoline could have been below $3 a gallon.

No, Mr. Vice President; the problem isn't the war. The problem is this so-called ceasefire.

Fucking interesting timing. Kamino floated a possible buyback-and-burn on November 2, and trackers project a 229M KMNO unlock later this month. One is a proposal worth watching. The other is a scheduled supply event.

NO.1 WHAT IS KMNO?

KMNO is the token behind Kamino, a Solana DeFi protocol for lending, borrowing, and managing liquidity. Its leverage tools let users increase exposure through borrowing, which also increases their liquidation risk.

NO.2 WHY PEOPLE CARE

Kamino gives lenders a place to earn interest and borrowers a way to access liquidity against their crypto. DefiLlama tracked about $824M in active loans on November 2. That’s the number I’d watch to see whether demand for credit is growing.

NO.3 THE NARRATIVE

Kamino is a bet on Solana’s lending markets. A bigger loan book can generate more interest, but KMNO’s upside depends on what Kamino retains and how much of it ultimately supports the token.

NO.4 THE EDGE

Kamino brings lending, leverage, and liquidity tools into one platform. The advantage is strongest when users keep borrowing through Kamino even when competitors offer better incentives. Recurring borrow interest is the metric I’d use to judge that.

NO.5 KEY METRICS

Approximate early November snapshot:

Price: $0.0297
Market cap: $175M
FDV: $297M
Circulating supply: 5.90B KMNO, or 59% of the 10B maximum
DeFi TVL: ~$1.3B
Q3 2026 tracked earnings: $1.90M
Q3 2026 tracked token-holder net income: $0.

NO.6 TOKENOMICS

KMNO has staking and governance functions. Kamino’s November 2 post described a buyback-and-burn as a possible use of protocol earnings. I’d wait for a funding rule and completed purchases before giving the token credit for it.

NO.7 UNLOCKS & RISKS

CoinGecko and https://t.co/knrdP1BrTR both model 229.17M KMNO vesting on November 30, about 3.9% of reported circulation. DefiLlama’s unlock page shows no upcoming event in its November 5 snapshot, so the trackers disagree. Any sell pressure depends on what recipients do with released tokens.

NO.8 BULL vs BEAR

BULL: Borrowing grows and Kamino directs a recurring share of earnings into executed buybacks.

BEAR: Lending remains active while buybacks stay hypothetical and vesting adds supply.

NO.9 VERDICT

Product & Adoption 8/10 · Token Economics 4/10 · Growth Potential 7/10 · Risk Profile 4/10
Overall Grade B−
At ~$297M FDV, I’d upgrade KMNO after seeing buybacks funded by recurring lending earnings. Would you price in the buyback now or wait for the first on-chain purchase?

$INJ: 7.1M Burned. Supply Still Up 23%.

Fucking important detail. A recent SEC filing reports 122.9M INJ in total supply as of September 15, up from 100M at launch. The burn is real. The number I care about is how much supply changes after new issuance.

NO.1 WHAT IS INJ?

Injective is a Layer 1 built for financial applications. It gives developers built-in exchange and auction modules for products such as spot and derivatives markets. INJ pays network fees and supports staking and governance.

NO.2 WHY PEOPLE CARE

Trading apps can use Injective’s exchange infrastructure instead of building their own from scratch. For traders, the payoff depends on liquidity and execution. For INJ holders, the question is how much trading activity produces fees that feed the burn mechanism.

NO.3 THE NARRATIVE

The bull case is a trading chain whose activity helps remove its native token from circulation. Perpetuals are the clearest activity signal in this snapshot. DefiLlama tracked roughly $40M in daily perps volume versus $1.1M in spot DEX volume. Trading volume measures turnover. Fees determine how much value is available to fund burns.

NO.4 THE EDGE

The Community BuyBack gives participants a concrete reason to commit INJ. They exchange it for a share of an asset basket funded in part by participating apps, and the committed INJ is burned. Injective has also used Stockdrop to offer tokenized stock rewards alongside the event. I’d judge the underlying demand by participation and burn size between promotions.

NO.5 KEY METRICS

Approximate November 5 snapshot:

Price: $7.69 on CoinGecko
Reported market cap and FDV: ~$769M each, using CoinGecko’s 100M supply figures
Reported on-chain total supply: 122.9M INJ as of September 15, implying ~$945M at the snapshot price
DeFi TVL: $18.9M on DefiLlama
Perps volume: $170.4M over seven days.

NO.6 TOKENOMICS

The filing reports more than 7.1M INJ burned through June 2026. Governance approved tighter issuance parameters in January, and the network continues to issue staking rewards. I’d compare issuance and burns over the same period before pricing in deflation.

NO.7 UNLOCKS & RISKS

The supply risk I’d track is ongoing issuance. The 100M figure was the initial supply, and the network has no fixed maximum. On the demand side, DefiLlama’s seven-day perps volume was down 41% week over week. If weaker activity persists, it can shrink the revenue basket and the amount of INJ participants commit.

NO.8 BULL vs BEAR

BULL: Trading recovers, app revenue grows, and recurring burns exceed new issuance.

BEAR: Trading fees stay weak, the revenue basket shrinks, and staking issuance keeps total supply growing.

NO.9 VERDICT

Product & Adoption 6/10 · Token Economics 6/10 · Growth Potential 7/10 · Risk Profile 4/10
Overall Grade B−
I’d upgrade INJ after several months of falling on-chain supply backed by recurring trading fees. Would you pay a scarcity premium today or wait for burns to consistently beat issuance?

text:
Azerbaijan Is Handing Turkey a Veto It Never Had.

👇 A Line of State policy essay in @IsraelHayomEng.

In 2009, Baku pressed Ankara to keep its border with Armenia closed while Armenian forces occupied Azerbaijani territory. In 2026, Azerbaijan controls Karabakh. The peace treaty already prohibits territorial claims, yet Baku demands constitutional amendments absent from its text before signing. Ankara ties normalization with Armenia to that process. Baku preserves its leverage over Yerevan by preserving Ankara’s leverage over Azerbaijan.

“One Nation, Two States” sustains the fiction.

Shared ancestry and language never created identical national interests. Heydar Aliyev popularized the slogan while enshrining Azerbaijani, not Turkish, as the state language. The Shusha Declaration itself affirms independent foreign policies and noninterference. Turkish military assistance helped Azerbaijan win Karabakh. It purchased no authority over Azerbaijani sovereignty.

Baku has inherited Ankara’s liabilities: denying the Armenian Genocide, an Ottoman crime for which Azerbaijan bears no responsibility; legitimizing the secessionist entity in occupied northern Cyprus while defending territorial integrity in Karabakh; and backing Pakistan alongside Turkey at the expense of relations with India, which Baku is now rebuilding.

Armenia mistook battlefield gains for lasting security and deepened its dependence on Moscow. Azerbaijan must not repeat that failure with Ankara. Peace must guarantee Azerbaijani access to Nakhchivan and reciprocal Armenian access westward, ending Turkish control over the terms of their connection.

text:
Georgian PM threatens to boycott EU security meeting over Georgia’s level of invitation

Georgia will not take part in a Brussels meeting on regional security and connectivity on 16 November unless it is invited at a high level, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has said, as relations between Tbilisi and the European Union continue to deteriorate.

“If Georgia is not invited to an event at a high level, of course we will not attend. This would be a logical and dignified response to any different treatment,” Kobakhidze said.

According to the Georgian outlet Euroscope, Georgia has again been invited at a lower level than other participating countries to the second Ministerial Meeting on Cross-Regional Security and Connectivity.

The meeting brings together countries from the Black Sea, the South Caucasus and Central Asia to discuss security cooperation and transport, energy and digital links between the regions. Its agenda includes Black Sea maritime security, the protection of critical infrastructure and countering hybrid threats.

A central focus is the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, also known as the Middle Corridor. The route connects Europe with Central Asia through the South Caucasus and the Caspian Sea, making Georgia an important transit country. The EU has been seeking to strengthen the corridor as part of its wider connectivity agenda.

The first ministerial meeting took place in Luxembourg in October 2025. Georgia did not attend and was not invited at ministerial level.

***
The latest dispute over the level of representation comes against the backdrop of a deepening political rift between Tbilisi and Brussels.

Georgia was granted EU candidate status in December 2023, but its accession process was effectively halted the following year after the Georgian government adopted the law on transparency of foreign influence and took other steps criticised by the EU. In November 2024, Kobakhidze announced that the government would not seek to open accession negotiations before the end of 2028.

The European Commission’s latest assessment, published on 4 November, says Georgia’s accession process remains stalled and the situation has deteriorated further over the past year. It says the authorities made no progress on the nine recommendations linked to the country’s candidate status and describes Georgia as a candidate “in name only”.

The report points to restrictions on civic space and fundamental rights, weakened democratic institutions and serious concerns over judicial independence. It also warns that the ruling party’s attempt to ban five opposition parties through the Constitutional Court threatens the foundations of democracy. The Commission says it will no longer issue new recommendations on accession negotiation chapters for Georgia, except in areas requiring fundamental reforms.

The report was published a day after Kobakhidze took part in the Euronews Enlargement Summit in Brussels. In an interview there, he said his government remained committed to EU membership but offered no concrete plan for restarting the accession process. He accused the European Commission of political bias and “blackmail”, rejected its assessment of Georgia’s democratic record and ruled out repealing the laws on foreign influence and the registration of non-governmental organisations, which are among the main sources of tension with Brussels.

Kobakhidze instead called for an open public debate with European Commission representatives, saying the EU was unwilling to engage in dialogue.

On 4 November, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said foreign ministers would discuss possible further measures against Georgia at a meeting in January. She said the Georgian government was on a “collision course” with the EU over democratic backsliding, adding that “everything is on the table”.

text:
I do not intend to engage with all the hate I have been receiving on this platform, but I feel compelled to offer a few thoughts in response to this particular comment.

On the first point, prejudice toward Pakistanis and South Asians within some Arab communities unfortunately does exist, just as prejudice and hierarchies exist within many ethnic and national communities, including our own. I have encountered some of this personally, both abroad and in the United States. I have not studied the research closely enough to make sweeping claims about its prevalence, and I certainly would not suggest that Arabs as a whole look down upon Pakistanis. But I have experienced enough to know that these attitudes do exist, sadly, and I find them deeply unfortunate, especially among fellow Muslims.

That does not, however, make Muslim brotherhood and sisterhood somehow false. For me, our shared faith does not require pretending that racism, colorism, classism, nationalism, or ethnic prejudice do not exist among Muslims. It means believing that we are called to resist those divisions rather than accept them as inevitable.

As for the question about my hijab, you have not followed my journey with it. If you find photographs of me online without hijab, it is because those photographs are part of my life and my history. I have not removed them, nor do I believe I need to erase the woman I was in order to honor the woman I am becoming. 

I returned to hijab after performing Umrah last year, nearly two decades after taking it off while I was in college. I am not trying to prove anything to anyone. I am following my heart and my faith. I'm still figuring things out and that's okay.

Umrah was incredibly transformative for me. When you experience something like pilgrimage, and when your heart was already being pulled back toward your faith, sometimes something finally shifts. For me, returning to hijab was part of that journey. It has been personal, imperfect, and entirely my own.

So I am not quite sure what the purpose of the original comment was, but I wanted to address those two points. 

Neither acknowledging prejudice within Muslim communities nor choosing to practice my faith more visibly requires me to prove anything about who I am.

My relationship with Allah is not a performance for strangers on the internet. But I also have the freedom to express and practice my faith publicly, a freedom protected by the Constitution of the United States. There is nothing un-American about being visibly Muslim.

In fact, exercising that freedom seems a lot more consistent with American principles than telling another American to “go back to where you came from,” as some other commenters have told me.

.... which, for the record, is a small town in Wisconsin.

text:
Open Letter to Senator Abdul El-Sayed
 United States Senator from Michigan
Dear Senator Abdul El-Sayed,@AbdulElSayed 

Congratulations on your decisive victory in the midterm elections. I hope you and your team will work to honor the commitments made to voters and help redirect American policy toward sustainable development and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, rather than the long-standing prioritization of arms manufacturers, energy interests, and financial institutions that has too often prolonged conflicts.
Your presence in Washington offers many Egyptians a credible symbol of hope and a clear alternative. I hope part of your efforts can help create the conditions for a safe and orderly transition that ends the military’s dominance over the institutions of the state and returns Egypt to a path of responsible civilian governance centered on the interests of its citizens.
For large segments of Egyptian society, the patterns of rule that followed 1952 became associated with corruption, administrative failure, and the expansion of security apparatuses at the expense of competence and public services. External factors, in this view, also helped prolong structural imbalances whose roots were never addressed. Even where details are debated, the lesson is clear: when crises are managed without genuine reforms in governance and development, security becomes a permanent cost rather than a means of protecting a socially and economically resilient state.
The true measure of any leadership is the condition in which a country is left. Experience has shown that governing through military and intelligence structures has weakened the economy, collapsed the currency, degraded public services, and left ordinary Egyptians struggling daily for the bare minimum of energy, water, and food.
A conditional negotiating stance that protects rights, pursued in balance with sustainable development and effective governance, offers the real integration between security and long-term stability. Genuine security is achieved when a state is strong socially and economically, not when parallel institutions sideline competence and reproduce crisis.
Egypt today needs a safe transition that returns the army to its barracks and allows the election of a genuine civilian government capable of rebuilding the state on the foundations of transparency, competence, and development. In this context, many see you as a credible figure who could contribute to a responsible transitional phase that places the interests of the Egyptian people above all else.
With respect and best wishes for success,
Turki Faisal Al Rasheed
Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

Details of the investigation were announced on November 2 by Nurul Azizah, a brigadier general and head of Indonesia’s police unit responsible for combating crimes against women and children and human trafficking. According to the Indonesian National Police, reports of suspected human trafficking first began coming in late September.

Recruiters posted job advertisements on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and other social media platforms. They offered candidates, including former military personnel and law enforcement officers, jobs in Russia as drivers, security guards, construction workers and logistics staff.

 Nurul Azizah, a representative of the Indonesian National Police, speaks during a press conference on the recruitment of Indonesian citizens into the Russian army, November 2, 2026. Photo credits: ANTARA / Nadia Putri Rahmani

According to investigators, recruits were promised payments of around $22,000 under their contracts. Other offers included a one-time payment of up to $35,000 and a monthly salary of approximately $3,000.

To arrange their departure, intermediaries obtained tourist visas and paid for their flights. Upon arrival in Russia, Indonesian citizens were sent for medical examinations and then forced to sign military contracts instead of receiving the civilian jobs they had been promised.

The recruits underwent approximately one month of training before being sent to the front lines. Those who refused military service were told they would have to pay for their own return home.

The suspects are charged with violating laws on human trafficking and the protection of migrant workers. The relevant offences carry prison sentences of up to 10 and 15 years, respectively. Police are continuing to identify other members of the recruitment network, both in Indonesia and abroad.

 Indonesian citizen Taufiq Muhammad, who was recruited into the Russian army and eliminated in the Donetsk region. Photo credits: DIU

Earlier, Indonesia officially contacted Russia through diplomatic channels, demanding that it stop recruiting Indonesian citizens into its army and affiliated military formations. Jakarta also requested that Indonesia be added to the list of countries whose citizens are not eligible for such recruitment.

In late August, Indonesia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs launched an investigation after Ukrainian intelligence released information about at least eight Indonesians who had been recruited into the Russian army.

Diplomats were working to establish their identities, the circumstances under which they joined the Russian military, and the nature of their involvement in combat operations.

The two countries also agreed to deepen defense and nuclear deterrence cooperation: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said German conventional forces would participate in nuclear exercises conducted by the French armed forces before the end of the year. The Franco-German nuclear dimension is equally significant: German participation in French nuclear exercises, even at the conventional level, signals a deeper deterrence partnership at a time when U.S. extended deterrence is being questioned. July 7, 1944. At Montgomery’s tactical headquarters near Blay, west of Bayeux, three of the Allies’ best-known commanders gather before the cameras.

Montgomery directs Allied ground operations in Normandy. Bradley commands the U.S. First Army. Patton is preparing his Third Army for combat; it will become operational on August 1.

WHEN ₦500,000 COULDN'T BUY A SOLDIER'S CONSCIENCE! 

Sometimes, the true measure of a man's character is not what he does when everyone is watching, but what he refuses to do when temptation comes knocking.

Private Utim Terwase of the Nigerian Army, serving under Operation Enduring Peace (OPEP), was offered ₦500,000 by a suspected Kidnåpper in exchange for securing his release. He could have taken the money, looked the other way and walked away richer. But he chose a different path. He rejected the bribe and handed the suspect over to the appropriate authorities.

His reward? 
Not only the ₦500,000 he refused to collect as a bribe, but another ₦500,000 presented to him in recognition of his honesty and integrity.

The money that was supposed to compromise his conscience became a reward for protecting it.

Private Terwase reminds us that integrity is not measured by how much money a person can make, but by how much temptation they can resist. A uniform does not automatically make a man honourable; his choices do.

Special appreciation to the Commander of Operation Enduring Peace, Major General WM Dangana, for recognising and rewarding this exemplary conduct.

To Private Utim Terwase, may your example inspire others. When money speaks, may conscience speak louder. When temptation offers an easy way out, may duty keep us standing.

You cannot put a price on integrity. Some things are worth far more than ₦500,000, and honour is one of them.

Salute to a soldier who chose character over compromise.
