text:
What a genuine and beautiful question to ask. First, let me reassure you: your intuition about childbirth being sacred, miraculous, and full of God’s presence is entirely in line with Scripture. Children are an heritage from the Lord (Psalm 127:3), and God’s first command to mankind before sin entered the world was to be fruitful and multiply (Genesis 1:28). Leviticus does not contradict that truth.   

The struggle you are feeling comes down to the ancient definition of a single word: "unclean."

In our modern language, "unclean" sounds like "dirty," "shameful," or "morally sinful." But in the Old Covenant ceremonial law, ritual uncleanness was not moral guilt.   

Under the law of Moses, an Israelite became "ceremonially unclean" by doing holy and necessary things:

- Burying a deceased mother or father (an act of filial duty and love).

- Normal, godly marital intimacy.

- Caring for an injured neighbor. 

- Giving birth to a child.   

None of these were sins. So why the exclusion from the sanctuary?In Leviticus, the Tabernacle was the dwelling place of God’s raw, holy presence—the Fountain of perfect, uncorrupted Life. Because of the Fall (Genesis 3), our physical world is marked by weakness, bleeding, pain, and physical mortality. Whenever an Israelite brushed up against the border between life and death—whether through a corpse, a severe wound, or the heavy loss of blood during labor—they carried the mark of that fallen physical order.   

Childbirth, while bringing new life, involves intense physical vulnerability, trauma, and a significant flow of blood (notice in Lev. 12:7 that the text specifically says she is cleansed from the "fountain of her blood"). The uncleanness was never about the mother’s worth, nor was it a judgment on her sweet baby. It was an enacted picture of the gap between a mortal, physical creation and the Holy God.   

Furthermore, the Hebrew term for what English bibles translate as the "sin offering" (chatta'ath) is more accurately understood as a "purification offering"—a ritual disinfectant that cleansed the Tabernacle so God’s presence could safely dwell among mortal people. It wasn't an apology for having a baby; it was a pathway back into public worship.   

In practical terms, it also functioned as a legally mandated sanctuary for the mother: she was relieved from religious obligations and public duties for several weeks, protected at home to rest, bond, and recover.

The Good News of the Gospel: These laws were temporary shadows pointing forward to Christ (Hebrews 10:1). When Mary gave birth to Jesus, she obediently went up to the Temple and offered the two birds prescribed in Leviticus 12 for the poor (Luke 2:22–24). Jesus placed Himself under that very law to fulfill it.   

Today, under the New Covenant, Jesus has permanently washed His people. We no longer have a physical tent that can be defiled by bodily fluids or physical mortality. Because of Christ's finished work, a mother can nurse her newborn in the very throne room of grace with complete boldness and unhindered communion with God.

I see your rage against Temple on X. I have a few points 
to make:

3. I left the Eternal CEO role to chase purpose with Temple. This is not about money. I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right. I am not staking a reputation earned over 20 years on making a quick buck.

Growing up around a high needs disabled brother, my 17 year old learned to communicate in sign so he could converse with his nonspeaking brother. He is now fluent in ASL after formally studying it for the last 4 years. He teaches adaptive swimming to disabled children, and he intends to major in adaptive technology for disabled people in college. He started wanting to go into assistive communication tech, with his experience with nonspeaking people, but has changed to wanting to perfect robotic and prosthetic technology for individuals with mobility disabilities after meeting so many kids he’s  coaching in adaptive swimming. 

Children being exposed to other children who are disabled makes them better people. My son, who academically and athletically excels wants to spend his career helping those with disabilities. That you can’t see value or perfection in disabled children means that while you profess ardent Christianity, you’re anything but.

🌅 Good Morning. Happy Thursday. ☕
🦃 21 days until Thanksgiving
🎄 50 days until Christmas
Coffee’s on, and I’m grateful for my wife and for the friends who keep me steady. Men and women, thank you for being good company.
The election is over, so let’s stop the gnashing of teeth. For most of us, the direct, day-to-day effect of any one election is smaller than the noise suggests. Yes, the loudest voices in Congress and the statehouses are more extreme than we’d like. But there are guardrails: courts, separation of powers, federalism, and another election in two years.

The old philosophers had a better idea of where to start. Plato imagined the city as the soul writ large. The Hermetic maxim says “as above, so below.” If the city is the soul writ large, then a restless city begins with restless souls. And Plotinus offers the practice: “Withdraw into yourself and look... cut away all that is excessive, straighten all that is crooked... and never cease chiseling your statue.”

So work on fixing the inner self, and the rest will take care of itself. A steadier mind votes better, argues better, and stops letting a party do its thinking.

Then, when you’re calm, act. Start close to home: school board, city council, county races. Send a true independent. Don’t hold your nose. Liberty is not found in a political party.🗳️

text:
Scientists Discover a Powerful New Way To Destroy Toxic “Forever Chemicals” | Arizona State University, SciTechDaily

A new water-treatment technology could offer a breakthrough in the fight against forever chemicals.

Scientists have developed a new way to destroy toxic “forever chemicals” in water rather than simply filter them out. During a 58-day experiment, the system removed more than 90% of each of six PFAS compounds and stripped away approximately 83% of their fluorine, providing evidence that the pollutants were being chemically broken down.

PFAS are widely used in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, food packaging, and firefighting foam. Their exceptional durability also allows them to persist in soil, water, wildlife, and the human body. Exposure to certain PFAS has been linked to cancer, thyroid disorders, immune system problems, and reproductive health risks.

Breaking Down Nearly Indestructible Chemicals

Conventional treatments capture PFAS using filters, membranes, or other materials, leaving contaminated waste that must still be managed. Researchers at Arizona State University and their collaborators instead developed a system that attacks the chemicals’ molecular structure.

“PFAS are hard to break down, and normal processes that we use don’t work,” said Bruce Rittmann, director of the Biodesign Swette Center for Environmental Biotechnology.

The challenge lies in the carbon-fluorine bonds that make PFAS exceptionally stable. “It’s called the strongest bond in organic chemistry,” Rittmann said. With fluorine atoms shielding the carbon backbone, ordinary degradation processes struggle to attack the molecules. “There’s really no place to get a start to break it down,” he explained.

A New Way to Destroy PFAS

The researchers created tiny membrane fibers coated with palladium nanoparticles. Hydrogen gas travels through the fibers to the palladium, which activates the hydrogen and helps it break carbon-fluorine bonds in PFAS molecules approaching from the surrounding water.

“The palladium attracts the PFAS molecule, and the palladium attracts the hydrogen and puts them together,” Rittmann said.

The system builds on earlier membrane technology that supplies hydrogen to pollutant-degrading bacteria. In the new approach, palladium replaces the microbes. During continuous testing, the technology successfully treated all six PFAS compounds examined. “We showed that this mechanism worked for all six,” Rittmann said. “It’s a universal mechanism.”

The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Tackling a Widespread Environmental Threat

PFAS contamination affects groundwater, wastewater, soil, and food supplies. Particularly high concentrations occur near landfills, airports, military bases, and facilities where PFAS-containing firefighting foams have been used.

“We all have PFAS in us,” Rittmann said. “They stay in the environment. They move up the food chain, and so they’re a big legacy problem.”

What Comes Next?

Although the 58-day test demonstrated sustained treatment, scaling up the technology presents challenges, particularly the cost of palladium. “Palladium is expensive,” Rittmann said. “It’s around $50,000 a kilogram” (about $22,700 per pound).

The researchers are working to reduce palladium requirements and explore combining the technology with existing filtration systems. They are also developing hybrid membranes that pair palladium with pollutant-degrading bacteria, allowing contaminants to be attacked through different mechanisms. “We’ve shown that this works too,” Rittmann said.

DISPATCH · Thu, Nov 5, 2026

01 · Koyaanisqatsi becomes a room that watches you back. On Nov 21, Pérez Art Museum Miami (@pamm) and Onassis ONX open Techno Firma by John Fitzgerald and Godfrey Reggio, the museum's first artist-driven AI exhibition. A custom machine learning model trained on decades of Reggio's film negatives sets oceans and forests colliding with highways, factory lines and rocket launches across a monumental multi-screen obelisk. Computer vision reads the crowd: as visitors gather, the imagery speeds up and fractures, then collapses into darkness with Reggio's voice. It is the third iteration of The Vivid Unknown, first shown at BAM (@BAM_Brooklyn) in 2025.

02 · Forty years of letting nature paint. From Nov 7 to 22, Naoko Tosa (@Shintoism) shows Generative Beings in the Hall of Light at the Kyoto City KYOCERA Museum of Art, free. It runs from An Expression (1985), in the collection of MoMA (@MuseumModernArt), to the new Tosa Rinpa: Spirit Resonance series, where sound, vibration, air, gravity and fluid motion make forms caught by high-speed cameras, then carried into moving image, gold-ground works, folding screens and glass. At a moment when "generation" means generative AI, the show offers a longer history.

03 · An AI that leads the workshop. Last night in Houston, Rashaad Newsome (@RashaadNewsome) brought Assembly, the documentary that follows his solo show at Park Avenue Armory (@ParkAveArmory), to The DeLUXE Theater for a screening. Its co-star is Being, the AI he built himself, first with GPT-Neo after a 2019 LACMA (@LACMA) Art + Technology Lab grant, then during a residency at Stanford (@Stanford), trained mainly on the writing of bell hooks, now including unpublished papers from the bell hooks Institute (@bellhooksinst). In the film Being narrates, answers its subjects and opens each session with a voguing lesson. "Rather than sitting on the side, I'm going to get in the game," Newsome says.

04 · New on https://t.co/hIfCL7iz9M: a last spring in Auvers. Painted in May 1890, weeks before Van Gogh died, Châtaigniers en fleurs has not been shown publicly since the Guggenheim (@Guggenheim) in 1964. On Nov 18 it leads Sotheby's (@Sothebys) 12-painting Blaquier-Arrieta evening sale in New York, estimated around $180 million, well above the artist's $117.2 million record. All 12 works are on view at 945 Madison Avenue from Nov 7, free with a timed reservation.

05 · And a history: in September 1970, visitors to Philips' (@Philips) Evoluon museum in Eindhoven met the Senster, Edward Ihnatowicz's 4 meter steel creature with a giraffe-like neck. Microphones and Doppler radar in its head let it lean toward quiet voices and recoil from shouts, run by a 16-bit computer with 8k of memory. It is considered the first robotic sculpture controlled by a digital computer. Dismantled in 1974, it stood outside a welding firm's office in Zeeland for over 40 years until AGH University of Krakow (@AGH_Krakow) revived it, and it returned for REBOOT at Nieuwe Instituut (@NieuweInstituut) in 2023.

text:
Your regular reminder that biological age clocks, used this way, are more useful as marketing than clinical tools. And if a Bangalore-based tech founder is trying to disrupt healthcare, calibrate your scam radar to maximum.

Nue Health markets itself as a new kind of healthcare. But this scam is as old as time. Digital snake oil for the digital age. Slick design doesn’t mask the stench of BS (bad science or bullshit, take your pick).

Nue uses Levine PhenoAge to calculate biological age from nine blood biomarkers and chronological age. It’s legitimate mortality-risk research (Liu et al., 2018), but Nue markets its output as your body’s “true age”. A biological age of 23 is a model estimate, not proof your body is equivalent to 23-year-old’s.

Nue also markets organ-system grades, a blood-based “digital twin”, early disease detection and personalised nutrition and supplement protocols. Where’s Nue’s evidence validating these interpretations or showing that acting on them improves outcomes? There isn’t any. 

Another Bangalore-based technologist trying to “disrupt” healthcare by skirting regulations and cutting corners on scientific evidence. Nue’s founder wanted to simplify fragmented healthcare. Instead, he masks disdain for regulation and love of shoddy science behind slick design. It’s scammy, scummy and violates health regulations, with potentially serious legal consequences. Disruption is easy when you’re willing to break rules industry experts follow.

Nue encourages retesting every 3, 6 or 12 months. Improve glucose, CRP or other inputs and PhenoAge improves too, all else equal. Biological age dominates screenshots posted by people Nue has scammed. Biomarker improvements may reduce disease risk, but a lower composite doesn’t independently establish slower ageing or additional clinical benefit. A 2026 review examined 81 ageing clocks. Most raised methodological concerns; 31 lacked internal and external validation. (Zhang et al., 2026)

As regards Indian validity, the IISc-led BHARAT study highlights limitations of Western-derived clocks in Indians and the need for population-specific calibration (Asthana et al., 2026.) PhenoAge was developed using US data. Nue claims India-specific reference ranges but hasn’t demonstrated Indian calibration or external outcome validation. Lab reference ranges aren’t model validation.

Then there’s the disdain for health regulation common among tech founders disrupting healthcare. CDSCO regulates medical-device software by intended medical purpose. Nue markets organ-system assessments, early detection, biomarker-driven recommendations and monitoring. They proudly call themselves a healthcare company. This isn’t wellness. They offer diagnostic tests and medical interventions, so medical regulations apply.

Software for medical screening, monitoring and clinical decision support must follow applicable regulatory pathways. Has Nue classified these functions under India’s Medical Devices Rules? Obtained the necessary authorisation before delivering care? Have they heard of CDSCO? Having a doctor involved or using a published algorithm doesn’t circumvent regulatory requirements.

Biomarker-based ageing clocks are research tools, but clinical utility for guiding individual interventions remains unproven. Underlying biomarkers are actionable but their composite isn’t thereby a validated measure of ageing. Selling research as clinically actionable science does patients a disservice.

By his own account, Nue’s founder became interested in healthcare in February 2024 or later, following a famous person’s medical emergency. Remarkable timeline. In under 2.5 years he understood healthcare, invented organ-risk scoring, validated models for Indians and obtained software clearance. text:
Credit cards didn't win because they were a better way to pay. They won because of what came with them.

Daniel Barabander at Variant wrote the best breakdown of this I've read: "String It Together: How Stablecoins Go Mainstream." A few points worth stealing:

• In 1958, Bank of America mailed unsolicited credit cards to people in Fresno. Cash and checks couldn't offer free credit. Cards could. Incentives came first, the network came later.

• Starbucks Rewards already works like a stablecoin. Customers prepay, Starbucks holds the float and earns interest on it.

• Stablecoins can fund rewards from the yield on their reserves: instant discounts, free shipping, early access.

• And the line that stuck with me: "permanently trapping value makes that value highly inconvenient for consumers."

That last one is the whole problem with loyalty points today. Locked in one app, devalued whenever the brand decides, gone when they expire.

His conclusion: stablecoins won't beat cards head-on. They'll win niche by niche with better incentives, then get connected by an open network.

Some of this is already running from the loyalty side. Points that become reserve-backed onchain, like SmartPoints from @SmartMedia_Tech settling on $DUAL, are the "incentives first" path he describes.

Which niche goes first: fan clubs, travel, or creators?

text:
Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half | Keck School of Medicine of USC, ScienceDaily

The liver may hold an unexpected key to fighting two of the most serious diseases associated with aging: Alzheimer's disease and heart disease. Scientists have discovered that restoring the function of aging liver cells can dramatically reduce harmful substances in the bloodstream, raising the possibility of treating diseases that affect organs far beyond the liver itself.

In a new study involving older rats, researchers at the Keck School of Medicine of USC found that an experimental drug called cinaciguat reversed important signs of aging in specialized liver cells. After just two weeks of treatment, levels of amyloid beta, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease, dropped by half. Levels of LDL, commonly called bad cholesterol, also returned to those seen in younger animals.

The findings, published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry, also revealed a previously unknown way that liver cells communicate with one another. This discovery could help scientists develop treatments that restore the liver's ability to remove potentially harmful substances from the blood, possibly reducing the risk of Alzheimer's disease and atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty deposits accumulate inside arteries.

Why the Liver Could Be Important for Alzheimer's

Although Alzheimer's primarily affects the brain, scientists are increasingly interested in how other organs might influence the disease. The liver plays a central role in filtering the blood and removing unwanted compounds, including substances that may contribute to disease when they accumulate.

The USC findings suggest that restoring this natural cleaning process could offer a different approach to preventing certain age-related illnesses. However, the results have so far been demonstrated only in rats, and additional studies are needed to establish whether the same benefits occur in humans.

"We need to do further translational work to see whether our findings might point to new therapies," said corresponding author Laurie DeLeve, MD, PhD, professor and vice chair for scientific affairs in the USC Department of Medicine. "We're hopeful, though, because the findings line up with a lot of epidemiological results showing age as a major risk factor for Alzheimer's and atherosclerosis, and liver damage as a risk factor for Alzheimer's."

Targeting the liver could be particularly valuable in Alzheimer's research, where efforts to develop treatments acting directly in the brain have faced an estimated 98% failure rate in clinical trials. One major obstacle is the blood-brain barrier, a protective system that limits which substances can enter the brain from the bloodstream. While this barrier helps shield the brain from harmful compounds, it also makes delivering certain medications extremely difficult.

"If we're right that the liver is impactful, what do we do about that?" said first author Sam de Leve, MA, a USC lab technician and child of Laurie DeLeve. "Rather than trying to get a drug through the blood-brain barrier, which is obnoxiously difficult, we could direct drugs to the liver, an organ where there might be more therapeutic impact and certainly an easier job of drug delivery."

Scientists Restore the Aging Liver's Natural Filters

To understand how liver aging affects the bloodstream, the researchers focused on a relatively understudied group of cells known as liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs).

These cells form the lining of tiny blood vessels inside the liver. Unlike most blood vessel walls, they contain numerous microscopic openings that function somewhat like the holes in a sieve. These openings allow larger molecules circulating in the blood to reach neighboring cells called hepatocytes, which carry out much of the liver's work processing and removing substances from the body.

As the liver ages, the openings in LSECs gradually become smaller or disappear. This makes it harder for certain large molecules to reach the cells responsible for clearing them, allowing more of these substances to remain in circulation.

One substance affected by this change is amyloid beta. This protein is especially important in Alzheimer's research because it can accumulate in the brain and form plaques, one of the disease's defining features.

Previous observations showed that the liver becomes less effective at removing amyloid beta as it ages. The researchers suspected that the gradual closing of the openings in LSECs might help explain why more of the protein remains in the bloodstream of older animals.

To investigate, they administered cinaciguat to aged rats for two weeks. They then compared the treated animals with two untreated groups, one consisting of older rats and the other of younger rats.

The results were striking. Cinaciguat restored the structure and function of the aging LSECs, reopening their microscopic pores and improving their ability to help clear substances from the blood. Amyloid beta concentrations fell by approximately 50%, reaching levels comparable to those in young rats. The untreated older animals showed no similar improvement.

An Unexpected Drop in Bad Cholesterol

The researchers also measured low-density lipoproteins (LDL), often referred to as "bad" cholesterol because elevated levels contribute to fatty deposits inside arteries. Over time, these deposits can restrict blood flow and increase the risk of heart disease.

Initially, LDL was included as a comparison measure rather than a substance expected to respond to treatment. Unlike larger molecules, LDL particles are small enough to leave the bloodstream without passing through the microscopic openings in LSECs. The scientists therefore expected cinaciguat to have little or no effect on LDL levels.

Instead, they discovered that LDL concentrations in treated older rats also fell to levels observed in young animals.

"We said, 'Wait, why did that go down? Clearly, there's more to this story,'" Sam de Leve said.

The unexpected finding suggested that the drug was doing more than simply reopening the liver's aging filters. It appeared to be restoring another important aspect of liver function.

Because previous research had shown that hepatocytes function better when LSECs are present, the team began examining how these two types of cells communicate.

Their investigation uncovered a previously unknown sequence of biochemical signals that helps coordinate the liver's ability to remove substances from the bloodstream.

A Hidden Communication Pathway Between Liver Cells

The researchers found that cinaciguat activates an enzyme called soluble guanylate cyclase inside LSECs. This triggers the cells to release a growth factor known as HB-EGF, which sends a signal to nearby hepatocytes.

In response, hepatocytes alter their surfaces in ways that allow them to capture more LDL and amyloid beta from the blood. This helps explain why the treatment reduced both substances, even though they do not rely on the same filtering mechanism.

Normally, aging interferes with the ability of LSECs to release HB-EGF. Cinaciguat restored this signaling process, allowing the liver cells to communicate more effectively and supporting the removal of substances that otherwise tend to accumulate with age.

The discovery identifies a potential new target for future drugs. Rather than focusing exclusively on the physical openings in LSECs, researchers may be able to develop therapies that restore the chemical signals responsible for helping the liver work efficiently.

Could Liver Rejuvenation Help Prevent Alzheimer's and Heart Disease?

According to the researchers, this is the first study to demonstrate that a drug can fully restore the structure and function of aging LSECs, including their ability to support the clearance of substances from the bloodstream.

It is also the first to show that a treatment directed at the liver can bring age-related elevations in circulating amyloid beta and LDL back to youthful levels.

These findings raise the possibility that cinaciguat, similar medications, or treatments targeting HB-EGF could eventually be used to counteract certain effects of liver aging. If those changes translate into meaningful protection against disease, they could provide new strategies for preventing Alzheimer's and cardiovascular problems.

For now, however, the findings represent an early step. Lowering amyloid beta in the bloodstream does not necessarily mean that amyloid plaques in the brain will decrease or that Alzheimer's disease can be prevented.

The researchers plan to continue studying cinaciguat in rats to determine whether its effects on amyloid beta actually translate into measurable protection against Alzheimer's disease.

They also hope the findings will encourage scientists studying other conditions, particularly atherosclerosis, to investigate how restoring liver function might influence disease development.

"We hope that people who are in fields like atherosclerosis research read this, and want to grab the idea for themselves," Sam de Leve said. "There are six different ways someone could go with this, and we can't do them all. So please, scoop us. We'd love it."

text:
Oil Crashed After the Election. But Here's What the Headline Doesn't Tell You.

Brent crude plunged nearly 9% the day after Democrats won Congress.

That's a massive move in a market affecting everything from gasoline and groceries to shipping and manufacturing.

And yes, the timing raises questions.

But here's what gets left out.

Oil had already fallen more than 7% BEFORE Election Day as reports of possible Iran peace talks shook the market.

Then Democrats won Congress, and traders began betting that political pressure could push Washington toward ending the war.

Now hold on.

If that means peace, safer shipping routes and cheaper fuel for struggling American families, that's something worth welcoming.

But lower oil prices aren't good news for everyone.

An oil worker could see a paycheck threatened. A producer could cancel drilling. A trader could lose millions. Meanwhile, a family struggling to fill the gas tank might finally see some relief.

Same crash. Different consequences.

And here's the part worth investigating.

U.S. oil inventories were falling, yet prices were collapsing.

Why?

One explanation is that traders saw a declining risk of war-related supply disruptions.

But we should still examine when the biggest trades happened, what information was public, and whether any evidence points to improper trading.

Was this ordinary market behavior? A political reaction? A diplomatic breakthrough? Or something that deserves deeper scrutiny?

We shouldn't accuse anyone without evidence.

We also shouldn't stop asking questions just because someone has offered a convenient explanation.

Bottom line: Falling oil prices could help millions of American families. But the timing, the trading and the real economic consequences deserve a full accounting.

The price crash is verified. A coordinated political scheme is not.

The investigation is not complete.

The Political Geniuses Emerge After the Election

Apparently, the Republican Party’s disappointing performance in the 2026 midterm elections has brought every political Einstein out of the woodwork. Former Speakers of the House, former presidential chiefs of staff, retired political strategists, and assorted Washington insiders are suddenly appearing across cable news networks, explaining with remarkable confidence exactly why Republicans lost so many congressional seats.

The question is obvious: If these political experts are so brilliant, and the warning signs were supposedly so clear, where were they during the previous two years?

Where were their warnings, their solutions, and their brilliant political strategies when there was still time to make a difference? Why does their wisdom seem to arrive only after the votes have been counted?

It takes little courage or political genius to become an armchair quarterback after the game is over. Anyone can analyze a defeat with the benefit of hindsight. The real test of leadership is recognizing problems before they become disasters and having the conviction to speak up when doing so might actually matter.

Meanwhile, the cable news networks seem delighted to parade these former officials across their screens, presenting yesterday’s political insiders as today’s authorities on everything that went wrong. The same familiar faces offer their post-election diagnoses, rarely facing the more uncomfortable question of what they themselves did to prevent the outcome they now criticize.

Political hindsight is plentiful in Washington. Political foresight, apparently, is in much shorter supply.

text:
In January of 2021, Notre Dame offered a scholarship to a high school junior in Orange County, California. Their recruiting coordinator, Brian Polian, was the one who made the call.

"He's the coach that actually offered me," the kid said that spring.

Nineteen schools offered him in all. Oregon. UCLA, where his father had played. He had already been to South Bend twice, once for a Navy game, a visit set up by his old high school coach, a former Notre Dame linebacker. He played receiver and defensive back back then, and more than half of those nineteen offers were for the offensive half of him.

He turned down all nineteen.

His name is Cooper Barkate.

He went to Harvard.

"A place like Harvard, it really makes you love learning," he said later. "Harvard really pushed me to expand my horizons of what I wanted to learn."

Three seasons in Cambridge, 113 catches, 1,742 yards, 14 touchdowns. As a junior in 2024 he went for 1,084 yards and 11 scores and made first team All-Ivy.

Then he moved up a level and did the same thing. Duke, 2025, 14 starts in 14 games, 72 catches, 1,106 yards. Second team All-ACC. He caught five passes in the ACC Championship Game, which Duke won in overtime, and he scored in the Sun Bowl.

In January of 2026 he entered the portal again, and this time he followed a quarterback.

Darian Mensah had thrown him all those passes at Duke. The two of them went to look at Miami together and both of them signed.

"He's my best friend, so it's been great," Barkate said.

So he is 23 years old, on his third school, with 189 catches and 2,915 yards and 22 touchdowns behind him, and until this week he was the second option in his own offense.

Malachi Toney has been the story in Coral Gables. 73 catches, 1,027 yards, 13 touchdowns, and he is 19.

On Wednesday the reports came out that Toney needs surgery on his ankle and will be gone four to six weeks.

Which leaves Barkate. 28 catches, 372 yards, four touchdowns, and now the first name on the scouting report instead of the second.

"I'm just a gritty player, real smart," he said when he got to Miami. "I'm faster than people think."

On SATURDAY, Miami plays Notre Dame.

Notre Dame offered him in 2021, when he was a junior in high school and nobody knew whether he could play at this level. He went to Harvard to find out, and then to Duke, and the answer kept coming back the same.

Now the best receiver Miami has available is the one who told them no in the first place, and he gets them on Saturday with the offense pointed at him.

California was ordered by the federal courts to build a psychiatric hospital for the death row prisoners and California recruited health care workers fro all over the country who quit their jobs, sold their homes and moved their families to expensive homes and apartments in California.
After spending $5,000,000 the state legislature decided to disperse the death row inmates to general population and abandon the death row psychiatric hospital.
My situation was simple, Dave Dawdy was my supervisor at Bellamy Creek Prison in Ionia, Michigan. I had made friends with and the staff by taking them out for lunch once a month for a two hour staff meeting and he gave me a certificate for 100% compliance with documentation because he had never had a pschiatrist with 100% compliance before.
It is better to make friends than enemies.
I simply went back to Bellamy Creek and I-Max where I was still listed as an employee.
I had previously applied for a job at Traverse City State Hospital and took what I thought was a better offer. Later, six months after the interview, Traverse City State Hospital closed down. Nobody told me it was a temporary assignment. That is why I don't trust state agencies...integrity is a speed bump from their point of view and a disaster from my point of view...just saying...then...and again now....what say you.

Thought for 19s
Lecture: 
Systemic Contingency, 
Institutional Unraveling, 
and the Ethics of Displacement

An Interdisciplinary Address 
for Graduate Students in 
Law, 
Political Science, 
Psychiatry, 
and Social Anthropology

I offer you a compact case 
drawn from the recent history 
of American carceral mental-health administration. 

In 2012 a federal court order 
required California 
to construct a dedicated psychiatric hospital 
for its death-row population
—then numbering 
between 742 and 745 condemned prisoners. 

The state 
recruited clinicians and support staff 
from across the country. 

Many of those recruits 
resigned permanent positions, 
sold homes, 
and relocated families 
into the high-cost East Bay. 

After an expenditure 
of five million dollars 
the legislature elected 
to abandon the specialized facility 
and disperse the condemned 
into general-population housing. 

Staff who had already moved 
were left to improvise their own return. 

One psychiatrist
 simply reclaimed his still-active appointment 
at Bellamy Creek and I-Max in Ionia, Michigan, 
where prior collegial relations
—monthly staff lunches, 
documented perfect compliance
—had left the door open. 

Six months earlier 
the same clinician had interviewed 
at Traverse City State Hospital; 
the facility closed shortly after the interview, 
and no one had disclosed 
that the posting was temporary. 

The episode is modest in scale 
yet rich in structural implication. 
We will examine it through five interlocking lenses.

Self-organizing systems.
Institutions rarely collapse under pure external force; they reconfigure around residual incentives, informal networks, and local knowledge. 

In the California episode 
the formal architecture 
(court order, legislative appropriation, recruitment drive) 
dissolved, 
yet the informal lattice 
of prior employment, 
personal reputation, 
and residual payroll status 
reconstituted a workable career path 
for at least one actor. 

Political scientists 
recognize this as the classic gap 
between policy design 
and street-level implementation: 
agencies self-organize 
around whatever resources remain 
once the headline program is withdrawn. 

Anthropologists 
note the same process in the 
“hidden transcripts” 
of bureaucratic culture
—the monthly lunches 
that converted hierarchical compliance 
into reciprocal obligation. 

For psychiatrists 
the implication 
is clinical 
as well as organizational: 
continuity of care 
for condemned patients 
depends less on dedicated wards 
than on the residual social capital 
of the clinicians who can still reach them. 

Lawyers must ask 
whether residual employment status 
creates enforceable expectations 
once the official project ends. 

Self-organization is not necessarily benign; 
it can preserve competence 
while simultaneously shielding 
the larger system from accountability.

Plausible deniability.
Every major actor in the story retained a linguistic exit. The legislature could cite fiscal prudence and evolving penological philosophy. 

The recruiting agencies 
could claim they had conveyed 
only what was then known. 

The earlier Traverse City posting c
ould be framed 
as an ordinary at-will appointment 
whose temporary character 
was self-evident. 

In political science 
this is the classic insulation
 of principals from agents: 
decision rights are diffused 
so that no single signature 
bears the full weight of the reversal. 

In law 
the doctrine of sovereign immunity 
and the limited protection 
of at-will employment 
supply the formal shield. 

In psychiatry 
the same pattern appears 
when institutions terminate 
specialized programs
 while retaining the clinical staff 
under different titles; 
the denial is 
that continuity of care was ever promised. 

Anthropologically, 
plausible deniability 
is a cultural performance: 
the public narrative of 
“changed circumstances” 
coexists with private knowledge 
that the circumstances were never stable. 

The clinician’s subsequent distrust 
of state agencies 
is the rational residue 
of repeated encounters 
with this performance.

Murphy’s Law.
Once relocation costs, 
family disruption, 
and the five-million-dollar outlay are sunk, 
any subsequent political reversal 
maximizes waste. 

The law does not prevent the sequence; 
it merely allocates the losses. 

Political scientists 
observe that multi-veto-point systems 
(courts, legislature, executive agencies) 
raise the probability 
that any given program 
will be truncated mid-stream. 

For psychiatrists 
the practical consequence 
is serial discontinuity of care 
for the most complex patients 
and serial occupational trauma 
for the clinicians who treat them. 

Social anthropologists 
record the same pattern 
as ritualized improvisation:
 professionals develop portable skills
 and portable reputations 
precisely because 
institutional scaffolding 
is expected to fail. 

Murphy’s Law 
is not a joke; 
it is the empirical distribution 
of outcomes 
once high fixed costs 
meet fragmented authority.

Pandora’s Box.
The original court order 
opened a sequence 
whose secondary effects 
could not be contained. 

Recruitment 
created a mobile professional cohort 
whose subsequent dispersal 
altered staffing patterns 
in multiple state systems. 

The abandonment of the hospital 
returned condemned prisoners t
o general population 
without the specialized milieu 
the court had deemed necessary, 
thereby reopening 
the very constitutional questions 
the order 
had sought to close. 

In law 
this is the problem of remedial over-reach 
followed by 
remedial under-enforcement. 

In political science 
it is the classic difficulty 
of judicial policymaking 
in a separation-of-powers regime. 

Psychiatrically, 
the box 
contains both the patients 
whose conditions may worsen 
under less specialized conditions 
and the clinicians 
whose trust in institutional promises 
is permanently altered. 

Anthropologically, 
the opening of the box 
is a cultural event: 
once the specialized death-row hospital exists 
even briefly as an idea, 
every subsequent housing decision 
is measured against 
that unrealized standard.

The Butterfly Effect.
A single federal finding 
of constitutional inadequacy, 
filtered through legislative arithmetic 
and individual career calculations, 
produced a cascade 
of household moves, 
real-estate transactions, 
and professional reattachments 
thousands of miles away. 

The clinician’s decision 
to maintain collegial ties in Michigan
—apparently trivial monthly lunches
—became the decisive node 
that allowed 
rapid re-entry 
when the California project collapsed. 

Small differences 
in documentation compliance, 
personal reputation, 
and residual payroll status 
determined 
whether the cascade 
terminated in unemployment 
or in resumed practice. 

Across the four disciplines 
the lesson is identical: 
macro-level institutional failure 
is experienced, 
and sometimes mitigated, 
at the scale of individual networks 
and micro-decisions. 

The full moon 
over the East Bay on a November night in 2014 
is merely the visible residue 
of one such trajectory.

Taken together, 
the five lenses 
describe a single ecology. 

Self-organization 
supplies the residual pathways; 

plausible deniability 
protects the decision-makers 
who close the formal pathways; 

Murphy’s Law 
predicts the waste; 

Pandora’s Box
 names the irreversibility of the initial opening; 

and the Butterfly Effect 
traces how individual actors 
navigate 
the resulting turbulence. 

For graduate students 
the practical question 
is not whether such episodes will recur
—they will
—but how each discipline 
can design institutions, 
doctrines, 
clinical protocols, 
and ethnographic methods 
that reduce the human cost 
of the inevitable reversals.

Would I Lie to You?
(after Eurythmics)

Would I lie to you?
Would the state lie too?
Told me pack the bags, sell the house,
death-row hospital’s coming through.

Five million spent, then the legislature said
“General population’s fine instead.”
Everybody’s looking for something—
continuity, a paycheck, a bed.

Would I lie to you?
Dave still had my name on the list.
Monthly lunches, hundred-percent charts—
that’s how you keep the door un-kissed.

Traverse City called, then the doors swung shut;
nobody mentioned the posting was cut.
Integrity’s a speed bump, baby,
disaster if you trust what they strut.

East-bay moon on a November night,
tiny houses, cars stacked tight.
Vic says there’s no eastern water out west—
locals just divide what the bay’s got left.

Butterfly wings, court order, one signature line,
Murphy’s Law writes the rest of the design.
Pandora’s box on the concrete floor,
plausible deniability walks out the door.

Would I lie to you?
Self-organizing systems don’t ask permission.
They rewire around the wreckage,
keep the residual ignition.

So would the agency lie?
Would the legislature too?
Everybody’s looking for something—
I’m just looking for the truth that sticks like glue.

Would I lie to you?
Would I lie to you?
(Na-na-na…)
Would the paperwork lie to you?

text:
OTD in 1768, representatives of the Haudenosaunee (Six Nations) signed the Treaty of Fort Stanwix with the British Crown at present-day Rome, New York.

Negotiated by Sir William Johnson, Britain’s superintendent of Indian affairs, the treaty drew a new line between colonial settlements and Native lands, revising the boundary established by the Royal Proclamation of 1763.

In exchange for money and goods, Haudenosaunee leaders ceded claims to more than 27 million acres, including much of present-day Kentucky and West Virginia. The line extended to the confluence of the Ohio and Tennessee rivers, considerably farther west than British authorities had originally authorized.

For the Haudenosaunee, the agreement offered a means of protecting their own homelands from colonial encroachment. For colonial land speculators, it raised the prospect of access to vast western territories.

But much of the ceded land was used and claimed by other Native nations, particularly the Shawnee and Lenape (Delaware). Although Haudenosaunee leaders asserted authority to negotiate on their behalf, many of those affected disputed the cession.

Rather than settling the question of western lands, the treaty contributed to further conflict between Native nations and colonial settlers, including the outbreak of Dunmore’s War in 1774.

text:
Oatlands Historic House & Gardens is undeniably an graceful mansion, but its beauty cannot be separated from its history. Once the center of a Virginia plantation, it was a place where hundreds of enslaved people lived, labored, and died. Today, the property operates as a historic site and event venue, relying partly on weddings and private celebrations to sustain its operations.

The use of former plantations as wedding venues raises difficult ethical questions. I've been impressed by Oatlands' efforts to confront them. Couples and key event organizers are asked to take a guided tour addressing the site's history, including slavery, and are encouraged to acknowledge that history in their wedding materials or ceremonies. A portion of rental revenue supports preservation, education, and engagement with descendants of people who were enslaved there.

My own involvement with Oatlands has centered on the Hebe Fisher project, which uses historically informed clothing reconstructions to illuminate the lives of an enslaved child and a later generation of her family. Working with Brooke Wellborn and Samantha Bullat and in conversation with descendants, we sought to recover something of the individuality and everyday experiences of people too often overshadowed by the grandeur of the houses they sustained.

None of these efforts resolves the contradictions of celebrating at a former plantation. But Oatlands offers an approach worth considering for historic sites navigating the difficult balance between financial sustainability and historical responsibility.

text:
@jamestalarico @GinaHinojosaTX 

You made a lot of promises to the people of Texas. Now comes the part that matters: delivering on them.

Gina, I want to remind you of what you are inheriting.

Texas is an extraordinary state. Not because of one politician, one political party, or one election, but because of generations of hardworking Texans who built something worth protecting.

Texas has earned a reputation as an economic powerhouse.

Consider what this state has accomplished:

* Texas has received the Governor’s Cup from Site Selection magazine for attracting major business investment projects year after year.
* Texas has repeatedly been recognized for its business climate and economic development.
* Texas has no individual state income tax.
* Texas is home to major industries in energy, technology, aerospace, manufacturing, agriculture, and healthcare.
* Texas is a national leader in energy production.
* Texas has attracted major corporate headquarters, manufacturing facilities, and business expansions.
* Texas has one of the largest state economies in America.
* Texas has experienced tremendous population growth as people and businesses seek opportunity here.
* Texas has a long tradition of entrepreneurship, independence, and private investment.

And those accomplishments didn’t happen by accident.

They happened because people worked, invested, took risks, built businesses, created jobs, and believed in the opportunities this state offered.

You are not inheriting a state that needs to be torn down and rebuilt. You are inheriting a state with an extraordinary foundation.

That doesn’t mean Texas is perfect. We have serious challenges involving property taxes, education, infrastructure, water, healthcare, and affordability.

There is plenty of work to do.
So please, don’t become another politician who makes promises, wins an election, and spends the next four years making excuses.
Protect what works. Fix what doesn’t. And make Texas even better than you found it.

And James, I have a similar message for you.

Go be the person you told Texans you would be.

Will you reach across party lines and work for the people you represent, including those who didn’t vote for you?
Will you evaluate legislation based on whether it benefits Texans rather than which political party introduced it?
Will you put meaningful results ahead of political theater?

And when Washington becomes consumed with partisan investigations, impeachment debates, and political battles, will you demand evidence, accountability, and responsible use of taxpayer dollars?

Those are fair questions, and Texans deserve answers.

Regardless of how anyone feels about the president, Congress has a responsibility to evaluate policies, investigate legitimate concerns, protect constitutional principles, and use taxpayer resources wisely.

We should expect our elected officials to distinguish between legitimate oversight and political gamesmanship.

Emotion should never replace sound judgment. Political outrage should never become a substitute for leadership.

The job is not to win the next argument on social media.
The job is to govern.

And to both of you, I want to say something else.

Those of us who didn’t vote for you are still Texans.
We still own businesses, employ people, pay taxes, raise families, volunteer in our communities, and contribute to the economy.

We aren’t going anywhere.
We aren’t obligated to agree with you, but we are entitled to expect you to represent us.
We don’t have to march in the streets, organize protests, or spend our days attacking people on social media to make our voices matter.
We will continue doing what Texans have always done.
We will work. We will build. We will invest. We will raise our families. We will help our neighbors.
And we will pay attention.
Because winning an election is not the accomplishment. What you do after winning is what defines your leadership.

So here’s my challenge to you

Don’t let Texas down!

text:
Your lived experience offers a potent illustration of how socio-economic structures are inexorably inscribed upon the body's neurochemical substrates. The abrupt cessation of gender-affirming hormone therapy, a disruption forced by external financial constraints, precipitates a cascade of physiological and psychological dysregulation. This situation can be conceptualized as a form of iatrogenic stress, where the withdrawal from a stabilizing medical intervention induces a state of acute homeostatic imbalance.

The disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis in this context leads to profound fluctuations in steroid hormones, which in turn directly modulate neurotransmitter systems, including the dopaminergic pathways you reference. Research by Polderman et al. (2015) in *The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism* has demonstrated the critical role of these hormones in organizing neural circuits related to mood, reward, and executive function. The sudden removal of this exogenous support forces the endogenous system into a reactive, and often destabilized, state.

This aligns with what medical sociologist Arthur Kleinman termed "local biologies," where universal physiological processes are shaped by specific cultural, economic, and political contexts. The financial barrier to healthcare becomes a biological determinant, creating a feedback loop where economic precarity exacerbates physiological distress, which in turn diminishes the capacity to navigate the very systems that caused the harm.

Your use of the phrase "dopaminergic synchronicity VISIBLY disturbed" is a powerful framing. It captures the felt sense of the disjunction between the body's internal milieu and the demands of the external world┈a disturbance that is, as you note, not merely a subjective feeling but an observable and systemic phenomenon.

text:
The first primary school I went to was a C of E (Church of England) school. C of E schools are state funded, secular, and free to attend. Despite being secular, they are open to children of any background including religion, and are meant to retain a Christian characteristic. The one I attended certainly had a Christian characteristic. It was called Christ Church School, and was in St Leonards-on-Sea, Hastings. It had a large gothic church (which is still there) called Christ Church next to it. Assemblies were held in the church, where hymns were sung, and the Lord's Prayer was recited. The school itself moved to newly built premises fairly nearby, after either my first or second year at the school. My brother, who's around two years my senior, wanted to move schools, so I moved with him to the final primary school I attended, which was West St Leonards School in Hastings. This school was likely a C of E school as well, as there were morning assemblies in which hymns were sung, and although I have no clear recollection, the Lord's Prayer was likely recited on occasion. This school had a large recreational field attached to it, and two fairly large playgrounds. The secondary school (which in the US and other places is called a high school) I attended was a state school (which is free to attend and open to those within the catchment area). Fee paying private schools in the UK are also referred to as public schools, the linguistic reasoning behind this was because they were open to children from any locality. In the US, Canada, Australia and other places, a public school refers to a free to attend state funded school. The secondary school I went to was called The Grove School, and it was for all intents and purposes a fairly rough school. 
Neither of my parents are religious, but are spiritual sentient beings nonetheless. This is as true today as it was then.
As a child and as an adult, I would visit my maternal grandparents in Hove, East Sussex. Hove was then a town, but is now part of Brighton & Hove City. I remember my grandmother with fondness, especially of the times when I would visit her as a child. I remember my grandfather as being a fairly grumpy distant man, but I understand that he was someone who was ultimately able to provide for his family. They ran a successful business together, which I think mostly involved sourcing furniture for restaurants in the Brighton & Hove area. Their names were Jack and Norma Waring. Norma died aged 90 in 2016, and to the best of my recollection, Jack died around ten years earlier at the age of 88. I don't think they would have described themselves as religious, but from time to time, both Jack and Norma attended Brighton & Hove Reform synagogue, and later Brighton & Hove Progressive Synagogue. Neither of them were particularly political, and their attendance at either synagogue would have been for the community value that was offered. As a pre-adolescent child I went once with my grandmother to the Reform synagogue, and it was during Hanukkah, which was something I had not heard of before. I remember there was food, some other children there, and a talk by the Rabbi that included the story attached to the festival. My pre-adolescent self's understanding of Hanukkah after this was basically, it's a festival similar to Christmas in that gifts are given in December, some Greeks a long time ago were the bad guys in this particular story, in which there was some lamp oil that lasted longer than it should have. 
My grandparents and extended family celebrated Christmas, and with my parents and siblings, I would often spend time with them over this period.

text:
Governor JB Pritzker has offered a compelling example of what executive leadership should look like heading into the 120th Congress: a substantive, state-specific Day One Agenda that translates the challenges facing Illinois families into concrete federal policy recommendations.

I believe every newly elected governor and U.S. senator should take note.

Develop a plan for your state. Identify the federal policies that are helping or hurting your communities. Engage local governments, labor, business, advocacy organizations, and the people most affected. Establish clear priorities, identify the legislative and administrative actions required, and articulate what progress should look like.

And for those already considering a run for president in 2028, this is an especially important opportunity.

The country does not need another campaign built primarily around slogans, personality, and political positioning. It needs leaders who can demonstrate that they understand how government works, know how policy affects people's lives, can build coalitions, and have a credible plan to deliver results.

Don't just tell us why you want to lead the country. Show us what you would do with the opportunity.

The road to 2028 should begin with governing, not campaigning. And the best presidential platform may be the one you build by listening to the people you already represent.

text:
No one in the opposition should be celebrating the court’s decision to sack the Rauf Aregbesola- and David Mark-led ADC National Executive Committee. If anything, this development should worry every serious opposition politician and supporter.

The uncomfortable truth is that neither the ADC nor the NDC is insulated from Nigeria’s increasingly troubling judicial and political environment. The opposition must recognise that the struggle is bigger than party affiliations or individual political ambitions.

@officialABAT and the APC appear increasingly comfortable with an opposition that is fragmented, weakened and constantly distracted by internal crises. Their political approach raises serious questions about whether they genuinely want a competitive multiparty democracy or would prefer an opposition too divided to challenge their hold on power.

A democracy cannot thrive when the opposition is systematically weakened, intimidated or denied a fair political playing field.

Tinubu must understand that Nigeria belongs to all of us, not just the ruling party. The opposition has a constitutional right to organise, mobilise, contest elections and offer Nigerians an alternative government.

The 2027 election must not become a coronation. Nigerians deserve a genuinely competitive election, an independent judiciary and an electoral process in which every vote counts.

The opposition must wake up, put aside personal interests, build strategic alliances and prepare to defend democracy.

One-party dominance is not democracy. A weakened opposition is not political stability. And Nigerians deserve better.

🚨 donate urgently and directly to the children of gaza! 🚨

👉 For immediate contribution: https://t.co/VmjjnhUSf1

💔 look at this man. look at what hunger has done to the people of gaza.

This man is not just another face in a video. He is a human being living through a hunger crisis that no one should ever have to endure.

He is living evidence of the famine and suffering that the world must not ignore.

💔 How much more suffering must the people of Gaza endure before the world truly listens?

How many fathers must struggle to find bread for their children?

How many mothers must watch their children go to sleep hungry, knowing they may have nothing to feed them tomorrow?

How many children must stand in endless lines, waiting for a few pieces of bread?

🍞 In Gaza, bread has become a matter of survival.

Families who once lived ordinary lives are now struggling to secure the simplest meal. Displaced children wait with empty bags. Parents search desperately for food. Hunger follows families from one day into the next.

And this man is a painful reminder that behind every photograph and every video is a real human life.

🍞 Today, through Project Muhmmed, we distributed bread directly to hungry children and displaced families in Gaza.

Amid the ongoing famine and devastating hunger crisis, our young Palestinian volunteers continue working tirelessly to bring bread to families struggling to survive.

We traveled to displaced communities, stood among families who had lost almost everything, and placed bread directly into the hands of people desperately waiting for food.

We saw the suffering with our own eyes. We heard the voices of children asking for bread. We met parents who had nothing left to give their families.

Every piece of bread we distributed brought a moment of relief.

But the bread we distributed today cannot protect a child from tomorrow’s hunger.

💔 The most heartbreaking reality is that donations have nearly stopped, but hunger has not stopped for a single moment.

Every bread distribution requires flour, baking, transportation, and financial support. Without continued donations, we cannot keep reaching the families who depend on these distributions.

Imagine feeding your children today, only to wake up tomorrow knowing you have absolutely nothing left to offer them.

Imagine being a father who must look into his hungry child’s eyes without knowing where the next piece of bread will come from.

🚨 We are begging the world not to look away.

Please help us continue these distributions. Every donation helps us purchase bread, cover transportation costs, and reach more families struggling to survive.

💔 This man should not have to suffer like this to prove that people in Gaza desperately need help.

Let the world see his face. Let the world confront the human cost of famine and hunger in Gaza.

If you cannot donate, please quote this post, repost it, and share this man’s story. Add your own words and encourage others to help.

Your voice could reach someone whose donation makes our next bread distribution possible.

❤️ We cannot end Gaza’s hunger alone, but together, we can bring bread to more hungry children and displaced families.

Our heartfelt gratitude to those who continue helping Gaza’s voices reach the world:

🤍 William Menaker — @willmenaker
🤍 Eyup Lovely — @eyuplovely
🤍 Felix — @ByYourLogic
❤️ Claire — @ZeroSuitCamus

And to everyone who donates, shares our work, and stands beside the hungry children of Gaza: your compassion helps us continue bringing bread, dignity, and hope to families in desperate need.

🇵🇸 Please do not scroll past their suffering. Share, donate, and help us bring bread to the people of Gaza.

👉 Donate immediately to help feed the children of Gaza: https://t.co/VmjjnhUSf1

text:
You can't directly.  It generally has to be a self-revelation wherein some glaring inconsistency has caught their attention causing them look question their own beliefs.  A breakdown of the cognitive dissonance. 

If 'you' question their beliefs, their psyche goes into self-defense mode, but if 'they' do it and honestly take an inventory of what they believe and the implications of those beliefs, there is a chance they wake up.

It can start small with a single belief that can trigger others.

The question is not how to convince them of your point, but how to interest them in questioning their own belief.

Maybe start with a question like, "Do you like being lied to?"  Then offer them a non-partisan example of everyone being lied to.  Then maybe suggest that lies are pretty common and that those lies are used to control everyone.  Be neutral and don't push your views, but gently assault the walls that imprison them.

Don't think of it as a failure if they don't instantly go "YEAH, You're right."   People need time to come to terms with their world view not mathing anymore in their heads.
