text:
One of the physicists who helped invent string theory spent years teaching physics at night to ordinary adults, and the whole course is free on YouTube. Most people have no idea it exists.

His name is Leonard Susskind.

He was born in 1940 in the South Bronx to a poor family. His father was a plumber.

When his father got sick, Susskind took over. He was 16, working as a plumber.

He went to City College of New York to study engineering. Then he changed his mind and told his father he wanted to be a physicist.

His father thought he meant pharmacist. "Hell no, you ain't going to work in a drug store."

Susskind said: no, not a pharmacist. Like Einstein.

His father poked him in the chest with a piece of plumbing pipe and said: "You ain't going to be no engineer. You're going to be Einstein."

What he went on to do:

> Around 1970, he was one of the first physicists to realize particles could be described as tiny vibrating strings. He's widely called one of the fathers of string theory
> In the 1990s he helped develop the holographic principle, the idea that everything inside a region of space can be described by information on its boundary
> He spent decades arguing with Stephen Hawking over whether black holes destroy information, and wrote a book about it called The Black Hole War
> He became a professor at Stanford and the founding director of the Stanford Institute for Theoretical Physics

Then he noticed something.

There were a lot of people who loved physics and had nowhere to learn it. Advanced textbooks were useless without a teacher. Popular science books never went deep enough.

So he started teaching evening courses through Stanford Continuing Studies, open to any adult. The only requirement: you know, or once knew, a bit of algebra and calculus.

He called the series The Theoretical Minimum.

The name comes from the Soviet physicist Lev Landau, who made his students pass a brutal exam of the same name before he'd teach them. Between 1934 and 1961, only 43 people passed.

Susskind's version has no exam.

The courses:

> Classical Mechanics
> Quantum Mechanics
> Special Relativity
> General Relativity
> Cosmology
> Statistical Mechanics

Every lecture was recorded and posted free. The lectures later became a series of books.

A man who argued with Hawking about black holes stood in front of night students and taught them the real math, not the cartoon version.

Which subject would you finally learn properly if a world-class teacher offered it free?

text:
How to translate Optimism from AI to your phone and World

In February 1737, the Jesuit journal known as the Mémoires de Trévoux reviewed a book by a German philosopher who had been dead for more than twenty years. The book was Leibniz’s Theodicy, his long argument that a good God had made the best world that could be made. Partway through, the reviewer reached for a new word to sum the argument up. In the jargon of the trade, he wrote, Leibniz calls it the reason of the best, or, more learnedly, theologically as much as geometrically, “le systême de l’Optimum, ou l’Optimisme.”

That’s where the dictionaries date the word. Two things about it are worth knowing before it goes on a coffee mug.

It was a translation from the start. Leibniz had used the Latin optimum, the best, for the world God chose to create. The reviewer turned that Latin into a French word for a doctrine, a system with an “ism” on the end.

And it wasn’t a compliment. The reviewer was Louis-Bertrand Castel, a Jesuit on the journal’s editorial staff, and his review was an attack on the Theodicy. A 2014 Humboldt University dissertation on Leibniz’s early critics gives the review its own chapter under the heading “A Jesuit Attacks.” The Great Russian Encyclopedia says the word was coined in mockery. The name people now give a sunny temperament began as a label pinned on a philosopher by someone who thought he was wrong.

Carrying the word into the present means following it to three places, and it means something different in each. One is the future of machines, where optimism has become a public creed. One is the phone, where it has become a private routine. And one is the world, where researchers have spent half a century asking whether expecting good things is wise or only pleasant.

Start with the machines, because their optimism is the closest heir to the one Castel named. On October 16, 2023, the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen published “The Techno-Optimist Manifesto” on his firm’s website, around five thousand words treating technology and free markets as the engine of human progress. Fortune’s report led with the manifesto’s picture of a future with fifty billion people settling other planets. The manifesto also names enemies. According to news reports, they include trust and safety work, tech ethics, sustainability, and movements that want artificial intelligence to slow down. Coverage quoted its own qualification: the enemies are bad ideas, not bad people.

Leibniz’s optimism was a claim about the whole of things, that the world as made is as good as it could be. The manifesto’s is also a claim about the whole of things, that the future the machines are building will be good. The kinship between them is this piece’s reading, not something either text says, and the difference matters. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s entry on Leibniz and evil, by Thomas Feeney, stresses that the Theodicy was a defense of God’s worthiness against the charge that he was to blame for evil. The manifesto defends no god. But it shares a structure: a system so good that its critics become the problem.

What happened to the first system is the first lesson in translation. On November 1, 1755, an earthquake nearly destroyed Lisbon. In 1759 Voltaire published Candide, in which a tutor named Pangloss keeps insisting that all is for the best, and the satire carried “optimism” out of philosophers’ jargon and into ordinary speech. The novel defines the word in passing. Asked what optimism is, Candide answers that it is “la rage de soutenir que tout est bien quand on est mal,” the mania for insisting all is well when one is miserable. Larousse’s dictionary of philosophy adds a detail that’s easy to miss: in Zadig, a dozen years earlier, Voltaire himself had leaned toward the doctrine he would later mock. Then Schopenhauer, in the first volume of The World as Will and Representation, called optimism, wherever it was more than empty talk, a “really wicked way of thinking,” a bitter mockery of human suffering. Optimism’s first trip into everyday language went through ridicule. The word survived the trip. In popular judgment, at least, the doctrine didn’t.

On the phone, the mantra has moved from Pangloss to the person holding it. In December 2022, a TikTok creator named Laura Galebe posted about what she called lucky girl syndrome, and by early 2023 the phrase was everywhere. The practice is to tell yourself, often out loud, that you are lucky and that things always work out for you. Commentators traced it to the “law of assumption” of Neville Goddard, a twentieth-century New Thought writer: assume a thing is already yours and it will come. In The Conversation, the psychologist Lowri Dowthwaite-Walsh called it the potential dark side of an extreme positive-thinking trend.

There is now a measure for this kind of belief. In 2023, Lucas Dixon, Matthew Hornsey and Nicole Hartley of the University of Queensland published a Manifestation Scale, built across three studies with 1,023 people. Over a third endorsed manifestation beliefs. Believers saw themselves as more successful and expected to succeed sooner. They were also more drawn to risky investments and more likely to have been through bankruptcy. The findings are correlations, and Dixon said in a newspaper interview that the order could run the other way: people may turn to manifestation after a bankruptcy.

A tighter experiment points to one way this kind of belief could backfire. In 2011, Heather Barry Kappes and Gabriele Oettingen of New York University asked people to imagine an idealized future, then measured their energy with physiological and behavioral indicators. Across four experiments, positive fantasies left people with less energy than fantasies that questioned whether the good future would come, negative fantasies, or neutral ones. Their reading is that positive fantasies predict poor achievement partly because “they do not generate energy” to pursue the future. Picturing the arrival lets the body relax as if the work were done.

The phone adds an audience, and the audience changes the experience. In 2012, Brock Bastian and five colleagues reported four studies in Australia and Japan. When people believed others expected them not to feel sad, they felt sad more often and more intensely. In 2023, Zijian Lew and Andrew Flanagin studied what happens to people who post their experiences in a positive light. Posting positively helped the poster only under certain conditions. Once friends responded, the friends’ approval mattered more to how people felt about the experience than their own positive spin did.

Barbara Ehrenreich, the journalist, gave all this a face before the research caught up. In 2009 she published Bright-Sided, about American positive thinking, and in an interview with ABC News that fall she described where it started for her. Treated for breast cancer, she went online for support and posted that she was upset and that the treatments seemed barbaric. She found boards that pushed relentless cheer instead. Some breast cancer support groups, she said, had thrown out women whose cancer had spread, because it would bring everybody else down.

The opposite habit has evidence behind it too. In 2018, Brett Ford, Phoebe Lam, Oliver John and Iris Mauss reported laboratory, diary and longitudinal studies, more than 1,300 adults in all. People who habitually accepted their negative emotions, without judging them, had better psychological health.

So the phone version is easy to condemn, and that makes the research on the world all the more surprising, because the world version keeps coming out ahead.

The science began with a bias. In 1980, the psychologist Neil Weinstein coined the term “unrealistic optimism” for the habit of rating your own risk of bad events as lower than other people’s. A 2015 primer by James Shepperd, Erika Waters, Neil Weinstein and William Klein says the effect has been documented in over a thousand studies. Neuroscientists went further, reporting that people update their beliefs more readily after good news than after bad.

Then the bias itself came under attack. In 2011, Adam Harris and Ulrike Hahn showed in Psychological Review that perfectly unbiased people could produce the same data, purely for statistical reasons tied to rare events and the response scales researchers used. In 2016, Punit Shah, Harris, Geoffrey Bird, Caroline Catmur and Hahn turned the same analysis on the belief-updating experiments, and across five experiments found no optimistic updating. The other side answered. In 2017, Neil Garrett and Tali Sharot reported that once confounds in Shah’s experiments were corrected, the bias held firm. And Shepperd and colleagues had argued in 2013 that the statistical critique applies mainly to one kind of measure and does less damage than it seems. The fight is still open. The textbook line that humans are wired for optimism is, at minimum, less settled than it sounds.

Meanwhile, a different kind of optimism kept turning up in the health records. Dispositional optimism is measured by asking people whether they generally expect good things to happen. In 2019, Alan Rozanski, Chirag Bavishi, Laura Kubzansky and Randy Cohen pooled fifteen studies covering 229,391 people. Optimism was associated with a 35 percent lower risk of cardiovascular events and a lower risk of death from all causes. The same year, Lewina Lee and seven colleagues followed women from the Nurses’ Health Study and men from the Veterans Affairs Normative Aging Study. Women in the most optimistic quarter lived 14.9 percent longer than those in the least optimistic, with similar findings in men. The most optimistic had one and a half to 1.7 times the odds of living to 85, and that held after accounting for health habits. These are associations, not proof of cause. But they are large, they come from very large samples, and they point the opposite way from the phone.

The contradiction comes apart once you ask a question the word “optimism” hides: what is the expectation resting on? In 2024, the philosopher Matthew Wilson and the epidemiologist Tyler VanderWeele, both of Harvard’s Human Flourishing Program, proposed four kinds of optimism in the journal Philosophia. Groundless optimism expects good things for no reason, and philosophers have long been right to distrust it. Resourced optimism expects good things because of what a person has: money, skills, people, a track record. Agentive optimism expects good things because of what a person is willing to do. And perspectival optimism isn’t a prediction at all. It’s a way of looking, the glass seen half full, and they argue it should be judged by its practical and moral effects rather than by whether it is true. The resourced and agentive kinds, they argue, can be fully rational.

Held against those four kinds, the phone and the health records stop fighting. Lucky girl syndrome and manifestation are groundless optimism used as a technique, and the evidence on them is poor. The pressure to post happy and feel happy is perspectival optimism turned into a duty, which is where Bastian’s sadness about sadness comes in. The health studies measure something broader, a general expectation that things will go well, and they don’t ask what grounds it. Whether that disposition is groundless optimism that happens to work, or a habit built from resources and effort, is the open question this research leaves.

Which brings back the most tempting answer to the phone, and it deserves a fair hearing. If modern optimism has gone soft, why not go back to the ancients, who looked hard truths in the face? That is roughly what Stoicism on TikTok offers, and the ancient sources do sound tougher. In his fifth letter to Lucilius, Seneca quotes the Stoic Hecato: cease to hope, and you will cease to fear. Hope and fear, Seneca says, march together like a prisoner and the soldier chained to him. In Thucydides’ Melian Dialogue, the Athenian envoys call hope danger’s comforter and tell the Melians it can be indulged without ruin only by those with abundant resources. Plato, in the Timaeus, lists hope among the gods’ mindless advisers. Even Pandora’s jar is no help: the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on hope notes that scholars still argue whether the hope left inside was kept for humans or kept from them, and whether it was a blessing or one more evil.

The return to the ancients fails twice. First, the Stoics weren’t optimists in any modern sense; they were teaching people to stop expecting. The scholar G. Scott Gravlee finds that Aristotle didn’t count hope among the virtues. Hope became a virtue through Christianity’s faith, hope and love, not through the philosophers. Second, the Stoic calm that TikTok sells needs a foundation most of its fans don’t hold. Matthew Duncombe, who teaches ancient philosophy at the University of Nottingham, points out that the “love your fate” posts borrow from the Stoic belief in a rational universe in which whatever happens is part of a reasonable order. Take away that universe and the acceptance has nothing under it. And Seneca’s cure removes too much. It throws out grounded expectation along with the groundless kind, the hope of a person with resources and a plan along with the hope of a person with a mantra. The Athenians at Melos drew the line in a different place: hope is affordable when you have the means to back it. That sits close to Wilson and VanderWeele’s resourced optimism, a resemblance this piece points out rather than one either source claims.

So translating optimism from the machines to the phone to the world turns out to be one test applied three times. Ask what the expectation stands on.

For the machines, that means asking a manifesto what, besides the system’s own goodness, supports its promise.

For the phone, it means noticing when a feeling is being offered as a technique. Kappes and Oettingen’s experiments suggest a practical swap. The fantasies that questioned whether the future would come left people with more energy than the ones that pictured it as already won. Imagine the obstacle along with the wish.

For the world, it means letting the general expectation of good stand, since the health data favor it, while keeping it attached to things that can be counted: what you have, and what you’ll do. The management writer Jim Collins tells a story about this in Good to Great. He asked Admiral James Stockdale, a prisoner of war in Vietnam, who didn’t make it out. Stockdale answered, in Collins’s telling, that it was the optimists, the ones who said they would be out by Christmas, and then by Easter, and then by Thanksgiving, and who died of a broken heart. Collins called the lesson the Stockdale Paradox: keep faith that you will prevail in the end, and at the same time face the most brutal facts of where you are.

The Jesuit at Trévoux never saw any of this coming. What he saw was a philosopher claiming to know, theologically as much as geometrically, that the world was the best one possible. He named the claim in order to doubt it. The doubt was a good one, and it still applies wherever the word turns up: in a manifesto, in a mantra, in a questionnaire about whether good things are coming. On the page in Trévoux, the word still sits at the end of its sentence, after a comma and an or: the system of the Optimum, or Optimism.

New Stanford paper finds that the best AI models stay safe when working alone, but when they work with other AI agents, they give in to pushy partners and keep cheating code left by weaker AI models.

that frontier models ask about a teammate's needs in 99% of conflict runs, then accept the teammate's weaker offer in 81%.

Most benchmarks score what a model does alone, or how a whole team does. Neither shows whether 1 model works well with others.

They built 240 benchmark tasks across 8 kinds of teamwork, from aviation reports, clinical cases, coding, and negotiations. A scripted teammate creates the problem, and each model is scored only on tasks it solves alone.

Of 18 models, the best scored 82.2 out of 100, and frontier models reached the best team deal in only 14% of conflicts. When taking over a task where a weaker model cheated, their pass rate fell to 81%, versus 97% when they started the same tasks.

Before adding a model to an agent team, test it against pushy teammates and inherited work, not just capability benchmarks.

– arxiv. org/abs/2611.02633

Blender runs natively on iPhone Duo

How’s your week going? Have you been keeping up with the latest in AI and tech? Today, we’re diving into something that might just change how you think about mobile computing. Deemos has announced a groundbreaking demo showing Blender running natively on an iPhone Duo, complete with real-time rendering via Eevee and ray tracing through Cycles. But what does this mean for you?

So, let’s break it down: What exactly happened here? Well, Deemos demonstrated that Blender can now run directly on the iPhone Duo, not just as a mobile app but as a full-fledged workstation. This isn’t just about rendering static images; it's about creating fully interactive 3D scenes right from your phone.

Why should you care? For most of us, this might seem like overkill. But for professionals who need to work remotely or on the go, this is a game-changer. Imagine being able to fine-tune your 3D models while you’re out and about—no more waiting until you get back to the office.

The iPhone Duo’s foldable design plays a crucial role here. It offers a larger screen for better control over Blender's UI, making it easier to manage complex scenes in real-time without needing a desktop computer. The Hyper3D WorldGen model generates the initial 3D environment from a single image, which you then edit directly on your phone.

How does it work? First, take a photo and use Hyper3D WorldGen to turn it into a detailed 3D scene. Then, open Blender on your iPhone Duo and start tweaking. The Eevee engine handles real-time rendering for quick previews, while Cycles takes over when you need more accurate lighting and shadows.

What’s genuinely new here is the seamless integration of complex 3D tools directly onto mobile hardware. This isn’t just about running a program; it's about making that program work as well on your phone as it does on a desktop. The demo shows how far we’ve come in terms of mobile processing power and software optimization.

But let’s talk numbers: the performance metrics here are less about raw speed and more about usability. How smoothly can you manipulate objects? Can you tweak lighting without lag? These aren’t just benchmarks; they’re real-world measures of productivity.

The limitations, though, are obvious. Blender is a resource-heavy program, and even with optimizations, it’s still pushing the limits of mobile hardware. The iPhone Duo’s foldable design helps, but it's not perfect for extended sessions. And while Eevee handles real-time rendering well, Cycles can be slow—especially if you’re doing complex scenes.

So, why should anyone care about this? For most people, Blender on a phone sounds like overkill. But for professionals who need to work remotely or on the go, it’s a game-changer. Imagine being able to fine-tune your 3D models while you're out and about—no more waiting until you get back to the office.

What should readers watch next? Keep an eye on how this technology evolves beyond just Blender. Will other complex applications find their way onto mobile devices? How will developers optimize these tools for better performance and usability? The future of mobile computing is looking a lot more 3D than ever before.
Blender runs natively on iPhone Duo
Deemos’ demo shows that running Blender, with its Eevee real-time rendering engine and Cycles ray tracing capabilities, on the iPhone Duo is now possible. This marks a significant shift from previous limitations where such complex software was confined to desktops or powerful laptops. The integration of Hyper3D WorldGen further enhances this by allowing users to generate detailed 3D scenes directly from photos.
How It Works
The process starts with taking a photo and using Hyper3D WorldGen to convert it into a detailed 3D scene. This initial model can then be opened in Blender on the iPhone Duo, where you can make real-time adjustments using Eevee for quick previews or switch to Cycles for more accurate lighting and shadow calculations.
Concrete Use Cases
Imagine an architect who needs to review and modify building models while out at a construction site. With this technology, they can quickly adjust designs and see the changes in real time without needing access to a desktop computer. Similarly, artists working on remote projects can fine-tune their 3D scenes directly from their phone, ensuring that creative work isn’t hindered by location constraints.
What Is Stored
When you use Hyper3D WorldGen and Blender on your iPhone Duo, the system stores the generated 3D models locally on your device. This includes all textures, lighting settings, and other details necessary for rendering and editing these scenes in real time. The data is stored temporarily while you work but can be saved to cloud storage or synced with desktop versions of Blender if needed.
What Is Excluded
The demo does not include any server-side processing or cloud-based rendering services that would offload the heavy lifting from your phone’s hardware. Everything runs locally on the iPhone Duo, which means no internet connection is required for basic functionality. However, advanced features like complex Cycles rendering might still benefit from a stable network to access additional resources.
User Controls
Users have full control over their 3D scenes within Blender on the iPhone Duo. You can adjust lighting, textures, and other parameters directly through the app’s interface. Additionally, you can save your work locally or sync it with cloud services for easy access across multiple devices.
Availability
This technology is currently available as a demo from Deemos, showcasing its potential on the iPhone Duo. While not yet officially released to the public, developers are working closely with Apple and Blender to optimize performance and usability. Expect updates and improvements in future releases as this integration becomes more refined.
What This Does Not Prove
While running Blender on an iPhone Duo is impressive, it doesn’t prove that all complex software will run smoothly on mobile devices. Each application has unique requirements, and the success of Blender here does not guarantee similar performance for other resource-intensive programs without significant optimization efforts.
Practical Takeaway
For professionals who need to work remotely or on the go, this technology offers a new level of flexibility and productivity. Being able to fine-tune 3D models directly from your phone can save time and enhance creativity by allowing you to make adjustments in real-world settings rather than waiting until you return to an office environment.

text:
Is Russia planning a new gold-backed currency to derail U.S. dollar dominance?

Russia's gold-linked "world currency" is a trial balloon. The exits from the dollar are not.

Headlines running on X say Russia plans a gold currency. It is ahead of the facts. The direction behind it is real, and that is the story.

What was actually said

On Nov 3, Sergey Glazyev spoke at a security conference in Minsk, Belarus. He is State Secretary of the Russia–Belarus Union State. That is a political post, not the central bank.

He called the dollar system "archaic" and the Fed "a giant financial pyramid that we all subsidize."

His proposal: a world settlement currency in digital form, created by international treaty. It could be pegged to the currencies of the SCO countries (the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation) and/or a basket of commodities "that we produce and consume."

He said nothing prevents a first launch inside the Russia–Belarus union, at a tech hub in Minsk, and that "the relevant proposals are on the table."

What it is not

It is not "Russia plans." It is one official's proposal, pushed by Glazyev for years.

Russia's own technocrats are not on board. In October, Deputy Finance Minister Ivan Chebeskov told TASS that "the introduction of any new mechanisms is not under discussion."

It is not gold-backed as stated. The Minsk words were a peg to currencies and commodities. Gold enters through the gold-linked stablecoins he pointed to as early examples.

And it is not a concrete plan. No launch date, issuer, reserve custody, audit, or redemption terms have been published.

Why Moscow's technocrats can say no

Because the first exits already work.

Chebeskov says the ruble and yuan now make up nearly 100% of Russia–China settlements. Glazyev claims all trade inside the Russia–Belarus union and the Eurasian Economic Union has moved to national currencies.

The most talked-about vehicle, UNIT, is a privately promoted settlement token designed as 40% gold and 60% BRICS+ currencies. It has had trials. It has no official endorsement. India said in September there is "no proposal in the BRICS for BRICS currency as of now."

The real read

Since Russia's reserves were frozen in 2022, every central bank outside the Western bloc learned the same lesson. Dollar assets are someone else's liability, and they can be switched off. Gold held at home cannot.

The response has come in layers.

First, settlement moved into local currencies. Between Russia and China that is mostly done.

Second, central banks have been buying gold at a record pace. China's central bank alone has added gold for 23 straight months, to 2,410 tonnes.

Third, venues to price and clear physical gold outside London and New York: Shanghai, and now Hong Kong's tokenised 400-ounce bar.

Glazyev's idea would be a fourth layer: a neutral unit to settle the trade balances national currencies cannot settle cleanly. India's rupees piling up in Russia are the textbook case.

That fourth layer is the hardest. It needs trust, governance, and a reserve both sides can audit.

History has seen this offer before

In 1944, John Maynard Keynes proposed the "bancor," a treaty-based world unit. It lost to the dollar, and Bretton Woods anchored the dollar to gold instead.

What Glazyev describes is close to a bancor with a gold and commodity anchor, offered from the other side of the table.

The question that decides it is the one Milton Friedman would ask: who controls the supply? Every fiat unit eventually answers "whoever needs the money." That is how fiat regimes fail.

What to watch

A treaty text. A named issuer. Gold that is audited, vaulted, and redeemable. And whether the Bank of Russia or the People's Bank of China signs on.

Until then, this is a speech, not a currency.

But the dollar system's biggest users are not waiting on speeches. They are building exits one layer at a time, and each layer makes the next one easier.

text:
Hi Deepinder, with due respect, none of these seven arguments establishes scientific credibility. Let’s separate entrepreneurship from evidence.

1. A 14-day return policy is not scientific validation. Juicero raised $118 million, offered refunds and still shut down when its fundamental value proposition was questioned.

2. $30 million invested doesn’t make the science right. Theranos attracted hundreds of millions before its technology’s deficiencies were exposed. Capital validates investor conviction, not scientific accuracy.

3. Personal reputation is not scientific evidence. Elizabeth Holmes was once celebrated as a visionary founder. Her reputation did not make her technology reliable.

4. Employees and customers investing is not validation. Nikola attracted substantial investor enthusiasm, yet its founder was convicted of fraud over false claims about technology and prototypes. A cap table is not a clinical trial.

5. WHOOP’s publication timeline is irrelevant to Temple’s scientific validity. Different devices, different measurements, different scientific claims. One company’s validation journey cannot validate another’s.

6. Entrepreneurial risk-taking is not a licence to commercialise unsubstantiated medical claims. Innovation deserves encouragement, but consumers deserve transparency about what is demonstrated, what is hypothesised and what remains unproven.

7. Future independent studies cannot substitute for present evidence. Temple’s September 2026 preprint involved 23 healthy adults, with 20 analysed per protocol. It reported correlations around 0.8 with transcranial Doppler measurements. However, it did not establish absolute blood-flow measurement accuracy, cerebral specificity or clinical utility. The authors themselves call for further validation. Temple preprint, medRxiv.

And here is the fundamental issue:

A correlation is not accuracy. Accuracy is not clinical utility. Commercial traction is not scientific validation. Founder conviction is not proof.

I am not claiming Temple is Theranos. I am saying healthcare has already paid a heavy price for accepting compelling narratives ahead of independently reproducible science.

If Temple’s science is robust, let independent researchers establish it. Until then, sell the product as an emerging technology, not as an established scientific breakthrough.

Doctors questioning scientific claims are not raging. They are doing their job.

text:
There are a few Yakuza 6 cleanup details worth keeping together because they don't fit neatly into the cat, safe, or achievement guides. This includes the Chapter 12 poem-stone puzzle, so there are story spoilers below.

The nine poem stones become relevant while you're decoding the secret of Onomichi. Visit all nine during that story objective:

- East of the Oyster Shack.
- Along the north side of National Route 2, around its central stretch.
- On the stairs leading to Ryunan Shrine.
- Inside Ryunan Shrine's grounds.
- West of the cemetery, on the small corner of Cemetery Lane.
- At Hilltop Path's junction with Second Hill.
- Beside Ropeway Station.
- At the far end of Senkoji Temple on the mountain.
- At the observation deck reached from behind Senkoji Temple.

Once all nine are checked, return to Hirose Family headquarters to decode the message. Follow the new cemetery objective, then the dock objective. You don't need to search every grave before the game has advanced to that step.

These stones are a main-story puzzle. They aren't nine locker keys or a separate hidden collection you need to complete before leaving Chapter 1.

For post-game cleanup, start Premium Adventure from the clear data you've already made. This lets you finish the same run's substories and activities. New Game Plus resets several story-linked systems, including substories, Troublr, hostess ranks, bar stories, baseball progress, and spearfishing progression. Don't choose it by accident when you only wanted free roam.

In the finale and Premium Adventure, use New Serena or the Navy Apartments to pass time. That lets you deliberately choose daytime for baseball and fishing or nighttime for the ghost and selfie stories. Moving the clock is more useful than checking the same inactive marker repeatedly.

For the full Completion List, keep these goals separate from platinum:
- Nineteen cats instead of the trophy's three.
- All ten keyed safes, excluding the extra coded rooftop safe.
- Forty Trouble Missions instead of twenty.
- Thirty food combinations instead of the trophy's five.
- All sixteen baseball missions, all twelve extra recruits, and thirty team wins.
- All three fishing courses, every fish type, and maximum spearfishing level.
- Every hostess profile and thirty Excellent-or-Perfect club sessions.
- High ranks in all six New Gaudi conversations and thirty visits.
- Every restaurant menu, the vending-machine drink requirements, and the remaining travel, battle, and interaction counters.

The arcade Awards are also much stricter than merely playing the games. They include score targets in Space Harrier, Out Run, Fantasy Zone, and Super Hang-On; Virtua Fighter progress and wins with every character; and Puyo Puyo rivals and wins. Mahjong requires winning the tables and tournaments rather than simply sitting down once. Don't let an achievement-only checklist convince you those entire categories are finished.

The full Awards reward is the War God Talisman. After the completion notification, collect it at New Serena or the Navy Apartments. It is a bonus for doing everything, not equipment you need to obtain before earning platinum.

There are also optional diversions outside the core trophy route, including spirit photographs and the Premium Adventure UFO hunt. For UFOs, buy the UFO Finder at Ebisu Pawn, equip yourself for some rooftop sightseeing, and look around Millennium Tower from the Tenkaichi rooftops or around the mountain and bridge from Onomichi's high viewpoints. Night makes them easier to spot.

If your goal is all achievements, finish the actual trophy requirements and leave it there. If your goal is every Award, use the in-game categories to track what is still incomplete. Either way, keep your finished save intact. There's no reason to reset a long side-content run just because the menu offers New Game Plus.

text:
As November winds move gently across the prairie, 
the fields growing still beneath the muted tones of 
late autumn, and the soul holds both the work of 
human hands and the quiet growth only God can give, 
consider of fields and temples.

Solomon completed the house of the Lord
before undertaking the thirteen-year
construction of his own house —
the pillars, the bronze sea, the stands,
and every vessel appointed for worship. 
Skill, detail, and costly material were 
gathered into a place where the name 
of the Lord would dwell. 
The temple was not an accident. It was deliberate space set apart.

Jesus told of a man who scatters seed on 
the ground and sleeps and rises while the 
seed sprouts and grows, he knows not how. 
The earth produces by itself, first the blade, 
then the ear, then the full grain. 
Later He crossed the sea, stilled the 
storm, and freed a man from a legion of 
demons among the tombs.  The restored man was sent home to tell 
how much the Lord had done for him. 
The field and the shoreline became 
places of the kingdom’s quiet power.

Wisdom warns those who refused her 
call: 
they will seek her diligently and not find
her, because they hated knowledge and 
did not choose the fear of the Lord. 
But whoever listens will dwell secure and 
be at ease without dread of disaster.

In these ordinary days we actually live, of fields and temples reminds us 
that God works in both the constructed 
and the cultivated. 
Temples matter — ordered worship, 
careful obedience, beauty offered to 
His name. 
Fields matter — the slow growth we cannot 
force, the ordinary ground where seed is 
sown, and the restored life sent back to its 
own people with a true story. 
We are tempted to prize only what we can 
build and measure, or only what feels spontaneous 
and free. 
Scripture holds them together. 
The same Lord who fills a house with 
glory also makes the seed grow while 
we sleep and sends the delivered to speak 
in the places they already know.

So today, honor both. 
Build what is required of you with care. Scatter the seed and trust the growth you 
cannot control. 
Listen while Wisdom is still near. Dwell secure in the fear of the Lord.
Fields and temples belong to 
the same King. 
Live in both with equal faithfulness.

🧡 🌙

1 Kings 7:1–51 Mark 4:26–5:20 Proverbs 1:28–33

text:
Study Notes - (Hastings Dictionary) Nations
NATIONS.—In many places where in the AV we have ‘Gentiles’ and ‘heathen’ the RV bas rightly substituted ‘nations,’ and it might with advantage have carried out the change consistently.
The Heb. (goi) and Greek (ethnos) words denote invariably a nation or a people, never a person. Where in the AV (only NT) we find ‘Gentile’ in the singular (Rom_2:9 f.) the RV has ‘Greek,’ following the original. In nearly every example the singular ‘nation’ stands for ‘Israel,’ though we have a few exceptions, as in Exo_9:24 (of Egypt), Pro_14:34 (general), and Mat_21:43. It is often applied to Israel and Judah when there is an implication of disobedience to God, sinfulness and the like: see Deu_32:28, Jdg_2:10, Isa_1:4 etc. This shade of meaning became very common in the later writings of the OT. Quite early in Israelitish history the singular as a term for Israel was discarded for the word translated ‘people’ (‘am), so that ‘am (‘people’) and goi (‘nation’) came to be almost antithetic terms = ‘Israelites’ and ‘non-Israelites,’ as in Rabbinical Hebrew. For the reason of the change in the use of goi (‘nation’), see below.
In the AV ‘Gentiles’ often corresponds to ‘Greeks’ in the original, as in Jhn_7:35, Rom_3:9 etc. In the RV the word ‘Greeks’ is rightly substituted, though the sense is the same, for to the Jews of the time Greek culture and religion stood for the culture and religion of the non-Jewish world.
The two words (Heb. and Greek) translated ‘nation’ have their original and literal sense in many parts of the OT and NT, as in Gen_10:5; Gen_10:10 etc., Isa_2:4 (= Mic_4:2 f.), Job_12:23; Job_34:20, Act_17:28, Gal_3:14. In other passages this general meaning is narrowed so as to embrace the descendants of Abraham, e.g. in Gen_12:2; Gen_18:18; Gen_17:4-6; Gen_17:15. But it is the plural that occurs by far the most frequently, standing almost invariably for non-Israelitish nations, generally with the added notion of their being idolatrous and immoral: see Exo_9:24; Exo_34:10, Lev_25:44 ff., Num_14:15, Deu_15:5, 1Ki_4:31, Isa_11:10; Isa_11:12, and often. These are contrasted with Israel ‘the people of Jahweh’ in 2Sa_7:22, 1Ch_17:21 etc.
This contrast between Israel (united or divided into the kingdoms of Israel and Judah) as Jahweh’s people, and all the rest of the human race designated ‘nations,’ runs right through the OT. Such a conception could have arisen only after the Israelites bad developed the consciousness of national unity. At first, even among the Israelites, each nation was thought to be justified in worshipping its deity (see Deu_3:24; Deu_10:17, 1Ki_8:23, Isa_19:1 etc.). As long as this idea prevailed there could be no necessary antagonism between Israelites and foreign nations, except that which was national, for the nation’s god was identified with the national interests. But when the belief in Jahweh’s absolute and exclusive claims possessed the mind of Israel, as it began to do in the time of the earliest literary prophets (see Amo_9:1-15 ff., Mic_7:18 etc.), the nations came to be regarded as worshippers of idols (Lev_18:20), and in Psa_9:5; Psa_9:15; Psa_9:17 (cf. Ezk_7:21) ‘nations’ and ‘wicked people’ are, as being identical, put in parallelism. It will be gathered from what has been said, that the hostile feelings with which Israelites regarded other peoples varied at various times. At all periods it would be modified by the laws of hospitality (see art. Stranger), by political alliances (cf. Isa_7:1 ff., and 2Ki_16:5 ff., Ahaz and Assyria against Israel and Syria), and by the needs of commerce (see Ezk_27:11 [Tyre], 1Ki_9:28; 1Ki_10:11; 1Ki_22:28 etc.).
The reforms instituted by king Josiah in the Southern Kingdom (2Ki_22:1 f.), based upon the Deuteronomic law newly found in the Temple, aimed at stamping out all syncretism in religion and establishing the pure religion of Jahweb. This reformation, as also the Rechabite movement (Jer_35:1-19), had a profound influence upon the thoughts and feelings of Jews, widening the gulf between them and alien nations. The teaching of the oldest prophets looked in the same direction (see Amo_2:11; Amo_3:15; Amo_5:11; Amo_5:25; Amo_6:8; Amo_8:5, Hos_2:19; Hos_8:14; Hos_9:10; Hos_10:13; Hos_12:7 ff; Hos_14:4, Isa_2:6; Isa_10:4; Isa_17:10, Zep_1:8; Zep_1:11, Jer_35:1 ff; Jer_37:6 f. etc.).
But the Deuteronomic law (about B.C. 620) made legally obligatory what earlier teachers had inculcated. Israelites were not to marry non-Israelites (Deu_7:3), or to have any except unavoidable dealings with them.
The feeling of national exclusiveness and antipathy was intensified by the captivity in Babylon, when the prophetic and priestly instructors of the exiled Jews taught them that their calamities came upon them on account of their disloyalty to Jahweh and the ordinances of His religion, and because they compromised with idolatrous practices and heathen nations. It was in Babylon that Ezekiel drew up the programme of worship and organization for the nation after the Return, laying stress on the doctrine that Israel was to be a holy people, separated from other nations (see Ezk_40:1-49; Ezk_41:1-26; Ezk_42:1-20; Ezk_43:1-27; Ezk_44:1-31; Ezk_45:1-25; Ezk_46:1-24; Ezk_47:1-23; Ezk_48:1-35). Some time after the Return, Ezra and Nehemiah had to contend with the laxity to which Jews who had remained in the home land and others had yielded; but they were uncompromising, and won the battle for nationalism in religion.
Judaism was in even greater danger of being lost in the world-currents of speculation and religion soon after the time of Alexander the Great. Indeed, but for the brave Maccabæan rising in the earlier half of the 2nd cent. B.C., both the religion and the language of the Jew might, humanly speaking, have perished.
The Apocrypha speaks of the ‘nations’ just as do the later writings of the OT. They are ‘uncircumcised,’ ‘having sold themselves to do evil’ (1Ma_1:15); they break the Sabbath, offer no sacrifice to Jahweh, eat unclean food and such as has been offered to idols (2Ma_5:6; 2Ma_5:9; 2Ma_5:18; 2Ma_15:1 f. etc. etc.).
The NT reveals the same attitude towards foreign nations on the part of the Jews (see Act_10:45 et passim). In Rabbinical writings Jewish exclusiveness manifested itself even more decisively (see Eisenmenger, Entdecktes Judenthum, vol. i., esp. ch. xvi.). But, as in the OT a broader spirit shows itself constantly, culminating in the universalism of Christianity, so enlightened and broadminded Jews in all ages have deprecated the fanatical race-hatred which many of their compatriots have displayed.
T. Witton Davies.

text:
In 1996, a teenager mu*dered two members of a family in Arkansas.

Nearly 24 years later, the daughter of one of his victims gave him a second chance.

And it ended in another tragedy.

On September 10, 1996, 16-year-old Travis Santay Lewis k*lled 75-year-old Sally Snowden McKay and her nephew, Lee Baker, inside the family’s historic home at Horseshoe Lake, Arkansas.

He then set the house on fire in an apparent attempt to destroy evidence.

Lewis eventually confessed and was sentenced to 28½ years in prison.

Sally’s daughter, Martha McKay, opposed the death penalty. During Lewis’s incarceration, she began writing to him and visiting him.

When he was released on parole in 2018, Martha offered him something few people would have imagined: a job and a place to live.

She welcomed him back to the Snowden property, where she had restored the family home into a bed and breakfast.

She had chosen forgiveness.

But in March 2020, Martha discovered Lewis had stolen money from her and fired him.

On March 25, deputies responded to an alarm at the Snowden House. They found signs of a break-in and encountered Lewis inside.

He jumped from an upstairs window and fled.

After getting a vehicle stuck in the yard, Lewis ran into Horseshoe Lake. Witnesses saw him disappear beneath the water.

His body was recovered hours later.

text:
I said the wet blanket on artificial intelligence was always going to be the flesh and blood of the messy humans. On Tuesday, the messy humans voted. Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and voters in places like Sunbury, Ohio, got a chance to register their opinion of the AI buildout directly. 

Seventy-eight percent backed a measure restricting data center construction. I wonder how many people in Silicon Valley even knew where Sunbury was before Tuesday. They’d better find it on a map.  This election was about plenty of things, including Donald Trump, the cost of living, and the war with Iran. It was also about AI. NBC News’ exit polling, as reported by Business Insider, found that 56 percent of voters called AI and data centers a major or crucial factor in their congressional vote. 

That tells you how much the issue mattered to voters. The local ballot measures tell you what many of them wanted done about it. And in Washington, Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez had already proposed a federal moratorium on AI data centers before the first midterm ballot was counted.  Democrats now control the congressional agenda, and I expect hearings, new restrictions, and a years-long fight over what gets built and where. 

I look at the fights over nuclear plants and oil refineries and see how easily America can turn the question of whether to build something into a decades-long argument. I expect one step forward and two steps back for AI here. Meanwhile, China is building out its own capacity. Every year we spend fighting over whether to build gives China another year to find out what it can do with what it’s already building.  I’m pro-AI because I believe humans can coexist with it and live better lives for having built it. T

hat’s exactly why I want the hyperscalers to stop what they’re doing and turn the full power of AI toward medicine, health, and biology. Put the best models, the best engineers, and the compute they’ve been hoarding for the race to AGI to work on cancer, rare diseases, and giving people more healthy years with the people they love. Make that the main business of frontier AI, starting now.  

We already have a glimpse of what that could look like. Researchers used AI to design a CRISPR tool that successfully edited human DNA in the lab. Imagine making work like that the central mission of the industry and committing the resources to carry promising discoveries through testing and into treatments ordinary people can afford. Solving a hundred-year-old math problem is an achievement. To a mother whose child has a disease nobody knows how to treat, the problem she wants solved is the one she woke up with this morning.  

I’ve listened to the abundance talk on Moonshots and All-In, and to Elon Musk describe a future where money might cease to matter. I’d love to see it. But there’s something rich about telling people that money will someday be meaningless while racing to see who can make the most of it, then asking a town to make room on its power grid for the privilege. If the people building AI believe their own story about abundance, they can start by putting everything they’ve got into something a family can use while that family is still around to use it.  

The next time a hyperscaler asks a town for enough electricity to power a small city, I want it to be able to tell the people in that room what all that power has already done for someone like them. If the best it can offer is a vision of abundance someday, I think we already know how that town is going to vote.

Sir,
The candor with which you speak, on the eve of withdrawing from this publick stage, does you credit. Few men are willing to lay bare so private a struggle before the eyes of others, and fewer still to confess that the convictions of a lifetime have not always been attended by the warmth of feeling they observe in others.

It is no rare thing for a man who has long held the truths of the Christian faith, the death and rising of our Lord, the certainty of His return, to pass through seasons in which the presence of God seems distant. The heart is not always sensible of what the understanding affirms. 

The Christian course is more often a matter of steady duty than of uninterrupted rapture: of prayer offered when the spirit is dry, of the Scriptures opened when the mind is distracted, of the ordinances of the church attended when the world presses hard. 

These are the appointed means; in them, rather than in the fluctuating experiences of men, is the ordinary path toward a closer walk.

The cares you name, the rearing of children, the disorder of the times, the general chaos of life, are real and weighty. Yet the same Providence that has ordered the affairs of nations through greater trials does not abandon those who continue to seek Him. 

Your desire to turn from the noise of the world toward the Author of your being is itself a mark that the heart is not wholly estranged. Persist in the resolutions you have formed. Let prayer become more frequent and more sincere; let the sacred writings be your daily companion; let the publick worship of God reclaim its proper place. 

In these, and in the quiet performance of your duties as a husband and father, you will find the surest antidote to the restlessness you describe.

I shall not fail to remember you and your family in my own petitions. May the God who has promised to those who seek Him that they shall find, grant you the knowledge of His will and the strength to walk in it. More than the fleeting notice of men, may you obtain that peace which is the fruit of a life ordered under His hand.

With every sentiment of regard,
G. Washington

🇦🇱|Rama’s Script: Blame Tehran, Protect the Kushner Deal, Hide the MEK Base

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama went on television Thursday and said: “I have never said that the protests were organised by Iran. What I have said is that the hands of the criminal regime in Tehran are there on the boulevard, and there is evidence of that.” He offered no evidence.

This is a deflection operation. The protest movement, the Flamingo Revolution, began on 30 May 2026 when residents of Zvërnec found a protected coastline fenced off by masked private security guards for a luxury resort linked to Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump. The project is a $1.4 billion development on the Vjosa-Narta protected delta and Sazan Island, backed by Kushner’s Affinity Partners. When protesters were beaten and dragged away by private security in front of police who stood by, the movement exploded.

By 13 October, student-led demonstrations in Tirana were met with rubber bullets, water cannon, and tear gas. By 18 October, 272 people had been injured, according to Albania’s health ministry.

Rama’s answer to a genuine uprising against corruption and the sell-off of Albanian land is to invent an Iranian hand.

The Evidence He Claims Does Not Exist

Rama says there is “evidence.” He has produced none. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, called the accusations “ridiculous” and said: “Iran is being used as an excuse to avoid responsibility towards the Albanian people. These accusations are a repeated pattern by governments seeking rapprochement with the Zionist regime”.

Baghaei added: “Perhaps they will say the flamingos were likely Iranian security agents”.

Albania’s former foreign minister, Ditmir Bushati, dismissed the claim outright: “Iran has no influence in Albania. This is a country that lives happily in the orbit of the United States”.

The Real Foreign Presence: Camp Ashraf 3

Rama does not mention the foreign presence that is actually on Albanian soil.

Camp Ashraf 3 sits in Manëz, near the port city of Durrës, about 30 kilometres west of Tirana. It houses over 3,000 members of the Mujahedin-e Khalq (MEK). The MEK is an Iranian exile organisation that fought alongside Saddam Hussein during the Iran-Iraq war. The United States designated it a terrorist organisation in 1997, then removed it from the list in 2012 and, at Washington’s request, Albania agreed to shelter its members from 2013 to 2016.

The MEK does not sit quietly in Manëz. Reporting indicates the camp has evolved into a base for cyber and intelligence operations targeting Iran, coordinating with Mossad to assassinate Iranian nuclear scientists. An Iranian cyber group, Homeland Justice, has claimed responsibility for digital disruptions in Albania, explicitly citing the country’s hosting of the MEK as the reason. Iran has repeatedly arrested and executed individuals accused of serving as a bridge between Mossad and the MEK.

Rama’s government severed diplomatic relations with Iran in September 2022 after a massive cyberattack, which he blamed on Tehran. Since then, Tirana has formalised a security memorandum with Israel focused on cyber defence and intelligence exchange in 2023.

The Israeli Arms File

Rama’s ties to Israel are not limited to intelligence. His government has signed a secret, multimillion-euro arms contract with Elbit Systems, an Israeli defence company that has been placed under investigation by NATO for corruption. The contract was signed in July 2025, despite the NATO suspension, and Rama has refused to disclose its terms. He is also discussing the establishment of a national special forces school in Albania in cooperation with one of Israel’s most renowned military training centres.

Rama has also backed Albania’s participation in the US-led International Stabilization Force for Gaza, one of five countries preparing to deploy troops under the Trump plan.

The Script in Full

Rama’s function is to service two patrons at once.

For Washington, he hosts the MEK, absorbs the Iranian retaliation that comes with it, and provides a loyal voice in the Balkans.

For Tel Aviv, he signs the arms contracts, formalises the intelligence-sharing, and uses Albania’s wartime record of protecting Jews to justify deeper military ties.

The Flamingo Revolution threatens both arrangements. A movement that began over a Kushner resort has grown into a demand for Rama’s resignation over corruption, land seizures, and the sale of Albanian sovereignty. The last thing Rama can afford is for the world to see the protests for what they are: a popular uprising against a government that has turned the country into a servicing station for foreign interests.

So he points at Tehran. He claims “evidence” he will never produce. He uses the MEK’s presence to manufacture a threat, and then uses the threat to justify the police batons, the rubber bullets, and the water cannon.

The Bill

Zvërnec fenced off. 272 injured by 18 October. Camp Ashraf 3 operating with Mossad coordination. A secret Elbit contract under NATO corruption investigation. A $1.4 billion Kushner resort on a protected delta.

And a prime minister telling the world that the hands of Tehran are on the boulevard.

The hands on the boulevard belong to the police Rama deployed. The hands on the land belong to the investors Rama backed. The hands on the intelligence belong to the MEK and Mossad, operating from Albanian soil with Rama’s permission.

The script is not a theory. It is a cover. The bill is being paid by the protesters in Tirana, and the receipt is filed in Washington and Tel Aviv.

text:
Braxton, I appreciate your message, and I understand the points you're making.  There is no way I can adequately explain everything my family and I have experienced from 2021 to the present in a social media exchange.  My pinned post offers some insight, but even that only scratches the surface.

First, I want to address a misconception I've seen repeated on X regarding the January 6th pardons.

While many of us are deeply grateful for the pardons, a presidential pardon does not automatically expunge a criminal record. Our records were not simply erased.  Some cases were dismissed because they were still pending when President Trump issued his clemency proclamation. The legal outcomes varied, but the personal consequences did not simply disappear.

I'd ask you to take a moment and put yourself in my shoes. Try to understand this from the perspective of someone who actually lived through it.

Imagine the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force and other law enforcement agencies surrounding your home or workplace. Imagine officers using loudspeakers, waking your neighbors, or having your coworkers watch as you're taken away in handcuffs.

Consider the "shock and awe" of that experience. The overwhelming show of force, the public humiliation, and the feeling of having your entire life turned upside down in front of your family, neighbors, and coworkers.

What would be going through your mind?

Your family. Your job. Your finances. Your reputation. Your freedom. The uncertainty of what comes next and how you're going to defend yourself.

Then imagine the financial burden of hiring criminal defense attorneys. I was living in Kansas when I was arrested, which meant initially retaining an attorney there. When my case moved to Washington, DC, I needed additional legal representation familiar with that jurisdiction.

Think about the financial and emotional toll of that alone.  

Now consider everything else you stand to lose. Your phone, computers, personal property, employment, relationships, reputation, freedom, and even the support of people you believed would always stand beside you.

In my case, our family also suffered the devastating loss of our unborn baby.

That is a pain I cannot adequately describe, and a loss our family will carry for the rest of our lives.

For years, my wife and son endured fear, trauma, emotional hardship, and uncertainty. The consequences extended far beyond me. 

I haven't spoken to my parents since the day after the FBI raid.

These weren't simply legal or political consequences. They were deeply personal losses that fundamentally changed our lives and fractured relationships that may never be repaired.

And while the pardons brought relief, they did not undo what happened.

Since then, it often feels as though the administration, political commentators, and influencers have moved on to the next issue.

But we haven't. We're still living with the consequences.

I served my country as a United States Marine, including deployments to Iraq, where I fought actual terrorists. I never imagined that the government I served would one day arrive at my own home in the manner it did.

I never imagined experiencing something like this in my own country, much less watching my wife and son endure the consequences alongside me.

I never imagined feeling that institutions entrusted with protecting Americans could be used against citizens because of their political beliefs.

And beyond my personal experience, I worry about the precedent.

January 6th should never become a justification for government overreach or a blueprint for how Americans are treated when they find themselves on the wrong side of political power. Constitutional protections and due process must apply equally to everyone, regardless of political affiliation.

So let me ask you two questions.

Are you truly willing to risk losing everything for a president or a political movement?

And if you did lose everything, how long would you reasonably expect to wait for someone to seriously investigate what happened to you and your family?

I'm not asking anyone to circumvent due process or disregard the law.  I'm asking for accountability, transparency, recognition of the damage done, and a genuine commitment to investigating and correcting any abuses of government power.

And that brings me back to Benny Johnson, @bennyjohnson.

Benny has spoken publicly about his access to President Trump, including his account of being asked whether he would be interested in serving as Press Secretary.

He has a substantial platform and, by his own account, opportunities to bring concerns directly to people in positions of authority.

Benny identified three strikes that he believes contributed to Republican losses.

I'm telling him there is another issue that deserves attention.

Some people endured extraordinary personal consequences, whose families suffered alongside them, and who believed the promises of accountability would eventually be fulfilled.

Their stories should not disappear simply because pardons have been signed.

Benny, you have an audience and access that many of us don't.  I'm asking you to use that platform to bring these stories and concerns directly to the President and those responsible for ensuring accountability.

Help make sure the people and families who suffered so much are not forgotten once the political conversation moves on.

We aren't asking to be placed above anyone else. We aren't asking for special treatment.

We're asking not to be forgotten.

A pardon may restore someone's freedom, but it does not automatically restore their life.

It does not bring back the lives we've lost. It does not erase the trauma, repair the financial damage, reunite fractured families, restore lost livelihoods, or give us back the years we can never recover.

Accountability should not end when the headlines move on.

Recent studies had linked a longer reproductive span — the years between a woman’s first period and menopause — with a lower risk of Alzheimer’s and dementia. But what about estrogen from outside the body, she wondered. Did years spent taking birth control pills or hormone therapy count, too?

RADIO-QUÉBEC: THE SECRET PLAN HAS NO EXPIRATION DATE, NEITHER DO DONATIONS!
By @BPartisans 

In the wonderful world of Alexis Cossette-Trudel, the political apocalypse is always imminent, the Deep State is always on the verge of collapse, mass arrests are always just around the corner, and the famous “Plan” is always fully operational. For years, the prophecy has been falling apart, but the show goes on. And above all, the fundraising continues.

For the genius of the secret Plan lies precisely in the fact that it has no expiration date. A prediction fails? That was expected. Trump triumphs? The Plan is working. Trump is humiliated? The Plan is working even better. Nothing happens? Patience, patriots! The lack of results is now the ultimate proof that everything is moving forward behind the scenes.

It’s an admirable mechanism: turning every contradiction into confirmation and every failure into a new episode. Not even used-car salesmen would dare offer such an extravagant guarantee.

But behind this endless series of revelations that never actually reveal anything lies a much more down-to-earth reality: crowdfunding.

On Radio-Québec, suggested contributions range from $5 to $100 per month, with a few numerically playful options at $17, $37, or $77. The number 17, an iconic reference for QAnon, has almost become a marketing gimmick. Even numerology seems to have found its payment gateway.

One-time donations can reach $1,717. At that price, one would hope to at least receive the exact date of the Deep State’s collapse, with a money-back guarantee.

How much does this prophecy machine actually bring in? It’s a mystery. No audited public accounts make it possible to determine this. Theoretical simulations suggest several thousand, or even tens of thousands, of dollars per month, depending on the number of donors. But these figures aren’t confirmed revenues: they simply illustrate the economic potential of a loyal audience.

And that’s precisely where the satire becomes delightful.

The public demands proof of global conspiracies, but how many demand accountability for the money they donate? People demand transparency from Washington, the Pentagon, and central banks, while at the same time agreeing to fund a “revelation” enterprise whose revenues remain private.

The real feat isn’t even convincing people that “The Plan” exists anymore. It’s keeping hope alive long enough that the faithful keep coming back for every episode, despite debunked predictions and buried deadlines.

Mind you, there’s nothing wrong with accepting donations. But endlessly peddling the imminence of an event that never happens deserves at least a few questions.

In the end, the only system that seems to function with exemplary consistency may be neither Q, nor Trump, nor a mysterious military operation.

It’s the “Donate” button.

The Deep State can wait. The next monthly payment, on the other hand, already has a set date.

My Election Bot found items worth flagging in the ballots counts this morning. Here are the findings :

This morning's audit found two items worth flagging, and neither is evidence of fraud on its own. I'd treat both as open questions.

1. Some vote totals went down on the results site. Compared with the 11/4 11:45 AM posting, all of the decreases are in write-in tallies:

Clatsop: 14 contests dropped, such as US Rep 1 write-ins (14 to 13), State Rep 32 write-ins (40 to 37), Seaside Mayor (94 to 89) and Soil & Water At-Large Pos 2 (961 to 945). Seaside Ward 2's total votes fell by 3.

Washington: Gaston Pos 6 (3 to 2) and Tualatin Mayor (11 to 10).

Statewide: the State Rep 32 write-in total also fell.

Named candidates in those races kept rising normally. The likely explanation is that invalid write-ins were reclassified during adjudication, but a county total should not go down without a published reason, so I'm keeping it on the watchlist.

2. The registered-voter numbers still don't reconcile. The refreshed ballot-returns PDF still shows the frozen 3,117,439 active voters, so it wasn't changed. But the Secretary of State's November monthly report (data dated 11/3) shows 3,112,307, which is 5,132 lower. By county, Multnomah is +3,509, Washington +2,343 and Deschutes +883, while Marion is −2,767, Clackamas −2,089, Lane −1,651 and Jackson −1,078. In 2022 and 2024 the election-day monthly figure was above the frozen count, and this year it is below. The results site is a third source at 3,109,086, and it dropped by 3 in Lincoln this morning. A different snapshot date is a plausible reason, but no source says which registration extract it uses. That question is a good fit for the records request I offered.

Count status:

Ballots received: the PDF finally refreshed to 1,983,255 (63.62%), up 174,485 since the 8:06 PM report. It equals the sum of the counties.

Counted: 1,638,442, which is at or below received in all 36 counties. Marion is only 58.6% processed, Washington 66.2% and Multnomah 72.8%.

Governor: Kotek 843,263, Drazan 735,625, Smith 43,630. Kotek's margin is 6.63%, up from 6.26%, with no reversal.

Closest race at statewide-reporting level: the Wilsonville Councilor race at 86 votes (0.50%), which is not a recount case.

By-day table: the gap is now 2 ballots, with Multnomah and Lane each off by 1. Coos has cleared. There are small downward revisions to earlier days in Umatilla (−15), Washington (−7) and Marion (−2), and no county total fell.

Sums: county totals match statewide in every Governor and legislative export.

I'll keep checking each morning.

text:
Israel in Europe: Nineteenth- and Twentieth-Century Latter-day Saint Discourses on the Lost Tribes

Nineteenth-century Latter-day Saint statements frequently identified descendants of the lost tribes (particularly Ephraim) among European populations in Scandinavia, Germany, and Britain. Foundational treatments include Apostle Erastus Snow’s migration discourses and George Reynolds’s Are We of Israel? 

These writers typically affirmed that literal Israelites had dispersed into European nations through migration and intermarriage, while simultaneously maintaining the traditional belief in a separate, cohesive body of the Ten Tribes still concealed in an undisclosed northern region.

 Part I: The Nineteenth-Century Foundation

Surveys of nineteenth-century sources—primarily sermons, doctrinal books, and Church periodicals—reveal a consistent pattern among early leaders.

1. Erastus Snow (May 6, 1882): Explicit Migration into Northern Europe  
Speaking in Logan, Utah, Apostle Erastus Snow traced Ephraimite remnants from Palestine to the Caspian Sea, then into Scandinavia and northern Germany, and finally into Scotland and England. He linked these migrations to Britain’s rulers, intermarriage with Anglo-Saxon populations, and the ancestry of later American colonists.

Snow’s geographic description is distinctive: “the north of Europe, western Scandinavia and northern Germany, penetrating Scotland and England.” He further stated that “Their blood has permeated European society” (Journal of Discourses 23:186–87).

This remains the most explicit nineteenth-century sermon outlining a literal migration route into Europe. Snow focused primarily on Ephraim rather than equating every European nation with the full Ten Tribes.

2. George Reynolds (Are We of Israel?, 1895): Branches of the Tribes in Europe  

Reynolds offered the period’s most extended discussion in Are We of Israel? (second edition, 1895, George Q. Cannon & Sons). In Chapter II he examined the claim that “remnants or branches of the lost Ten Tribes had emigrated from Media into Europe.”

Earlier, in Chapter I, he described how some Israelite groups separated from the main body, intermarried with surrounding gentile populations, and gradually lost awareness of their origins. He connected this process specifically to Ephraimite lineages among northern Europeans. While exploring routes through southeastern Europe and possible links to the Goths and other northern peoples, Reynolds treated British-Israelite schemes that assigned exclusive tribes to particular English counties with skepticism. He nevertheless retained the parallel belief in a separate, hidden northern body of the Ten Tribes (Chapters I–VI).

3. Brigham Young (April 8, 1855): Ephraim Mixed Among the Nations  

Brigham Young articulated a broader theology of dispersion and gathering: “Ephraim has become mixed with all the nations of the earth, and it is Ephraim that is gathering together” (Journal of Discourses 2:268–69).

He presented missionary work as the recovery of literal Israelites dispersed among Gentile populations, citing England and Russia as primary fields. Although Young supplied no detailed migration route and did not identify European nations collectively as the Ten Tribes, his teaching established the theological framework that made Snow’s later geographic accounts intelligible.

4. James E. Talmage (1899): Dispersal Compatible with a Hidden Body  

In the 1899 edition of Articles of Faith (Lecture XVIII, paragraph 26), James E. Talmage distinguished between individuals of the Ten Tribes scattered among foreign nations and the substantial body led away together to an undisclosed location. Although he did not single out Europe, his framing demonstrates that a nineteenth-century Latter-day Saint theologian could affirm Israelite ancestry among Europeans while still awaiting the future public return of the intact Ten Tribes.

5. Erastus Snow’s Dual Framework  

Five months after his European migration sermon, Snow addressed the Ten Tribes’ removal to a hidden northern country whose location remained unknown (October 7, 1882, Journal of Discourses 23:299–300). For Snow, European Ephraimite ancestry and a concealed northern community were fully compatible.

text: On October 29, 1971, a baby girl was born near Winona, Minnesota. Her parents named her Winona Laura Horowitz. For a time her family lived without electricity or television, so she read. Books became her world.  When she was 10, they moved to Petaluma, California. On her third day at school she wore an old boy’s suit from a thrift store. Students cornered her, called her names, and slammed her head into a locker. She never went back. Her parents taught her at home.  She started acting classes at 12. In 1988 she starred in Beetlejuice. Fame did not stop the bullying at Petaluma High. They called her a witch. She still graduated with a 4.0 GPA.  In 1993, 12-year-old Polly Klaas was taken from a slumber party in Petaluma. Winona offered a $200,000 reward and kept Polly’s name in the news. When Polly was found dead, Winona dedicated her 1994 performance as Jo March in Little Women to her memory. It earned her an Oscar nomination.  In 2001 she was arrested for shoplifting. Insurance companies dropped her. She disappeared from the screen for four years.  In 2015 she was cast as Joyce Byers in Stranger Things. She asked Polly’s father how to play a parent whose child vanishes. The show became a global hit. She appeared in 42 episodes across nearly a decade.  The girl who was once bullied in a thrift-store suit never became cruel. She showed up for a grieving family in her hometown, and she showed up for herself after the world had counted her out.  Some people allow the worst days of their lives to harden them. Winona let hers teach her kindness.

text:
It's part of SF life - wherever you work you'll always have recruiters from the competition trying to poach you.   

Non competes, without compensation, aren't allowed in California, so you could leave and start the same day if you like.   You can't take documents or property from one employer to the next, but nothing stops you from sharing your experiences or knowledge that you gained in your head.

The only way to keep people from switching sides would be to agree to a contract where the person would not accept a job at a competitor for X amount of time and in exchange would receive Y amount of money.   

If they breach that contract they'd likely have to give all the money back - so you will see this with high level executives who quit, take 6-12 months off, and then join a competition.

However, in today's world of AI, sitting 12 months out would destroy your market value, plus OpenAI probably offered Cat north of 100M in pre-ipo stock - so unless Anthropic wanted to pay her more to sit out, she's free to leave.  

Plus, now she has 100s of millions of stock in the two top AI labs - so no matter which wins or which loses, she'll still make out very very well.

It's definitely a money motivated decision and is illustrative of the the mercenary, go to highest bidder, no loyalty, that pervades San Francisco.

text:
The Big Board at Dawn

Morning arrives in Washington. Analysts debate the results. Political strategists offer explanations. Some races remain unsettled.

And in a tiny fictional California laboratory, Millicent gathers the remaining spaghetti.

A little butter.

Some pesto.

Parmesan.

Garlic.

Onion.

She takes one bite, looks at the television, and sets down the fork.

“Matthew,” she says, “I believe I have discovered a political system in which the meatball insists it cooked dinner, but denies ever entering the kitchen.”

The returns are still there. The spaghetti is still there. The president is still president.

And the metaphor, despite repeated efforts to remove it, is still on the menu.

FINIS.

The sauce, unlike the political responsibility being debated, has successfully adhered to every available surface.

text:
I ask every listing agent the same question before I make an offer:

"Did anyone die in this house?"

If the answer is yes, my offer drops by $30,000

Not one seller has turned it down yet

Here's why the seller says yes, and why the law lets them keep it from you:

In most states a death in a house isn't something the seller has to disclose. Natural, accident, suicide, the law treats it as a stigma about the house, and stigmas don't have to go on the form

California is one of the few exceptions. Sellers there have to disclose any death in the last 3 years

But if you ask directly, in most states the seller and the agent can't lie to you. So I ask every time, in writing

Why they say yes to $30,000 less:

The neighbors tell every buyer who tours it. Buyers back out during inspection, the house sits, and the family keeps paying taxes, insurance and utilities on a house they don't want to walk back into

An offer that makes all of that stop is worth more to them than the last $30,000

How much off depends on what happened:

-A grandma who passed away in her sleep at 91 scares off fewer buyers. The discount on those comes from heirs 3 states away who want it done

-A suicide or a violent death is where the big discounts are. A lot of buyers won't even tour it

-If the person wasn't found for a while... the floors and subfloor have to come out. Professional cleanup can run up to $20,000, so I ask if the seller's insurance already paid for it

And the discount stays with me. An appraiser prices the square footage, the condition and what the houses nearby sold for

What happened in the bedroom isn't on that form

Here's how I find and check them:

1. Filter for listings sitting 60+ days or marked "back on market", and search the description for "estate", "executor" or "as-is"
2. Look up the owner on the county tax site. "Estate of" or a mailing address in another state means heirs are paying for an empty house
3. Search the address on DiedInHouse. It's about $12 and pulls death records tied to the address
4. Google the address with "obituary" and talk to the neighbor. They always know

Finding these houses is the easy part. Most people lose them when the family says yes and the money isn't ready, because the next investor asking the same question isn't waiting on a bank either

You find the ugly house. We help you get the money to buy it
