text:
A THOUSAND-YEAR-OLD MYSTERY CARVED INTO THE ROCKS OF UTAH!

Hidden among the rugged sandstone canyons of Utah, USA, these remarkable ancient carvings have survived for more than 1,000 years. Created by the Fremont people, an ancient culture that lived across parts of the American Southwest, these mysterious images offer a rare glimpse into a world that existed long before modern civilization.

Look closely, and one figure immediately catches your attention. A tall, human-like character with an unusually large body, elaborate headgear, and mysterious geometric patterns covering its torso dominates the rock face. Around it are images of bighorn sheep and smaller human-like figures, carefully carved into the stone by ancient hands.

But what did these symbols actually mean? Were they connected to religious ceremonies, powerful spiritual beings, ancient stories, or beliefs about the natural world? The Fremont people left no written explanation, and despite years of archaeological research, many questions remain unanswered.

The bighorn sheep appear repeatedly in Fremont rock art, suggesting that these animals may have held an important place in their lives and beliefs. The larger human-like figures, often decorated with elaborate designs, are equally fascinating. Some researchers believe these carvings may have carried symbolic or ceremonial meanings, although their exact purpose remains unknown.

Perhaps the most incredible thing is that these images have survived centuries of wind, sunlight, and changing landscapes. Long after the people who created them disappeared as a distinct culture, their artwork continues to speak through the stone.

More than a thousand years later, we can still stand before these ancient carvings and wonder what their creators were trying to tell us.

Source: National Park Service (NPS), Capitol Reef National Park – Fremont Culture Petroglyphs.

If athletes are allowed to break commitment without penalty, schools should be allowed to yank their scholarship if they find a better player too. Now obviously that sounds ridiculous, but the relationship should be symmetrical.

text:
$MSFT Microsoft is tightening oversight of some data center projects and stepping away from ones it deems risky due to delays, regulatory snags, and high costs.

The company is debating internally whether to ink new neocloud deals, with some leaders expressing strong reluctance to add new capacity from third-party providers. $CRWV $IREN $CORZ $NBIS 

Microsoft is focusing on expanding its own data centers, having added more than $200 billion of new data center lease commitments over the last year, with the goal of bringing capacity online reliably and efficiently.

The friction was on display during Microsoft’s most-recent earnings call, when Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said that delays in the delivery of some third-party capacity was disrupting the company’s spending plans. It was the third time she has called out such issues on an earnings call.

Some of the recent hiccups involved issues with cabling at a site in Texas being developed by IREN, according to people familiar with the situation. Data center servers are connected by intricate networks of fiber-optic cables. IREN, an Australian firm that pivoted from cryptocurrency to AI in 2023, also suffered a generator fire at the campus in April and disclosed hardware delivery delays there in August.

IREN and Microsoft officials met last week and negotiated a revised timeline that may push back the site’s completion by several weeks or months, according to people familiar with the events.
Microsoft manages relationships with infrastructure partners “against our requirements and customer demand, including monitoring delivery and adjusting plans when circumstances change,” a company spokesperson said. “

These are normal and responsible practices for managing large, complex infrastructure projects, and they help us bring capacity online reliably and efficiently.”

IREN declined to comment.

Shares of IREN and Nebius both fell about 20% on Thursday amid a broader selloff of AI infrastructure stocks.

It’s a perilous moment for the neoclouds, which were created to capitalize on a shortage of computing power by speeding up the deployment of artificial intelligence infrastructure, including chips from Nvidia Corp.

Industry analyst Gartner Inc. recently estimated that 80% of neocloud providers could be consolidated or closed by the end of the decade. Elon Musk — whose SpaceX also sells computing power — offered a similarly bleak outlook of “guppy-level death” for many neoclouds because they’re struggling to raise sufficient funds to operate.

These fears were compounded after a series of victories this week by Democratic candidates for governor, who made more aggressive data center regulation a central part of their campaigns. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa in particular has called for an immediate moratorium on data center development until more thorough regulation is established.

Microsoft was the nascent industry’s most crucial early patron, providing the likes of CoreWeave Inc. and Nscale with massive contracts that let them get big quickly. Even though Microsoft has a huge fleet of data centers, it was willing to pay up to meet demand it couldn’t handle on its own.

“We’ve had to pinch our nose and borrow GPUs from some of our competitors,” Microsoft Executive Vice President Mat McBride said of the company’s neocloud deals during a conference hosted by Evercore in June. “We’ve done that because we have a very, very strong demand signal.”

Each week, CFO Hood chairs a meeting about computing capacity – when it’s coming online, from where and which part of the company will get it. A common point of discussion at these sessions is whether the neoclouds’ timelines are credible and what Microsoft can do to accelerate them, according to people who’ve been involved with the meetings.

Increasingly, Microsoft is putting boots on the ground. In recent months, the company has dispatched workers to neocloud sites to make sure facilities are being built to its specifications and following regulations, according to job listings and people familiar with the matter. For example, Microsoft sent workers to a Nebius site in New Jersey that was fined $1 million for running generators without permits. Microsoft has also sent people to projects in Texas being built by Nscale and IREN.

In other cases, Microsoft is walking away from sites it no longer considers tenable, including multiple Nscale projects. It declined to expand its deal with Nscale in Texas, and some of that capacity ended up being taken by Figure AI. Microsoft also stepped away from a letter of intent to lease 1.35 gigawatts from the company in West Virginia.

And last month it cancelled a roughly $3 billion Nscale deal tied to a UK data center owing to multiyear delays in getting grid power, according to people familiar with the deal. Nscale said at the time that the UK withdrawal didn’t impact its other deals with Microsoft.

The Information and Financial Times previously reported some details of Microsoft’s IREN and Nscale deals.

Microsoft is currently focused on expanding its own data centers rather than adding new neocloud deals, according to those who’ve spoken with leaders inside the company. The company hasn’t entirely sworn off new neocloud deals, but many company leaders express strong reluctance, the people said.

Over the last year, Microsoft has added more than $200 billion of new data center lease commitments. Some of this includes neocloud capacity, according to a spokesperson. All of this spending is being directed toward major expansion of its own server farm capacity in the coming years, Bloomberg previously reported.

Buying third-party computing capacity was always controversial at Microsoft. Executives were concerned that even partial outsourcing would help prop up would-be competitors. They also fretted that Microsoft would be exposed to higher costs and execution risks because neoclouds had limited experience building and operating server farms.

Some of the competition fears came true: CoreWeave hired a handful of key executives from Microsoft, then did a deal directly with close partner OpenAI last year. This rankled many leaders inside Microsoft, according to employees who were present at the time. A CoreWeave spokesperson said that Microsoft was one of its first partners and collaborators, “and we continue to have a great relationship.”

Nebius has been unusually upfront with its competitive strategy. It will scale up by inking contracts with big customers like Microsoft or Meta Platforms Inc. knowing that they’ll abandon neoclouds in the long run, Nebius CEO Arkady Volozh said during a March conference hosted by Morgan Stanley.

“We treat this business as temporary,” Volozh said, referring to his company’s deals with customers like Microsoft and Meta. “They just cannot cope with the speed now — that’s why they’re outsourcing.”

Meanwhile, demand for computing power remains much higher than supply — and is expected to for the foreseeable future. So even if Microsoft decides not to sign new neocloud deals, Anthropic PBC and Alphabet Inc.’s Google have been accelerating their own commitments to the upstart data center operators.

text:
Stormy Daniels was paid $130,000 in 2016 to stay quiet about Donald Trump. In 2024, she paid Trump $627,500.

Her lawyer, Michael Avenatti, called himself her "biggest champion." He was later convicted of stealing nearly $300,000 of her book money.

In the video below, Trump is asked on Air Force One if he knew about the $130,000. "No," he says. Then Stormy tells Piers Morgan she'd go to jail before paying him a penny, CBS News reports his lawyers' offer, and she says what she finally paid.

In 2018 she sued Trump for defamation, a suit she says Avenatti filed against her wishes. A judge threw it out and ordered her to pay Trump's legal fees.

With appeals and interest, the bill reached $652,362 by July 2024. Then Trump's lawyer offered to cut it to $620,000 if she agreed in writing to make "no public or private statements" about their alleged past.

She refused. Her new lawyer told CBS News she paid $627,500. In the clip, she puts it at "nearly $700,000."

The case for Trump: the suit was filed in her name, she lost, and she owed the fees either way. He denies any sexual encounter with her.

Stormy now does stand-up, and the scandal is part of the act. Last year she said she was still getting threats telling her to "pay Trump what you owe him." Avenatti left prison in April for a halfway house. This week, Trump's lawyers asked a New York appeals court to throw out his hush money conviction.

Would you have paid $620,000 and stayed silent, or paid $627,500 and kept talking?

text:
"Haiti Is Not Here!"

This is a map of Central America and the Caribbean.

The country on the left, with no coastline along the Caribbean Sea or the Gulf of Mexico, is El Salvador.

That portion of an island on the far right—1,500 km away (roughly the distance between the Uruguayan border and the city of Rio de Janeiro)—is Haiti.

El Salvador has a navy limited to coastal operations, an air force that serves primarily a logistical role, and an army of 24,000 personnel trained exclusively for territorial protection (akin to a military police force).

Haiti has a population of 12 million, with an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 active gang members and over 100,000 weapons. This does not necessarily mean they are superior to a well-trained, well-equipped military force; however, history offers countless examples of highly trained and heavily armed militaries being decimated by paramilitary groups—sometimes consisting of little more than farmers wearing flip-flops.

This is due to the inherent complexities of urban guerrilla warfare: difficult, fortified terrain, the element of surprise, ambushes, intelligence provided by the local population, intimate knowledge of the landscape, and so on.

El Salvador is part of a coalition of nations—initially known as the Multinational Security Support (MSS) mission—which is set to be renamed the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) in 2026, following a transition in leadership to the United States, which stepped in after sanctions were imposed on the Kenyan leadership. Haiti is recognized as the only country to have experienced a successful slave revolution that led to its very founding. It is also a nation subject to constant North American interference and repeated international interventions—ostensibly for humanitarian aid or to combat criminal factions and gangs—despite having governments widely viewed as Western puppet regimes. Some lines of inquiry suggest that certain paramilitary groups may actually represent local resistance to Western domination (not to be confused with the militias or criminal factions found in Brazil). The military personnel allegedly held hostage by Haitian gangs were part of a "Gang Repression Force."

Now, where does this get interesting?

The four Salvadoran military personnel supposedly held captive by Haitian gangs—a pilot, two aviation technicians, and a sergeant—were reportedly in an armored vehicle, heading to purchase food and supplies in a "red zone." The vehicle, which was carrying explosives, was ambushed and caught fire; after the men fled the vehicle, there was no further word from them, and all communication ceased.

No gang has claimed responsibility for the attack, nor has any group reached out to the GSF to negotiate the release of the captives. An NGO reportedly delivered four sets of human remains to the GSF headquarters in Port-au-Prince. According to *The New York Times*, the bodies were severely burned, requiring forensic analysis for identification. Meanwhile, the President of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, has rejected the claim that the remains belong to his country’s soldiers, citing reasons that lack scientific rigor—such as "they were wearing uniforms from another country, their heights did not match, and they were carrying documents that did not belong to them." The questions to be asked in this case would be:

1 - What would a contingent of aviation technicians and pilots be doing on a supposed humanitarian food-resupply mission at a public market located in a "red zone" of a country experiencing urban guerrilla warfare? Such a task would be for soldiers; furthermore, one would logically use markets in secure areas, not zones controlled by hostile gangs.

2 - Why were these military personnel carrying explosives through civilian areas—even if they were "red zones"? This looks much more like a covert operation or an infiltration mission.

3 - If the objective—as suggested by the GSF—was to capture the military personnel in order to negotiate the GSF’s withdrawal, why did no gang come forward to claim responsibility for the ambush, nor open any channel for negotiation with the GSF? This begins to sound like a narrative reversal—a form of damage control for a suspicious operation that went terribly wrong.

4 - What is the truth? Were the bodies so badly burned—as indicated by The New York Times—or were they in a condition that allowed for the identification of uniforms, documents, and even height—as claimed by Bukele—without a properly conducted forensic examination?

5 - Why did President Nayib Bukele reject any form of contact or negotiation, opting instead to invade another country—an act that violates international law—even with the backing of (astonishingly) the United States?

Based on the data and the discrepancies—along with points that remain poorly explained—my assessment of what occurred is that an assassination attempt or a "false flag" operation likely went terribly wrong. Since one should never let a crisis go to waste, the subsequent damage control involved crafting an "ambush" narrative. This serves to justify the deployment of a larger military contingent for the purpose of invasion and territorial control—perhaps to secure a beachhead for a future, larger-scale incursion. El Salvador was chosen because it is part of the GSF (Global Security Force)—which already enjoys a degree of backing from the international community and the UN Security Council—and because of its well-known ties to the Trump administration. Direct intervention by the United States would have violated international law and risked dragging the U.S. into yet another quagmire, adding to the existing crises in Ukraine, Iran, Yemen, Syria, Lebanon, and Taiwan. Furthermore, Bukele needs to "pay" for the positive PR that painted him as the "beacon of the Latin American right" in the fight against urban violence.

How do I imagine it all unfolded?

Either a plan that went wrong, or one that went exactly as intended:
- Four Salvadoran military personnel were tasked with planting explosives in a popular market—either to assassinate a gang leader or simply to carry out an act of terror designed to spark international outrage. The goal was to blame Haitian gangs for the attack, labeling them as terrorists targeting the Haitian civilian population, thereby providing a pretext for a full-scale military invasion.
Things went wrong! But, as the saying goes, never let a good crisis go to waste. They leveraged their "soft power" apparatus to construct and disseminate a narrative about an "ambush" and the capture of these soldiers. This was then used as a bargaining chip in negotiations regarding the withdrawal of GSF forces—all while providing a convenient justification for a military invasion, now thinly veiled as a "rescue and humanitarian aid operation." OR

- The four military personnel were tasked with a mission as previously described, BUT, in reality, this was a "false flag" operation from the start. Explosives were intentionally detonated inside the armored vehicle, rendering the bodies unrecognizable—a scenario that allows any narrative to be propagated in the absence of evidence, footage, or official testimony.
THIS WOULD HAVE WORKED: it explains why the remains were, according to the *New York Times*, burned and unrecognizable. It also explains why Bukele so abruptly rejected the bodies—without any detailed forensic analysis—offering only a blunt, baseless dismissal: "It isn't [them], because I say it isn't—and that’s that." This false flag serves as the justification for an unauthorized (by the UN) incursion into the country by Salvadoran military forces unaffiliated with the GSF.

Layered on top of this is an alleged letter to the UN—purportedly sent by Lanmò Sanjou, leader of the "400 Mawozo" gang—as well as an interview with the AP, in which he claims the military personnel are dead. He asserts that he is personally raising a white flag and requesting an international delegation, led by the UN, to negotiate a peaceful resolution to Haiti’s problems. He further accuses international forces of killing civilians—including children and the elderly—via drone strikes under the guise of "hunting gangs." He also accuses local politicians of simultaneously arming these gangs while inviting international intervention, all to keep the country in a state of chaos and violence.

There is a $1 million bounty on Lanmò Sanjou’s head, stemming from his conviction in connection with the 2021 kidnapping of 17 "missionaries"—all of whom were eventually released unharmed. A representative for the unidentified group stated that this was not a kidnapping, but rather an action demanding justice regarding another missionary—one whom the group has accused of molesting and sexually abusing Haitian boys.

The missionary accused of abusing these boys was tried in an Ohio court, where he pleaded guilty and admitted to having abused approximately 30 boys, aged 8 to 18, between 2002 and 2019. He was also tried for abusing four other boys in Ohio. There is nothing new here; there are dozens of scandals involving the sexual abuse of minors perpetrated by "missionaries" from North American Christian groups. Apparently, no international pedophilia ring goes unpunished for those who expose and fight against them...

Thursday Soybean Report Thursday, November 5, 2026
The soybean market is experiencing widespread technical selling and harvest pressure this Thursday, breaking below the psychological $12.00 barrier to post multi-month lows across the active futures board. 

A sharp pullback in crude oil (/CLZ26 down to $90.55/bbl) is spilling over into vegetable oils, dragging soy oil (/ZLZ26 down to 62.24 c/lb) and soymeal (/ZMZ26 down to $318.00/ton) significantly lower. 

With national harvest advancing to 88% complete and favorable early planting conditions across Brazil, market participants are aggressively squaring positions ahead of next week's November WASDE report.

Futures & Market News CBOT soybean futures are trading sharply lower across all active contract months today, reflecting broader macro energy weakness and seasonal hedge pressure.

January 2027 (F) sits at $11.93 4/8 (/ZS[F27] at 1193.50), down 42 0/8 cents from last week's trade. March 2027 (H) is trading near $12.06 0/0, while May 2027 (K) is hovering near $12.18 4/8.

Key Driver: A steep decline in energy markets is acting as the main headwind today. 

Front month Crude Oil (/CLZ26) dropped over $10.00 from last week's highs to trade at $90.55/bbl, triggering heavy long liquidation in Soybean Oil (/ZLZ26 down to 62.24 c/lb) and Soybean Meal (/ZMZ26 down to $318.00/ton). 

Furthermore, traders are locking in risk parameters ahead of the USDA’s November 10 WASDE report, balancing the U.S. harvest tail end against expanding South American production potential.

USDA Soybean News: Crop Progress & Export Activity

National Harvest Nearing Completion: Monday afternoon's USDA Crop Progress report showed national soybean harvest advancing to 88% complete nationwide, pacing ahead of the 5 year historical average of 84%.

Core Belt Finished: Fieldwork across the primary I-80 corridor is effectively wrapped up, with states like Iowa, Illinois, and Minnesota passing 92% to 95% completion as combines park for the season.

Pre WASDE Positioning: The USDA will release its November WASDE on Tuesday, November 10. Market consensus expects ending stocks to remain comfortably padded near 310–315 million bushels, reflecting strong domestic crush baseline assumptions offset by expanding global supplies.

Commitments of Traders: Managed Money Speculative funds have expanded their net-short posture this week, pushing front month futures below the key $12.00 floor.

January 2027 futures (/ZSF27) have broken technical support at $12.00, with the next major chart baseline resting near $11.80 to $11.85. Technical resistance has lowered to the former breakdown zone of $12.15 to $12.20.

Crop & Weather Update Clear weather across the Midwest over the past week allowed growers to finish harvest with minimal interruption. Attention is shifting toward regional soil moisture recharge heading into winter.

In South America, central Brazil and Argentina are receiving timely early-season rainfall, supporting rapid planting progress and favorable crop establishment across key export regions.

Biofuel & 45Z Industry News The pullbacks in crude oil ($90.55/bbl) and soy oil (62.24 c/lb) have compressed short term processing margins, though domestic crushers continue to operate at robust run rates.

Long term domestic demand expectations remain anchored by the upcoming Section 45Z clean fuel rules, encouraging processors to maintain high crush capacity to serve domestic biofuel blending allocations heading into 2027.

Regional Cash Bids (Nebraska & Iowa) Country cash bids have adjusted sharply lower alongside the board's break below $12.00, though local processor basis remains historically steady relative to post-harvest baselines.

Strategies:

Commercials: Use current board weakness near $11.93 to lock in extended Q1/Q2 2027 crush coverage while spot soybean oil and meal values offer favorable input pricing.

Producers: With harvest 88% finished and futures below $12.00, avoid panic-selling off-the-combine bushels into chart weakness. Utilize commercial or farm storage to wait out seasonal harvest liquidation and capture post-harvest basis recovery toward late Q4.

text:
A lot of people who voted for Trump are complaining that he didn’t do this or dropped the ball on that.

Now it’s time to piss off my followers, so sit down and listen.

Yes, I’m talking to YOU.

You want America First? You have to show up in DC and do the work.

IDGAF if you live in Lubbock, Texas, Fort Wayne, Indiana, or Timbuktu.

Take a week off work, hop on a plane, land in DC, check into a hotel room, and start taking meetings.

The Republic is counting on you.

You can’t log into X, retweet something, and expect results.

This has been the most responsive administration in my lifetime. They do read those tweets. They do take action.

The problem is the follow-through. Not that there isn’t any. You might even get an entire executive order out of a single tweet.

But to make it stick you need to show up in DC, put on a suit, and take at least a dozen meetings to make absolutely certain that momentum is carried forward.

Seems simple enough, right? I don’t care if it’s the Little League championship or trivia night at the bar. You have to show up if you want to win.

We all know that. Yet how many of you are making regular flights to DC? How many of you have Diamond status because you spent over $10K on hotels in DC last year?

Now that I’ve chastised you, let me chastise the administration.

The most frustrating thing about the Trump administration so far, on a personal level, is that proximity matters.

I logged 20,000 miles in my car. I stayed at a friend’s house. I stopped at supermarkets.

And STILL, I spent an incredible amount of money and time traveling to THE most expensive city in America.

Democrats have no problem with Zoom. They have NGOs in every city. They have grassroots campaigns. They have no problem paying cold, hard cash for their people to descend on DC to hold a sign.

I get it. Trump, at his core, is a local businessman. He likes to shake hands and look you in the eye. The man dominated local construction in NYC. Then, when he could afford private jets, he expanded but continued putting in the time.

I don’t have a private jet. I can’t even afford to hop on a commercial flight and stay in a decent hotel in DC for a week.

And I’m worth millions of dollars and run my own company.

From battleships to maritime executive orders, I have accomplished more than I ever expected, but holy sh!t, was it expensive.

And I DROVE MY CAR. Six hours each way from Massachusetts, through the heat, snow, and freezing rain.

Now, it’s not like the administration didn’t try to accommodate me. They offered me an SGE position.

I wish I had never taken it.

Dozens of forms. Hours-long drives to get fingerprinted. Full background checks on everyone in my family.

Then someone in some corner of the administrative state “lost” something, and months went by trying to figure it out.

Then I got ghosted.

HOW THE FUCK does anyone in the administration think this is sustainable??

Accusations are flying around that the administration is corrupt. That it focuses too much on special interests. That it listens to billionaires like @BillAckman or @DavidSacks more than very smart, based people with almost as many followers who don’t have billions.

Accusations that the Israel lobby, Big Oil, or whoever has more access to the Oval Office.

I’ve spent a lot of time in DC. I see little evidence of outright corruption. I have no problem booking meetings with top officials for myself and my friends, with one caveat:

I HAVE TO SHOW UP.

There are no Zoom meetings because everyone is paranoid that a screen recording will leak to the press.

But what I absolutely 💯 DO see is that the rich, both inside and outside DC, can afford DC.

David Sacks can afford to fly his private jet in. I can afford to get a Tesla with self-driving to take me to a friend’s couch.

WTF can someone who really needs the administration’s help, who works 50 hours a week in Texas, afford?

Nada. 1/2

text:
🚨LEARN ABOUT VIRGINIA COURTS: Supreme Court of Virginia Launches Virginia Judicial Civics Week and New In Open Court Educational Website

The Supreme Court of Virginia is marking the start of the inaugural Virginia Judicial Civics Week, November 2–6, 2026, and introduced In Open Court,
https://t.co/XR9hVOCvBE, a new website offering educational resources to help
Virginians understand the judicial branch, the work of courts, and the rule of law.

In Open Court brings together educational resources for students, educators, families, and
community groups. Materials include graphic novels, classroom activities, and resources that
introduce the people, processes, and responsibilities of Virginia’s courts. Additional interactive
learning resources are planned as the initiative develops.

In Open Court is supported by a grant from the State Justice Institute. The website is part of the
broader Virginia Judicial Civics Initiative, which brings together educational resources,
community partnerships, and opportunities for public engagement throughout the year.

“Public trust in our courts depends in part on public understanding of what courts do and why
their work matters,” said Chief Justice Powell. “In Open Court will help Virginians of all ages
better understand their judicial system, the importance of the rule of law, and the responsibility
we all share in sustaining the principles of constitutional government.”

The Virginia Judicial Civics Toolkit, https://t.co/NjOalX0yGI, offers courts and community partners ideas and materials for participation, posters, classroom activities, and ways to share local efforts.

Virginia Judicial Civics Week expands upon the judiciary’s longstanding civic education efforts,
including Rule of Law Day at the Capitol, mock trial programs, courthouse tours, and the
Judicial Learning Center, https://t.co/rQtnWY8IH0. 

Courts and community partners are encouraged
to offer activities during the week or at other times throughout the year. Virginia Judicial Civics
Week complements the Commonwealth’s existing observances of Citizenship Day, Constitution
Week, and Civics Education Week, while placing particular emphasis on the judicial branch.

“Education has more of an impact when it extends beyond websites and classrooms and creates
opportunities for people to engage directly with the institutions that serve them,” Chief Justice
Powell said.

☑️About Virginia’s Judicial System
Virginia’s Judicial System is comprised of the Supreme Court of Virginia, the Court of Appeals

text:
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby flew with rival American Airlines, spotted something he liked and promptly emailed his own employees asking why United didn't have it.

Only to discover they were already planning it.

Kirby, who lives in Dallas, was travelling through American Airlines' hub at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport when he encountered the carrier's new automated boarding gates.

The technology allows passengers to scan their boarding passes before glass barriers open automatically, reducing the need for employees to manually check every traveller.

According to View from the Wing, Kirby was impressed enough to ask his United team why the airline hadn't introduced similar equipment.

Their response? Comparable gates were already planned for Houston.

And this wasn't an unusual trip aboard a competitor.

Kirby has reportedly flown American, Delta and Southwest at least three times each over the past year, deliberately studying what rival airlines do differently.

American introduced nine automated boarding gates at DFW's new Terminal C pier in September 2026.

Whether the technology actually speeds up boarding remains an open question, particularly when passengers still have to contend with crowded aisles and limited overhead bin space.

But Kirby's approach offers an interesting glimpse into airline competition.

Sometimes the best way to see what your rivals are doing is to buy a ticket and experience it yourself.

The connection between retired U.S. Army General David Petraeus and billionaire Tom Pritzker came to light through the public unsealing of over 3 million Department of Justice documents related to Jeffrey Epstein. 

The documents revealed a June 2011 email where Pritzker detailed an "adventure tourism" trip to Afghanistan to visit Petraeus, who was commanding U.S. and NATO forces at the time.

Pritzker’s connection to Petraeus was established through his involvement with Business Executives for National Security (BENS). BENS is a non-profit organization that regularly flew high-level corporate delegations and billionaire executives into active conflict zones to interface with top military commanders.

On June 6, 2011, Jeffrey Epstein emailed Pritzker asking to chat. Pritzker, who was celebrating his birthday on the trip, replied directly from Afghanistan: "I am in a remote valley of Afghanistan (its my birthday wish) with Boys with Toys. Spent time w(ith) Patraeus yesterday and he loaned me a chopper (actually two with one as a back up). Can't call till tomorrow.

The disclosure that military resources—specifically two helicopters—were allegedly diverted to accommodate a billionaire's personal birthday excursion in an active war zone drew immense public scrutiny.

In one of the emails to an unnamed recipient, Epstein reportedly addressed Pritzker as being “like family.” The convicted sex offender also offered to arrange a meeting with the billionaire. The emails show Epstein and Pritzker frequently planning, per Forbes. The outlet reported that in one of the emails, the financier told the Chicago billionaire:

“nice to see you , please come more often.”

Thomas Pritzker reportedly responded, “Always fun.” According to The New York Times, they also discussed invitations to the Pritzker Architecture Prize ceremony in Beijing.

Per the NYT, Tom Pritzker reportedly helped Jeffrey Epstein’s girlfriend, Karyna Shuliak, arrange a Southeast Asian trip in 2018. In the subsequent conversation, the billionaire asked Shuliak about the purpose of her visit, to which she replied:

“Going to try to find a new girlfriend for Jeffrey.”

Pritzker replied:

“May the Force be with you.”

In 2016, Thomas Pritzker was also named in a deposition filed by Epstein’s victim, Virginia Giuffre. She alleged that Pritzker was among the men she was trafficked to have sex with, but the billionaire’s spokesperson “vehemently” denied the allegations. Giuffre reportedly took her own life in 2025.

Thomas Pritzker has denied having any involvement in crimes committed by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. However, he retired as Hyatt Hotels Corporation executive chairman in the wake of newly surfaced email exchanges with the convicted sex offender.

****

Business Executives for National Security (BENS) is a powerful Washington-based non-profit network founded in 1982. It embeds roughly 450 top-tier corporate CEOs, private equity titans, and billionaires into the national security apparatus.

BENS markets itself as a pro-bono consulting firm, allowing industry leaders to apply corporate efficiency, technological insights, and supply-chain logistics to the military. Critics frequently point out that BENS functions as an exclusive bridge providing private-sector elites with extraordinary access to active war zones, high-ranking intelligence officials, and top military brass.

text:
Pam Geller

In the wake of Tuesday’s Republican rout, I wrote “Republicans Get Routed After Betraying Their Mandate.” My argument stands: Republican leaders failed the voters who gave them power. They asked for the House, the Senate and the White House. They got all three. Then they squandered the opportunity to turn a historic mandate into lasting law.

Now comes the predictable stampede to blame Trump. How convenient. The people who spent two years explaining why something couldn’t be done suddenly have absolute certainty about who caused their defeat.

There is much to learn from Tuesday’s shellacking: Republican leaders squandered their mandate and unapologetic conservatives who won offer a lesson the party cannot afford to ignore.

It’s what we must build on.

Start with the Republican leadership’s failure to pass the SAVE America Act. They squandered their opportunity to strengthen election safeguards and show the base that its most fundamental demands mattered. Instead, they delivered failed, again and gave their own voters another reason to lose faith. Passing it would have answered a central concern about election integrity; it would certainly have prevented fraud and changed the outcome.

Just as telling and just as important—is who actually won.

The unapologetic conservatives. The fighters. The unequivocals: Republicans with the courage of their convictions, willing to state them plainly and defend them publicly. Their victories deserve scrutiny before the same failed leadership prescribes another retreat. The party owes its voters principles it will defend and promises it will turn into law.

Look no further than Brandon Gill who won reelection in Texas. Gill is an unapologetic America First conservative who has made immigration enforcement, national sovereignty and government accountability central to his congressional work. Serving on the Judiciary, Budget and Oversight committees, including the DOGE subcommittee, he has focused on border security and cutting government waste. He introduced legislation seeking to restrict birthright citizenship for children of unlawful entrants and birth tourists, and another bill to eliminate exemptions from English-language and civics requirements for naturalization. These legislative proposals leave no ambiguity about his priorities. Gill gives voters a clearly stated conservative agenda and puts his name on legislation to advance it. On Tuesday, voters returned him to Congress.

Keith Self won in the 3rd. Michael Cloud won in the 27th. All three have belonged to the House Freedom Caucus. Steve Toth, who campaigned on his uncompromising conservative record, won the 2nd District. These candidates hardly offered voters a watered-down version of the Republican platform. Yet they prevailed—even as Republicans lost the statewide races for governor and Senate.

Look beyond Texas. Randy Fine, n outspoken, unapologetic conservative,  won reelection in Florida’s 6th Congressional District while Republicans elsewhere were being swept out. He hardly fits the establishment’s preferred portrait of a Republican who survives by keeping quiet and sanding down his convictions. His victory deserves a place in the Republican reckoning: before demanding that conservatives retreat, explain why a fighter like Fine prevailed.

Randy Fine is a fighter, and unapologetically pro-Israel conservative whose record includes concrete legislative victories. In the Florida Legislature, he sponsored measures enacted into law defining antisemitism and establishing security funding for Jewish day schools and preschools. He also sponsored the House resolution calling for Florida government agencies to disassociate from CAIR, which passed 98–15. In Congress, he introduced the No Antisemitism in Education Act, seeking to extend protections modeled on Florida’s law to the federal level. Fine’s politics are confrontational and his positions explicit. Whatever voters think of him, they have little reason to wonder where he stands.

Jim Jordan won in Ohio. James Comer won in Kentucky. Clay Higgins won in Louisiana.

Republicans who stood their ground and spoke without apology won. Those victories should shape the party’s path forward.

These victories deserve serious examination. They also require an honest comparison: winning a Republican district is different from winning statewide, and conservative Ken Paxton’s Senate defeat makes sweeping explanations inadequate. Geography, turnout, opponents and individual records matter. The results alone cannot tell us why every voter stayed home or changed sides.

But the establishment cannot wave away the conservatives who won while insisting that conservatism caused the losses. Republicans should study those victories as closely as their defeats.

My contention is that the party has exhausted its voters’ patience with promises followed by excuses. A majority is supposed to accomplish something. Voters are entitled to demand legislation, accountability and results.

The Republican leadership’s first question should be brutally simple: What did we deliver with the power we were given?

If Democrats can win with jihadis, communists and lunatics, Republicans can certainly win with rational, patriotic, unapologetic Americans who love this country and have the backbone to defend it.

Democrats are counting on the political rewards of the border chaos they created. We must elect officials who will enforce our immigration laws, deport those here illegally and reclaim our education system from the ideologues who have turned classrooms into political recruiting grounds. If it’s not too late….

text:
Jessica lost her virginity to a rapist on the pavement when she was 21. Within weeks she was on camera begging men to beat her harder and choke her because the pain made her feel like she deserved it. A porn producer at a party offered her $400 the day after she was raped, and she took it. She went from a church girl who had never been touched to the most violent sets in the industry because she believed her body was already ruined.

In the video below, she tells the full story of how she went from a preacher’s daughter to lying on her marble kitchen counter, crying, with money in one hand and a bottle in the other.

The first scene she ever shot was days after the worst moment of her life. Someone at a party coached her through what to do, she got booked, and before she even understood what was happening she was already in the industry. She had just lost her virginity to her rapist and now strangers were paying to use her body.

The money came fast. Marble floors, beautiful counters, a home that looked like she had made it. From the outside it looked like success. From the inside she was destroying herself one scene at a time.

She started requesting the most violent shoots she could find. Slapping, choking, whatever they wanted to do to her. The worse it got, the more she wanted it. “The more you beat me up, the more you slap my face, the more violent you are to me, the more I think maybe I deserve this.” That was not a role she was playing. That was how she actually felt about herself.

One shoot broke her in a way she still remembers. An old man on top of her, dripping sweat into her eyes while the cameras rolled. She drove home that night, climbed onto her marble kitchen counter, and just laid there crying. She stared at the money and thought: “The only difference between rape and that moment was the money.”

But the thing that destroyed her most was not the violence or the cameras. It was when clients would tell her they loved her. That one sentence gutted her worse than anything they did to her body. “You can do anything to my body,” she said, “but do not say that you love me.”

She lost every person in her life. She was swallowing pills by the handful and drinking until she blacked out, hoping every single night that she would not wake up. She tried to kill herself more than once. And every time she survived, she drank again because she hated the fact that she was still breathing.

Then one night she picked up the phone and called her parents. “I really messed up,” she said. And for the first time in years, they answered.

She got out. She traded porn for her family. Now they talk every single day. She says she wants to be a wife, a mother, and a friend. And she wants people to know the truth about what the industry did to her.

The marble floors are still there. But the girl who used to cry on them finally left.

text:
THE KINSHIP OF DEATH

You are in my thoughts every day—nourished by my fears,

You are the hope that will save me, the one who will take my final breath!

DEATH…

You are constantly, insidiously present in my life; I do not know when you first crept in.

You began to frighten me when I was a child, pressing down upon my very breath.

What I called "nightmares"—those moments when I couldn't breathe—were simply you, passing by my side.

To be a child—

A terrifying solitude;

Everyone and everything is vast; the light is dim, yet my eyes are sharp, focused intently on what is near.

One day:

In an unfamiliar house, by a window overlooking the garden, you caught me as I slept.

You appeared at the pane with your dark face—and you did not simply leave…

Then, again and again…

You never truly departed;

You always seeped into my restless slumbers with a hideous, savage intensity.

Suddenly, my breathless nightmare—a moment of sheer, petrifying terror—finds me on the precipice,

Standing in the middle of the *Sirat* (the bridge to the afterlife), barefoot, with the abyss of hell yawning below.

I yearn to fall and be done with it—yet there, my bare feet press against blades sharper than any sword…

I wake up drenched in sweat, grateful for the breath in my lungs; your spirit breathes life into me, O Death!

It turns out your desire was neither to kill nor to make physical contact;

Your true intent was to enter a child and hide within, spinning cocoons for all the time yet to come.

My mother, frightened by the terrors I harbored,

Took me to an old, white-bearded sage—

I was still just a child; prayers, endless prayers…

And then, the sage’s gentle, soft spittle—a blessing following the prayers. My mother is anxious; this child is different.

Will the prayers take hold?

The stroking of my hair, traces of innocent saliva on my face,

My fear-filled eyes hidden within the grandfather’s white beard…

Toward home.

We left that place, my mother and I;

My mother follows me—not my footsteps,

But the prayers…

And so, we arrive home, after the prayers.

I touch the balcony wall of our house—a game of tag with the void—

And the same nightmares return: giant figures walking calmly.

To spare my mother any sorrow—at just six years old, for the sake of love—

I learned to tell lies: lies about the prayers that all those malevolent beings supposedly cherish.

….

Prayers were recited over me once more, yet I could not find peace…

Like a temperamental, mischievous serpent, you would not let me sleep—

Into Your presence!

Just as the silence and its strange delight were about to pierce my heart, the villain from my recurring nightmares would appear—

Into Your presence!

Yet, in the scenes I witness, you are an executioner, a monster,

Killing me in my sleep, night after night…

How much of "me" is even left?

As for my inner self—I cannot reach its deepest depths, I know;

My deepest core is filled with filth; I haven’t even been able to bury my own corpses,

And I—I reek even worse than the corpses themselves…

Death!

When shall I finally come

Into Your presence?

It is not the scent itself,

But the most overpowering odors that bring blindness;

I am blind,

I cannot endure the heaviest of stenches.

A faint, fleeting trace of a rose’s fragrance drifts to my nose—

A runaway, a sinner, disobedient—I, the sinner,

So weak and wretched—when shall I finally pass into Your presence? A delicate scent of roses—and a fragrance that is yours—steals softly toward me,

And I defile it with my sins…

If the light were to reach out to me, its radiance would scatter filth across the world;

Let me come to you!

I am so utterly helpless…

…

Yet, you accustomed me to your presence, slowly and with such calm…

…

Little by little, I shall lay the weight of what remains of me upon your shoulders…

Life—the moments you offered me were beautiful, but I was selfish…

…

God shall take up my burden in my stead;

I shall walk toward a new path—I am the master of my own load—

Alone, and in despair, I shall tread the same stone-strewn, tainted paths of prayer—

Paths paved with the false hope that everyone else walks upon—

But this time,

Sheltering myself within those terrible sins,

Yet—

Without Him.

Hakan Karaduman

text:
A YEAR AFTER $28.90, FERMI $FRMI IS A $1.52 STOCK:

Fermi (FRMI) at $1.52, -$0.30 / -16.59% today.

Fermi stays off the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5, and today's fall took its market value under $1 billion for the first time, on nothing Fermi did. The shares fell with the whole market, to $1.44, the lowest since they listed. The price is now under every price at which Toby Neugebauer, the co-founder, has sold or offered shares since mid-October. The expansion permit Fermi asked Texas for in March already sits in a state pause that the governor-elect's promised ban would extend. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) at $416.67, -$72.11 / -14.75% today. AMD is the outside credit behind Fermi's tenant; by Fermi's own filing its support starts once the buildings are finished and rent is paid, not while they are being built, and our read is that today's sellers of AMD are pricing the guarantees it carries. Fermi has promised more on the lease by November 12, or sooner.

The Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5 prices a business under a cautious value of what it earns and waits for a dated event to close the gap; Fermi earns nothing yet, and its one event, a 15-year lease of the first 222 megawatts at Project Matador to the privately held TensorWave, passed its October 31 closing date without taking effect. Fermi said on Tuesday that the closing conditions were not all met, without saying which; they include project financing to build the leased buildings. What would put Fermi on the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5: that lease taking effect, with the construction money signed by a named lender. With no sales, Fermi is on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es, and the Quality Len5 wants a gross profit, which needs a paying tenant first.

The fall came with the market. SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) at $739.01, -$27.80 / -3.63% today.
- Open $1.78; low $1.44 at 10:50am ET, in the same five minutes as the S&P 500 fund's low; 19.7 million shares by 12:25pm ET, against 23.4 million on an average full day.
- Market value at $1.52: under $1 billion. A year ago today the shares traded as high as $28.90.
The Texas data-center stocks lost between 11% and 16% today, and Fermi is now priced as one of them.

Neugebauer, Fermi's co-founder and largest holder, has sold in three rounds since October 13, each cheaper than the last, and on Wednesday evening his trust gave notice of 94,000 more shares at $1.82, Wednesday's close. The stock has not traded at $1.82 today; its high of $1.80 came in the opening five minutes.

Texas has already paused the permit Fermi needs to grow. On September 21 Governor Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing data-center permits until the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the grid operator, finishes its audit of data-center projects, expected in December. Fermi's first air permits, for up to 6 gigawatts of gas-fired generation outside Amarillo, were approved in February, before the pause, and dwarf what the 222-megawatt first phase needs. The second application, filed March 27 for about 5 gigawatts more, is the one waiting: the commission canceled its August 24 public meeting on it and has set no new date. Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat elected governor on Tuesday, said in an October 22 video: "When I am governor I will issue a moratorium - a ban - on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the Legislature to protect Texans." She takes office January 19, after the audit is due, so the permit would pass from one governor's pause to the next governor's ban with no date on either.

AMD's October 13 credit-support agreement for the first-phase lease is the guaranty Lee McIntire, Fermi's chief executive, had called "our remaining work" in September. The fact sheet Fermi filed the next day says AMD's obligations begin only after construction is complete and rent starts on the final delivery phase, due in early 2028, and that the support helps the project financing Fermi still lists among the things to raise. It stands behind the rent, not the building. AMD said with its quarter this week that it could owe up to $8.5 billion under guarantees of its partners' data-center leases and borrowings if they default. Our read: today's sellers of AMD are pricing what those guarantees are worth. AMD is on none of the Len5es we weigh: 37% under its October 6 high is not Momentum's climb, and it pays no dividend.

McIntire said on Tuesday that Fermi expects to say more about the lease on November 12, "or sooner if appropriate." At $1.52, sooner is the word that counts: the state's calendar has a December audit and a January inauguration on it, the co-founder's has a lower price each time, and Fermi's has one date, a week from today.

Not investment advice.

text:
This an open letter by Angie Yates currently posted on Facebook:

AN OPEN LETTER TO JAMES TALARICO AND GINA HINOJOSA
You made a lot of promises to the people of Texas. Now comes the part that matters: delivering on them.
Gina, I want to remind you of what you are inheriting.
Texas is an extraordinary state. Not because of one politician, one political party, or one election, but because of generations of hardworking Texans who built something worth protecting.
Texas has earned a reputation as an economic powerhouse.
Consider what this state has accomplished:
* Texas has received the Governor’s Cup from Site Selection magazine for attracting major business investment projects year after year.
* Texas has repeatedly been recognized for its business climate and economic development.
* Texas has no individual state income tax.
* Texas is home to major industries in energy, technology, aerospace, manufacturing, agriculture, and healthcare.
* Texas is a national leader in energy production.
* Texas has attracted major corporate headquarters, manufacturing facilities, and business expansions.
* Texas has one of the largest state economies in America.
* Texas has experienced tremendous population growth as people and businesses seek opportunity here.
* Texas has a long tradition of entrepreneurship, independence, and private investment.
And those accomplishments didn’t happen by accident.
They happened because people worked, invested, took risks, built businesses, created jobs, and believed in the opportunities this state offered.
You are not inheriting a state that needs to be torn down and rebuilt. You are inheriting a state with an extraordinary foundation.
That doesn’t mean Texas is perfect. We have serious challenges involving property taxes, education, infrastructure, water, healthcare, and affordability.
There is plenty of work to do.
So please, don’t become another politician who makes promises, wins an election, and spends the next four years making excuses.
Protect what works. Fix what doesn’t. And make Texas even better than you found it.
And James, I have a similar message for you.
Go be the person you told Texans you would be.
Will you reach across party lines and work for the people you represent, including those who didn’t vote for you?
Will you evaluate legislation based on whether it benefits Texans rather than which political party introduced it?
Will you put meaningful results ahead of political theater?
And when Washington becomes consumed with partisan investigations, impeachment debates, and political battles, will you demand evidence, accountability, and responsible use of taxpayer dollars?
Those are fair questions, and Texans deserve answers.
Regardless of how anyone feels about the president, Congress has a responsibility to evaluate policies, investigate legitimate concerns, protect constitutional principles, and use taxpayer resources wisely.
We should expect our elected officials to distinguish between legitimate oversight and political gamesmanship.
The great coach Nick Saban has often emphasized the importance of discipline, preparation, and controlling emotions.
That’s a lesson worth remembering in politics.
Emotion should never replace sound judgment. Political outrage should never become a substitute for leadership.
The job is not to win the next argument on social media.
The job is to govern.
And to both of you, I want to say something else.
Those of us who didn’t vote for you are still Texans.
We still own businesses, employ people, pay taxes, raise families, volunteer in our communities, and contribute to the economy.
We aren’t going anywhere.
We aren’t obligated to agree with you, but we are entitled to expect you to represent us.
We don’t have to march in the streets, organize protests, or spend our days attacking people on social media to make our voices matter.
We will continue doing what Texans have always done.
We will work. We will build. We will invest. We will raise our families. We will help our neighbors.
And we will pay attention.
Because winning an election is not the accomplishment. What you do after winning is what defines your leadership.
So here’s my challenge to both of you:
Keep your promises.
Work across party lines.
Respect the taxpayers.
Protect the opportunities that made Texas successful.
Address the problems that genuinely need fixing.
And remember that you represent every Texan, not just the ones who voted for you.
Texas was great before you took office. Your responsibility is to leave it better than you found it.
Save this post.
Let’s revisit it in a year. And again in four years.
Not to measure your speeches, your social media following, or how many political opponents you’ve criticized.
But to measure your actual results.
We are watching. We are paying attention. And we expect you to deliver.
Don’t let Texas down!

Well said, Angie!
