text:
WHAT IS AGENT VIEW IN CLAUDE CODE

Agent view is a full-screen terminal dashboard in Claude Code that lists every background session on your machine, grouped by activity: still running, blocked on a human, or done. You open it with claude agents. It shipped as a research preview in Claude Code v2.1.139, tagged on GitHub at 18:43 UTC on May 11, 2026, and announced the same day by @claudeai. Everything below comes from the official Claude Code docs, the CHANGELOG.md in the anthropics/claude-code repository, the https://t.co/kAsbRIwDvw announcement, and posts from @claudeai and @ClaudeDevs, read on November 5, 2026, when the newest release was v2.1.318.

Naming and what the term does not mean

Agent view is the official name. The docs give it a dedicated page, the v2.1.139 changelog line labels it a research preview, and the launch post from @claudeai uses the same two words. The settings key and the /config menu spell it agents view, so both forms appear in the product. They are the same screen.

Three nearby things carry the word agents. The first is the command itself. The claude agents subcommand predates the feature: v2.1.50, published February 20, 2026, added it to print your configured subagents. On a build without agent view, or where the feature is unavailable, it still prints a subagent count and exits. The docs fix for that symptom is claude update, then a look at whether the disableAgentView setting, or its environment variable twin CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AGENT_VIEW, is switched on.

The second is the slash command /agents inside a session, and it is unrelated to the shell subcommand. Up to v2.1.197 it opened a wizard with a Running tab and a Library tab for subagents. Current builds print a reminder that custom subagents live in .claude/agents/ and ~/.claude/agents/, and that you ask Claude to write them or edit the files yourself. The Run agents in parallel page says outright that the two are separate.

The third is the word agent. A row in agent view is a whole Claude Code session with its own process, context window, and transcript. Subagents and agent team teammates spawned inside a session do not get rows. The docs call each row a background session.

What the screen shows

Agent view takes over the terminal and draws one table under these headers, top to bottom: Pinned, Ready for review, Needs input, Working, Completed. The headers do not map one to one onto states. Ready for review holds sessions whose pull request is open and awaiting review or failing checks, while Completed is a catch-all for sessions that succeeded, failed, or were stopped. Overflow folds into a line reading N more, and short terminals collapse the header into a single summary line so the live groups keep their space.

Each row has a name, a one-line summary, and an age. Age counts from session creation and freezes at the run length once the session finishes. The name carries the color you set with /color. A pull request label at the right edge reads #1234, or !1234 for a GitLab merge request, and it is a link even over SSH or tmux since v2.1.217.

The leading icon encodes state by color and process status by shape. Working is animated, Needs input is yellow, Idle is dimmed, Completed is green, Failed is red, Stopped is grey. A star-like glyph means the process is alive or the session needs you. A small dot means the process exited, and replying or attaching restarts it from the saved conversation. A third glyph marks a /loop session sleeping between iterations, with a run count and countdown on the row.

Needs input is stricter than it sounds. It covers a question only you can answer, a permission decision, a sandbox request for network access to a host, and an MCP server asking for input. It also holds an unattended session that ran a command needing a terminal, for example /install-github-app or opening the /mcp settings list, until you attach. Since v2.1.212 (July 17, 2026), sandbox, MCP input, and managed-settings prompts count as Needs input and not Working. A session whose turn ended and which is simply idle is not blocked, and the JSON interface reports it as done.

Pull request colors: yellow for pending or failed checks, green for passing with nothing blocking, purple for merged, grey for draft or closed. With several linked pull requests the label becomes a count such as 3 PRs. Linking comes from watching commands Claude runs: gh edits, comments, closes and ready-marks, gh pr checkout, and pushes. After a push, the lookup repeats following each of the next five commands (git, gh, glab, or curl) run in that directory, so a pull request opened later still gets linked.

While the view is open, the terminal tab title reads N awaiting input plus claude agents when something needs you. Local sessions that start needing you, complete, or fail also raise a terminal notification on your configured channel, and the Notification hook fires with type agent_needs_input or agent_completed. That arrived in v2.1.198 on July 1, 2026. Scheduled sessions such as /loop notify only when they need you.

How the one-line summaries work

A small Haiku-class model writes the row summary, and that is the status update behavior people ask about. While a session is working, row text refreshes at most once per 15 seconds, taken straight from the session's latest output without calling a model. When a turn ends, a fresh model-written summary replaces it, and a lengthy turn gets the same treatment at intervals of several minutes, which keeps busy rows current.

Each summary is a single small request sent through the provider you already use, governed by the data terms that cover the session itself. If your traffic goes through a gateway or a non-Anthropic provider lacking a Haiku-class model, the session's main model does the work instead, and ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL lets you pick one. The same class of model names sessions dispatched from the input. When you group by directory, each summary opens with a colored state word because the group header no longer names the state.

Opening agent view and leaving it

Run claude agents in a shell. An untrusted directory first triggers the workspace trust dialog, a check added in v2.1.225 on August 8, 2026. Before that, the command opened without asking.

From a regular session, press the left arrow while the prompt is empty. That backgrounds the conversation and opens the view with its row selected. One press suffices since v2.1.196 (June 29, 2026), where earlier builds needed two. The footer shows a left-arrow hint for the first ten seconds, then a count such as 2 agents while background sessions wait on you, or 99+ agents beyond 99, polled roughly every ten seconds when the terminal is focused. A brief done count follows successful finishes. The count shipped in v2.1.205 and reached third-party providers in v2.1.210.

Run /background, or /bg, inside a session, optionally with an instruction. In a brand new session with no messages /bg asks for one, while the left arrow works immediately.

Make it the default with /config, then Open agents view by default, or /config defaultToAgentsView=true. Bare claude then opens the view, and claude with a prompt still starts a normal session.

To leave, press Esc, which closes the peek panel, then clears the input, then exits. If you arrived by backgrounding, the last Esc returns you to that conversation. Ctrl+C twice exits to the shell. The shortcut has safeguards: if you just erased your draft or stepped through history, the first press only asks for confirmation. Running tools, foreground subagents, an unanswered permission prompt, or a queued message that cannot move delay the switch. Past roughly ten seconds Claude Code proceeds regardless in most cases, and a foreground shell command still running at that moment is stopped, unless you pressed Ctrl+B earlier to make it a background command. The leftArrowOpensAgents setting turns the shortcut off.

Dispatching work

Enter a prompt in the input and a background session launches. Every prompt gets its own session, so a second prompt runs alongside the first. Prompts under four characters are rejected. Images can be pasted, and long pasted text collapses into a placeholder but is sent in full.

Prefixes shape the start. A subagent name as the first word, or @name anywhere, runs that subagent as the main agent. @repo targets a repository, offering git repos one directory below where you launched, registered worktrees under the repository tree, and directories that already have sessions. A slash prefix suggests skills and commands as the first prompt. An exclamation mark turns the entry into a plain shell job that never calls a model. A pull request number or URL selects the row already working on it.

Some commands run in the view itself: /exit, /quit, /logout, /login, /model, /effort, /fast, and a bare /resume, which lists the repository's past sessions, deleted ones included, and resumes your pick in the background. Built-ins that need a terminal print a not-available hint and keep your text.

New sessions start in the directory where you opened the view. Open it elsewhere, use @, or run claude --bg from the target directory. In directory grouping, a dispatch goes to the selected row's directory.

Typing /model, /effort, or /fast changes the starting values for later dispatches, in that window only. Effort levels run from low through medium and high to xhigh and max, and the word default reverts a choice. Ultracode needs claude agents --effort ultracode. The /effort and /fast forms arrived in v2.1.299 on October 14, 2026. Defaults can also be set at launch: claude agents --model sonnet --permission-mode plan. The --agent, --restricted (v2.1.248), and both bypass flags work too, and the configuration flags --mcp-config, --strict-mcp-config, --settings, --add-dir, and --plugin-dir pass through to dispatched sessions.

From a shell, claude --bg followed by a quoted prompt starts a session and prints its short id. Combining --bg with -p is rejected. --name labels the row and --agent runs a defined subagent. An unknown agent name fails the launch since v2.1.191. To continue a conversation, claude --resume with a full session id plus --bg either continues it in place or starts a copy with a printed note, since v2.1.257. claude --bg --exec runs a plain command as a job, with output held in memory and the row cleared about five minutes after exit. That path came with v2.1.154 on May 28, 2026.

Peek, reply, attach

Space on a row opens a peek panel with the full sentence the row truncates: the exact question for a blocked session, the result for a finished one, the full status for a working one. Linked pull requests follow, plus a waiting-time line for blocked sessions. Replies go in the same panel. With predefined choices, a number key fills the input. For free-form questions, Tab accepts a suggested reply. A permission, sandbox, or MCP input dialog cannot be answered from the panel, so the reply waits in the queue until you attach. An exclamation prefix sends a Bash command.

On a working session, four commands take effect right away: /model, /effort, /rename, and /usage (v2.1.290, October 5, 2026). Other text joins the queue and does not interrupt. Other slash commands wait for the turn to end. A reply of exactly /stop ends the session at once. Undeliverable replies say whether they were saved, except those starting with an exclamation mark or slash, which are never saved.

Enter or the right arrow attaches. Claude posts a short recap, and the session runs fullscreen regardless of your tui setting. Left arrow on an empty prompt, or /exit, detaches. Ctrl+Z detaches to wherever you started. Ctrl+C keeps its interrupt role, and two presses on an empty prompt also detach. Leaving a session this way never stops it, and a waiting /loop keeps its schedule.

Shortcuts and filters

Up, Down, Page Up, Page Down, Home, End move the selection. Enter attaches or submits. Space peeks. Shift+Enter and Ctrl+J add a newline, and Ctrl+Enter dispatches and opens the session in one step on terminals where the help overlay shows that option. Alt+1 to Alt+9 jump to the first nine sessions of the focused session's directory. Tab on empty input browses subagents. Ctrl+S toggles state or directory grouping and remembers it. Ctrl+T pins. Ctrl+F finds by name. Alt+Up and Alt+Down jump between groups. Ctrl+R renames. Shift+Up and Shift+Down reorder. Ctrl+G opens your editor. Ctrl+X stops, and a second press within two seconds deletes. The question mark shows the live list.

Keys in the Agents keybinding context follow keybindings.json, which needs v2.1.257 (September 1, 2026). Filters narrow the list from the input: a: for an agent, s: for a state or group (s:blocked shows all that are waiting for you), n: for name or first prompt (v2.1.287, October 1, 2026), o: for result text, plus pull request numbers and URLs. Combine them with spaces, for example s:blocked a:reviewer.

By default the list covers every background session across all projects. claude agents --cwd limits it to one path (v2.1.141, May 13, 2026). Interactive sessions in other terminals appear only after you background them.

How file edits are isolated

A session dispatched from the view or with --bg starts in your working directory and moves into a git worktree under .claude/worktrees/ before it edits files, so parallel sessions read one checkout but write separately. Isolation is skipped for a session you backgrounded yourself, a session already inside a linked worktree, edits inside a linked worktree, a directory outside git with no WorktreeCreate hook, and writes outside the working directory. Setting worktree.bgIsolation to none, available since v2.1.143, makes sessions edit the working copy directly. Outside git, parallel sessions are not isolated from each other.

When a session changes code in a worktree it entered, Claude Code tells it to preserve the work: commit, push the branch if a remote exists, and open a draft pull request when the task calls for one. The instructions rule out three actions: pushes to main or master, forced pushes, and merges. Your own git instructions in the task, CLAUDE.md, or memory take precedence.

Two presses of Ctrl+X on a row delete the worktree Claude made for that session, along with any uncommitted edits. claude rm keeps a worktree with uncommitted changes. A worktree with commits not saved elsewhere blocks the delete and the message gives the branch and the number of unpushed commits. Deleting again discards them, and claude rm offers --discard-unpushed (v2.1.260) and --force-remove-worktree (v2.1.268). Transcripts stay available through claude --resume. A sweep also removes old Claude-made worktrees past cleanupPeriodDays, which defaults to 30.

The supervisor and persistence

A supervisor process hosts the sessions, so closing the view or your shell does not stop them. Claude Code starts it on first use. Working sessions, sessions paused on a dialog, and attached sessions keep their process. A session that finished or awaits your next message, left unattached for about an hour, has its process stopped, then resumes from disk on your next attach or reply. Pinning prevents that. When Claude Code auto-updates, the supervisor relaunches on the new build and migrates idle sessions in the background.

Sleep does not stop sessions. Shutdown does: within 48 hours a session shows failed and restarts from its saved conversation when you reply, and past 48 hours it shows stopped. If the supervisor itself dies on macOS or Linux, sessions are stopped roughly a minute later unless you rerun claude agents. State lives under ~/.claude, including daemon.log, daemon/roster.json, and jobs/<id>/state.json. Each session gets CLAUDE_JOB_DIR for scratch files. Setting CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR creates a separate instance.

Scripting and shell commands

Companion commands are claude attach, logs, stop (alias kill), respawn, rm, and claude daemon status, logs, and stop. Attach and logs take a partial name since v2.1.290. claude agents --json prints sessions as a JSON array. Add --all for finished sessions and --cwd to scope. Entries carry fields such as cwd, id, state, status, waitingFor, sessionId, and name. The state field holds one of five values: working, blocked, done, failed, stopped. Read state through this command and not the files in jobs, which are not a stable interface.

How it relates to other parallel features

Subagents work inside a single session with a separate context window and hand back a summary. Agent view dispatches separate sessions that report only to you. Agent teams are experimental and stay off until the experimental-teams environment variable (CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS) is set to 1. They organize a lead, a common task list, and teammate-to-teammate messages. Dynamic workflows run scripts that coordinate many subagents. Projects at https://t.co/78PQEW8GvU run parallel cloud sessions and are in public beta for Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers. Worktrees isolate edits, and agent view applies them automatically.

For work inside one session, /tasks lists background items and /workflows lists workflow runs. Cross-session messaging lets Claude message your other sessions, including dispatched ones, and needs v2.1.224 on macOS and Linux. A status line is a script-driven bar inside one session and not a cross-session list. v2.1.246 fixed its cost and duration resetting after a trip through agent view.

Backgrounding changed /fork. Since v2.1.212 it clones the conversation into a fresh background session, and the old forked subagent moved to /subtask. With agent view off, /fork keeps the subagent behavior.

Release timeline

The docs' version history table has 83 rows across 50 versions, from v2.1.139 to v2.1.299, and the changelog mentions the feature through v2.1.314. Dates are GitHub release tag times in UTC.

v2.1.139, May 11: launch as a research preview. The @claudeai post that day described one list of all your sessions, and its reply said each session keeps running without taking a terminal tab. The @ClaudeDevs thread framed the goal as more parallel sessions with less mental overhead, suggested packaging common workflows as skills and dispatching many at once, and ended by telling readers to run claude agents.

v2.1.142, May 14: dispatch flags for permission mode, model, effort, settings, directories, plugins, and MCP. v2.1.143, May 15: worktree.bgIsolation. v2.1.145, May 19: claude agents --json and voice dictation. v2.1.157, May 29: --agent. v2.1.169, June 8: --all plus id and state fields in the JSON. v2.1.198, July 1: automatic draft pull requests. v2.1.257, September 1: keybindings context. v2.1.288, October 2: Ctrl+F and Alt+arrow group jumps.

Where it runs and who gets it

Agent view is a terminal feature that needs an interactive terminal. The docs describe it for macOS, Linux, WSL, and Windows. The desktop and VS Code docs do not mention it, and the https://t.co/kAsbRIwDvw article says it improves sessions in the CLI. The announcement names Team, Enterprise, Pro, Max, Ultra, and Claude API accounts. Opening it by left-arrow works on Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry since v2.1.154. Sessions run on your machine, not in the cloud.

Costs and limits

The docs state that ten agents in parallel drain quota about ten times faster than a single one, since each session spends your subscription independently. Row summaries add short Haiku-class calls. Scheduled loops resend full context on each iteration, and cross-session messages start new turns in idle sessions.

Administrators can turn the feature off with disableAgentView or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AGENT_VIEW, enforceable through managed settings. Either one disables it, and the other cannot re-enable it.

Practical steps: first run

1. Update first. Run claude update, then claude agents from the repository root. If the output is a plain count of subagents and the command exits, the build or environment lacks the feature, and the checks to make are the version and the disable setting.

2. Accept the trust dialog if it appears. Declining exits immediately, and no session is created.

3. Before typing a task, type /model sonnet and /effort medium in the input and press Enter after each. They apply to every session you dispatch from that window until you change them. Replace the values with whatever your plan and task justify.

4. Type a task that names a verifiable outcome, for example a failing test file and the expected result, and press Enter. Repeat for the second and third task. Each prompt is a separate session with its own row.

5. Watch the table. A row under Working means a turn is running. A row under Needs input means a person is required. A row under Ready for review means a pull request is open and either needs eyes or has failing checks.

6. Select a Needs input row and press Space. Read the exact question, answer it in the panel, and press Enter. If the panel says the session is waiting on a permission prompt, press the right arrow instead, answer the dialog, and press the left arrow on an empty prompt to return.

7. When a row shows a pull request label with a green number, review and merge it in your normal tooling. Background sessions are instructed never to merge.

Practical steps: steering and stopping

1. To redirect a working session, press Space on its row and type the new instruction. It joins the message queue and takes effect when queued input does, without cutting off the current response.

2. To stop one session immediately, send the reply /stop from the peek panel, or select the row and press Ctrl+X once. A second Ctrl+X within two seconds deletes the row, so press Esc if you only meant to stop.

3. Before deleting a row that edited code, commit and push inside its worktree or confirm a draft pull request exists. Deletion from the view removes the worktree with any uncommitted changes.

4. To pick up a session that shows failed after a reboot, attach or reply within 48 hours of its last activity. Send an explicit instruction to continue, since the interrupted turn does not resume on its own.

Practical steps: keeping cost down

1. Treat parallelism as a multiplier. The docs put ten agents at roughly ten times the quota burn rate of a single one. Start with two or three and watch your plan usage before widening.

2. Choose model and effort per task type in the input, as in the opus then sonnet example in the docs. Reserve the heaviest settings for refactors that need them, and give routine test runs and reviews a lighter pair.

3. Remove idle self-paced loops. A /loop session wakes on schedule and sends its full context each time, as the costs page notes for scheduled tasks.

4. If sessions message each other, consider setting crossSessionInbound to hold, because each delivered message starts a turn in an idle session with the full context attached.

5. Pin only the sessions you will return to within the hour. A pinned process stays alive while idle, and unpinned idle ones are reclaimed by the supervisor.

Common mistakes

Typing a follow-up into the dispatch input and expecting it to reach the earlier session. It starts a new one. Use the peek panel to reply to an existing session.

Expecting subagents or teammates to appear as rows. Only whole sessions appear, and /agents inside a session is a different tool.

Assuming a reply answers a permission dialog. It only queues. Attach with the right arrow for those.

Deleting a row to tidy the list before checking its branch. The worktree goes with it, and commits that exist nowhere else trigger a refusal that identifies the branch and counts its unpushed commits, so read that message before confirming a second time.

Setting bgIsolation to none in a shared checkout and then running parallel sessions on overlapping files. With isolation off, or outside git, nothing separates their writes.

Counting on sessions to survive a shutdown. Sleep is survivable and shutdown is not, so long jobs that must outlive the machine belong in Projects or cloud sessions.

Sources

Agent view reference page: https://t.co/S1WxaWFWjU

Parallel agents comparison page: https://t.co/s5MMclLyxZ

Worktrees page: https://t.co/isFPyaiwTS

Subagents page: https://t.co/n1MSKVbrRm

Agent teams page: https://t.co/ztGqWBUbPD

CLI reference page: https://t.co/XwaahqwCV3

Settings reference page: https://t.co/X1jb4lkAes

Costs page: https://t.co/0A9uNjk37l

Cross-session messaging page: https://t.co/YjZC1Pypvx

Repository changelog: https://t.co/GxtYOf1IzJ

Release tag v2.1.139: https://t.co/xokplpvNFp

Anthropic announcement dated May 11, 2026: https://t.co/867QJNdqRG

@claudeai launch post: https://t.co/KxPAcb2MDn

@ClaudeDevs follow-up thread: https://t.co/azmPGXrWkE

PRESS STATEMENT

GOV. LAWAL DISTRIBUTES 300 VEHICLES, 2,000 MOTORCYCLES TO ZAMFARA GROUPS AND INDIVIDUALS, SAYS EMPOWERMENT GOES BEYOND RHETORIC.

Governor Dauda Lawal said empowerment means giving people and grassroots organisations practical tools to become self-reliant, restore dignity, and deliver democracy’s dividends, not rhetoric.

The governor on Thursday distributed vehicles and motorcycles to groups and individuals at a ceremony held at the Trade Fair Complex in Gusau.

The empowerment program recognises the immense contributions of groups and individuals to the State's overall development.

The distribution of 300 vehicles and 2,000 motorcycles is part of a state government empowerment program aimed at engaging people and groups in productive activities and boosting the local economy.

In his remarks, Governor Lawal said the event marks another milestone in his rescue agenda to reward dedicated people and groups contributing to Zamfara State’s socio-economic and political development.

He said, “It gives me great pleasure to be here for the official distribution of vehicles to various carefully selected individuals and political groups across Zamfara State. This gathering is particularly important because it offers me a unique opportunity to distribute these vehicles formally.

“Let me emphasise here that empowerment goes beyond rhetoric - it requires providing our people and grassroots organisations with the practical tools needed to be self-reliant, restore dignity, and deliver the real dividends of democracy. We remain fully committed to supporting our people in rebuilding and revitalising Zamfara to make it a more prosperous State.

“I therefore call on you as beneficiaries of the gesture to remain firm and committed to championing our drive to rescue the good people of Zamfara State. Your strategic role in partnering with the current administration remains vital.

“As you are officially presented with your vehicles, which will be performed shortly, I urge you to utilise them efficiently. This gesture is designed to facilitate mobility across the State and improve the local economy. 

"The present administration remains fully committed to sustaining its drive for infrastructure development, revamping our economy and restoring peace and stability in our dear State."

SULAIMAN BALA IDRIS
Spokesperson for the Zamfara Governor
November 05, 2026

text:
George Gurdjieff’s Self Remembering: An Ultimate Guide — Richard Ruach

SELF OBSERVATION: THE FOUNDATION

Self Observation is the prerequisite to Self Remembering. It is the study of the human machine and its three cylinders: intellectual, emotional, and moving.

This is Personality: the human mask shaped by heredity and the outside world. (More detail in the comments.)

Self Remembering is NOT Self Observation. It rests on a different teaching: the distinction between Personality and Essence.

ESSENCE is the “Divine spark,” the eternal element that passes from life to life. Personality is formed in this lifetime; Essence is perennial.

Self Observation is a technique. Self Remembering is a state of consciousness and being.

THE FOUR LEVELS OF CONSCIOUSNESS

Gurdjieff describes four levels:

1. Sleep.
2. Ordinary, everyday consciousness.
3. The awakened state (sometimes called Self Remembering).
4. Objective consciousness.

The technique for entering Self Remembering is DIVIDED ATTENTION (see diagram in comments).

DIVIDED ATTENTION: THE KEY

Imagine someone looking at a tree. An ordinary person sees the tree, but may not notice the representations and associations arising within them.

Divided attention means remaining aware of your inner world while also attending to your surroundings. Consciousness becomes BIDIRECTIONAL rather than moving in one direction; eventually, it can become MULTIDIRECTIONAL.

For example, imagine suddenly becoming sad while walking down the street, without knowing why. Through Self Observation, you would recognize why the sadness arose.

THE SECRET THIRD THING

With sustained practice, you may sense a “secret third thing” (Essence) observing the process: the arising and entering of an impression.

This is neither thought nor emotion. You are turning away from the human machine (Persona).

RECOGNIZING SELF REMEMBERING

P.D. Ouspensky describes its “flavor” as similar to being a child visiting a place you have never been before—not nostalgia or the “inner child.”

The state is slippery: you can enter it and lose it without noticing. Someone speaks to you, and suddenly it is gone.

Do not force or manipulate it. Remain as natural as possible.

Richard Ruach offers another technique, ROLLING ATTENTION, to maintain the state. See the comments for my notes and his fuller explanation.

THE GENIUS MIND AND THE FILTER

A genius can filter out distractions and concentrate on one thought. A chess master, for example, filters out bad moves rather than calculating every possibility.

But an extremely strong filter can disconnect you from reality. Intellectual people therefore struggle with Self Remembering.

The aim is not to strengthen the filter, but to LOOSEN it, allowing consciousness to expand and experience the world. This may help explain why geniuses sometimes have breakthroughs while dreaming.

THE EFFECTS OF SELF REMEMBERING

The area of consciousness expands and more impressions enter. You notice things previously overlooked; perhaps you hear something new or the world seems more vivid.

When looking at another person, an image or reaction may arise within you. Ruach describes this as not coming from you, but as that person’s internal world. He calls it “Extra-Normal Phenomenological Perception” (like telepathy, but not exactly).

Do NOT get caught up in this. Thinking about “having telepathy” can pull you out of Self Remembering.

BEING-PARTKDOLG-DUTY: THE DEATH OF THE OLD SELF

Everything in the human machine has arrived from an external place. Through Self Remembering, you attempt to draw solar force into the machine and reorganize it into something else.

Gurdjieff calls this “Being-Partkdolg-Duty” in Beelzebub’s Tales to His Grandson.

This is death: the old self is replaced by Essence.

It brings to mind Christ’s words:

“Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”
— John 3:3

Obligatory you had me up to sober...©️

But seriously, I agree.  We must break the mold of fear to offend when we speak the truth and speak the truth loud and often.  

I'll start.

The USA is not a democracy.  It's not a democratic Republic.  It is and has been a constitutional representative Republic since the Constitution was enacted.

The founders knew the difference and deliberately chose the latter.

In Federalist 10 James Madison defined a pure democracy as "a society consisting of a small number of citizens, who assemble and administer the government in person.". He warned that such systems "have ever been spectacles of turbulence and contention," have "been as short in their lives as they have been violent in their deaths," and offer "nothing to check the inducements to sacrifice the weaker party or an obnoxious individual."

A Republic, by contrast, is "a government in which the scheme of representation takes place.". The people elect representatives who filter and refine public opinion rather than simply ratifying the passions of the moment.

That's why we have:
A senate (equal representation of states, originally chosen by the state legislatures)
The Electoral College 
A written constitution that limits majority power 
A Bill of Rights
Separation of powers and federalism

John Adams put it bluntly: "Democracy never lasts long.  It soon wastes, exhausts, and murders itself.  There never was a democracy yet that did not commit suicide."

Benjamin Franklin's famous reply when asked what form of government the Constitution had created was not a democracy.  It was: "A Republic, if you can keep it."

Calling the USA a democracy is not a harmless shorthand.  It erases the deliberate design that protects liberty from pure majoritiarianism.  The system was built to restrain temporary majorities, not to empower them without limit.

We are a constitutional representative Republic.  The distinction matters.

text:
A few days have passed since the midterm elections, and after what was undoubtedly a difficult night for Republicans, I want to share a few thoughts.

First, a reminder: George Washington lost more battles than he won. But he won the war. There’s an important lesson in that.

This is democracy. Elections are won and lost, and frankly, much of what happened was not entirely unexpected. There are lessons to be learned, mistakes to correct, and serious conversations to be had.

But before getting into the bigger picture, I want to reflect on something closer to home.

Republican Serbs - Serbs for Trump, and our team have a great deal to be proud of.

Roughly 70% of the candidates we supported won their races. That’s a meaningful achievement, especially considering the broader electoral environment.

But one victory stands above the rest.

Jon Maples. Florida House District 87. President Trump’s home district.

Following Jon’s disappointing performance in the special election, we identified several weaknesses in his campaign. Our very first meeting with him was an honest conversation about those shortcomings and what we believed needed to change.

To his credit, Jon is a force of nature. He listened, understood that our intentions were genuine, and welcomed our involvement.

From that moment, we were determined to win.

This wasn’t just another legislative district. It was the district that includes Mar-a-Lago, the home of President Donald J. Trump. That carried special significance for Jon, for us, and for everyone involved.

And we won.

Jon’s campaign manager personally acknowledged our contribution, and made it clear how important that involvement had been to the campaign’s success.

Consider what that means.

In an election where Republicans suffered significant setbacks, Jon Maples flipped a Democratic-held district RED, the only Florida House seat to make that transition.

I’d say that’s a pretty good indication that our team has figured out a thing or two.
Maybe we’ve got a little of that special sauce after all.

But this isn’t just about celebrating a victory. It’s about understanding WHY certain campaigns succeed while others fail.
And that brings me to a much larger issue.

I’m not going to dissect every failure of Republican Party leadership or offer a complete assessment of what President Trump and the party need to do over the next two years.
My support for President Trump remains unwavering. I love the man, I believe in what he’s fighting for, and I will continue standing with him.

But supporting someone doesn’t mean pretending everything around them is functioning perfectly.
For too long, the Republican Party has behaved like a wagon attached to the locomotive that is Donald Trump. That needs to change.

Candidates cannot build their entire political identity around whether the president endorses them.
They need to know their districts, understand their voters, build their own organizations, and take responsibility for their own campaigns.

President Trump cannot carry an entire political party on his back forever.

But there’s an even bigger structural problem, one that our team has repeatedly raised with Republican leadership.

Republicans don’t just have a party organization problem. We have an ecosystem problem.

And the distinction matters enormously.

Democrats have spent decades building an extensive political infrastructure that operates far beyond election cycles.

Through nonprofit organizations, 501(c)(3)s, 501(c)(4)s, advocacy groups, community organizations, digital networks, and countless other institutions, they’ve created a political ecosystem that remains active and engaged year-round.

Every day. Every week. Every month. Every year.
Elections are simply one part of that operation. 

Republicans, meanwhile, too often operate in cycles. We organize, campaign, vote, and then much of the infrastructure goes dormant until the next election approaches. 1/2

This is the other side of the myth, the carefully built public image. While the world saw a ruthless drug lord, certain communities saw a man who built houses, handed out money, and filled the space the government left empty.

The camera doesn’t need to explain the contradiction. It’s right there in the greetings, the gratitude, and the quiet respect.

Monster to some. Benefactor to others.
And in places like this, both versions of him were true at the same time.
